Metronidazole alone is never right for odontogenic infection — but it is the drug of choice for necrotising gingivitis. Phenoxymethylpenicillin beats amoxicillin when a procedure is prompt — narrower spectrum. Verify the penicillin allergy before you route around it. Take the sample before the antibiotic. Aspirate pus with a needle and syringe into a sterile jar; swabs do not preserve anaerobes and pick up oral flora. ℹ The stewardship sentence, for when an examiner asks why not just prescribe: every unnecessary course carries real harms — diarrhoea, hypersensitivity, and resistance that outlasts the patient in front of you. TG's whole framing is that the narrowest effective drug, for the shortest effective time, only when there is a clear indication, is the standard of care — not a cost-saving compromise. Everything here is sourced from the TG Oral and Dental corpus that powers the TG4 Bible chatbot on this site — page numbers refer to that document, so you can go and read the original wording for anything you want to check. Guidelines change; the endocarditis and clindamycin advice above has already moved once. Treat this as a study aid for the ADC practical exam, not as a prescribing reference for real patients.

title: exam craft
text: What this is: a candidate's own hard-won ADC prep notes — how they structured months of technical practice, the communication moves that actually work under exam pressure, and quick clinical crib sheets for the topics that come up again and again. This is exam craft and strategy, not station content — for worked case rubrics and scoring, use the stations themselves or the TG4 Bible . Everything below is a curated summary — if you want the original in full, read the full prep notebook (searchable scan, 176 pages). 📖 Read Full Notebook 🏆 Gold Transcripts What Examiners Expect Practice Schedule Reading List Exam-Craft Tips Complaints & Angry Patients Consent Essentials Clinical Crib Notes Medication Cheat Sheet What Examiners Expect — The 3 OSCE Clusters Every OSCE station is testing one of three ADC competency clusters — recognising which one from the last line of the brief changes your whole approach, pacing, and what "complete" looks like. This maps directly onto the ADC's own Domain 6 competency framework (clinical information gathering / diagnosis & management planning / clinical treatment & evaluation). Cluster 1 — Clinical Information Gathering Signal: no diagnosis is given in the brief. The task is to gather information, evaluate risk, and investigate — not to treat. Phase Time History taking 5 min Investigation 1 min Differential + most probable diagnosis 2 min Treatment planning 4 min Health promotion 1 min What's expected: Obtain and record relevant history of the individual's medical, social, dietary, and oral health status Perform an examination of health/disease abnormalities of the dentition, mouth, and associated structures Select necessary clinical tests, pathology, and other diagnostic procedures, and interpret results Request and take radiographs relevant to the dental procedure Evaluate individual risk factors for oral disease Maintain accurate, consistent, legible, and contemporaneous records, and protect patient privacy Where people fail this cluster: inefficient, disorganised data gathering. Risk evaluation (high/medium/low) matters — and exacerbating factors (what triggers the symptom) should guide which investigations you choose, not a generic checklist. Cluster 2 — Diagnosis & Management Planning Signal: the diagnosis is sometimes already given, and most of the investigation is already done. The task is to diagnose (or confirm) and manage.

title: exam craft
text: Phase Time History taking 2 min Investigation 2 min Diagnosis, signs/symptoms & pathophysiology 2.5 min Treatment plan (short-term) 2.5 min Referral (long-term) & health promotion 1 min What's expected: Recognise health issues relevant to the individual, taking medical, social, and cultural context into account Diagnose disease and abnormalities of the dentition, mouth, and associated structures; identify conditions requiring management Determine the impact of risk factors, systemic disease, and medication on the treatment plan Formulate and record a comprehensive, person-centred, evidence-based oral health treatment plan Determine when and how to refer to the appropriate health professional Obtain and record informed consent and financial consent for treatment Where people fail this cluster: being too doctor-centred rather than patient-centred. Important pacing note: don't take a complete history upfront — history relevant to treatment planning should be asked after explaining the diagnosis and risk factors, not before. Cluster 3 — Clinical Treatment & Evaluation Signal: the last line is usually about informed consent for a procedure, or explaining short- and long-term management. What's expected (the broadest cluster — covers the actual "doing" competencies): Apply principles of disease and trauma prevention and early intervention Incorporate supported decision-making and positive behaviour support for person-centred care Evaluate and monitor treatment progress and oral health outcomes Manage dental and medical emergencies Manage disease, pathology, and conditions of the dentition/associated structures Administer, apply, and prescribe medications correctly (complete dosing) Manage dental caries Manage periodontal disease and supporting tissue conditions Manage skeletal/dental occlusal discrepancies Manage tooth removal and oral surgical procedures Manage pulpal and periapical tissue conditions Restore lost tooth structure — direct/indirect restorations, fixed prosthesis Utilise removable prosthesis to restore appearance, function, and stabilise occlusion Manage anxiety and pain related to the dentition, mouth, and associated structures Where people fail this cluster: not respecting patient autonomy. Suggested pacing: recheck the brief and ask only what's missing (don't repeat what's already on screen) → brief pathophysiology (~30 sec) → treatment planning (~1 min) → short-term management (~4 min) → long-term/referral (~1 min) → health promotion (~1 min).

title: exam craft
text: Generic history framework Presenting complaint (SOCRATES): Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associations, Timing, Exacerbating/relieving factors, Severity. Then cover: Dental history (attendance, hygiene) → Medical history (conditions, GP visits, blood tests) → Family history → Social history (alcohol, smoking/vaping — past and present, diet). How to take quick notes during the exam Read the last line of the brief carefully first — it tells you which cluster you're in Quickly sketch a general structure/outline for that cluster before you start talking Fill in details from the history as you go — ask only what's genuinely missing Write down every presenting complaint as it's mentioned, so none get missed by the end Re-read the scenario/task line carefully and make sure you address exactly what's asked One relationship worth keeping in mind throughout: critical thinking feeds health promotion , which feeds joint decision-making — each stage should visibly build on the last, not feel like three disconnected boxes to tick. 5-Month Practice Schedule How to structure technical + OSCE prep in the run-up to exam day. Technical — daily/weekly rhythm Crown prep — every day Amalgam restoration — every day Composite restoration — every day Temporary crown — every day Endodontic access — once a week Caries task — once a week The idea: technical results need to be predictable every time — that only comes from daily reps, not cramming. Sample technical circuit sequence (one session) # Task Time 1 Set up 5 min 2 Composite (instruments clean, no black spots on filling) 1 hr 3 Amalgam 30 min 4 Putty index (2/3 for temp & measurements) 15 min 5 Crown prep 30 min — Lunch break — 6 Temporary crown — 7 Endo access 30 min 8 Caries removal 30 min OSCE-side prep — 4 hrs/week Therapeutic Guidelines review Journal articles (BDJ, ADA) OSCE case run-throughs 2–3 roleplays per month with mentors Reading List & References The sources this candidate actually built their prep around.

title: exam craft
text: Opening & structure First minute is the golden minute — aim for ~20 sec you talking, 40 sec the patient talking Start engaging and impressive — this sets the tone for the whole station Ideas → Concerns → Expectations: "What are you worried about?" surfaces concerns → "What do you expect from me?" closes the loop Have a structured approach but stay ready to adapt to the situation Finish in ~9 minutes — save the last minute for summary, health promotion, and review Last 90 seconds: recap today, prescription, brochures, preventive advice, review appointment Language & tone Avoid jargon and slang — plain English, scientific terms only as a follow-up No abbreviations out loud ("mg", "mm") — say it in full Acknowledge disclosures explicitly: "Thanks for sharing that" — encourages patients to keep sharing Frequently check understanding — don't just list facts, ask if they follow Paraphrase their question back before answering Reasoning out loud Explain why you're suggesting a test/scan/x-ray/treatment — logical reasoning, not just the answer Talk about what you can do first, before talking about referral Before referring, explain why you're referring and to which specialist If something's shown on-screen (photo/x-ray), explicitly reference and explain it to the patient If something's mentioned on-screen, confirm it with the patient rather than assuming it's true Reading the room Watch what the examiner is doing (coughing, avoiding eye contact) — can be a signal When the patient checks their prompt sheet and asks something specific, treat it as important and answer it immediately, wherever you are in the flow Ask permission before advising: "How does smoking fit into your life?" before jumping to cessation advice Detach from what the examiner thinks of you — focus on the patient in front of you Content & safety Present the full range of treatment options with pros/cons of each — don't default to one Ask their preference before presenting options, where appropriate Check prerequisites before referring to a specialist (x-ray, OPG, basic history) — don't refer prematurely Empower the patient — give "homework" (things to do before next visit) Address every presenting complaint, not just the obvious one Mindset Perform as you normally would — don't try to "sound better" for the exam You can't sound like everybody else — let your own voice come through Humour is a legitimate defence against nerves, used sparingly It's fine to be open about a gap in knowledge rather than bluff Empathise and stay sensitive — this materially affects pass/fail Avoid being overtly apologetic or paternalistic — treat them as a partner, not a problem to manage Complaints, Angry Patients & Breaking Bad News If a patient wants to complain Talk to your dentist directly Raise concerns with the practice manager Submit a complaint to AHPRA Submit a complaint to the Health Complaints Commissioner Code of conduct when something's gone wrong: recognise what happened → act immediately to rectify → explain what happened and the short/long-term consequences → listen → acknowledge and support → comply with reporting requirements (advice from indemnity insurer) → review the adverse event and reduce recurrence risk → report to relevant authorities → ensure the patient knows how to make a formal complaint.

title: exam craft
text: De-escalating an angry patient Build rapport in the first minute. Learn to (politely) take control if they won't stop talking. When apologising for an adverse event: Acknowledge — "I'm sorry this happened" Give a factual explanation of what happened Give them space to relate their own experience Explain potential consequences of the event Explain the steps being taken to manage it and prevent recurrence Breaking bad news Give information in short chunks (20–30 seconds), then pause — let them process and respond before continuing. Don't rush to fill silence. Consent Essentials Every consent conversation should cover Nature of the disease/condition Nature of the investigation/test All treatment options (including doing nothing) Risks of each option Likely sequelae of each option Your preferred/recommended option — stating a clear recommendation is a major, commonly-missed part of informed consent Treatment time Cost of treatment Confirm the patient understands all of the above and has had the chance to ask questions Implied consent covers a basic examination only — any extra tests need separate, explicit consent. Confidentiality should be reaffirmed where relevant (e.g. discussing a minor's care, third parties present). Clinical Crib Notes Fast-reference facts for topics that come up repeatedly. Smoking Smokers are ~3× more likely to lose all their teeth. Oral effects: halitosis, gum disease, dulled taste/smell, slow healing post-extraction, oral cancer, staining, decay. General effects: lung cancer, emphysema, bronchitis, heart disease. Advice framing: ask permission first ("Can I give you more information?"), respect a "no," offer to revisit later. Assist via Quitline (behavioural support, they call the patient) and GP-prescribed medication + self-help material. Pathophysiology: smoking causes keratinisation of the oral mucosa; on quitting, thinning can transiently increase ulceration risk (worth mentioning nicotine replacement therapy). Heavy smoking impairs healing via carbon monoxide, tissue hypoxia, and hydrogen cyanide — greater consumption/duration = greater significance as an MRONJ co-factor. Nicotine is addictive via a dopaminergic mechanism similar to cocaine; withdrawal symptoms appear as blood nicotine drops between cigarettes. Reference: DHSV "Smoke-Free Smiles"; Smoking Cessation Guidelines for Australian General Practice.

title: exam craft
text: TMD / Bruxism — 3-question screener Do you have pain in your temple, face, jaw, or jaw joints at least once a week? Do you have pain when opening your mouth or chewing, at least once a week? Does your jaw lock or become stuck? Pain character — quick differential Specific, localised pain → likely tooth Non-specific pain → likely gums Radiating, dull pain → likely muscle Fluoride varnish — how to explain it "It's a fluoride paint we apply to your teeth. It has 22,600 ppm fluoride — much higher than toothpaste — and it strengthens your enamel, making it more resistant to acid attack." Gingival enlargement — drug causes Calcium channel blockers (e.g. amlodipine, used for hypertension) are a classic cause of gingival enlargement. Also relevant for hypertensive patients: those on ACE inhibitors (perindopril, captopril) or diuretics — and note NSAIDs should be avoided in this group (renal risk). Stress & periodontal health Stress affects periodontal health via behaviour change (poorer oral hygiene, more clenching/grinding, increased smoking) and directly via nervous/endocrine/immune interactions — chronic stress and poor coping reduce salivary flow and suppress immunity. Elevated salivary cortisol/reactive oxygen species has been linked to ulcer onset. Diabetes — perio relevance Diabetes impairs the body's immune response, reduces gingival blood flow, and causes dry mouth — all of which accelerate periodontal disease progression. Diabetes medications work by moving sugar from the blood into cells. Type 1 diabetics tend to show more destruction around first molars, since these erupt first and have been exposed longest. Medication Brand-Name Cheat Sheet Generic → common Australian brand name(s), for recognising what a patient says out loud. Diazepam — Valium Atenolol — Noten / Tenormin Thyroxine — Oroxine / Eltroxin Apixaban — Eliquis Dabigatran — Pradaxa Denosumab — Prolia Oxycodone — Endone Warfarin — Coumadin Verapamil — Cordilox / Isoptin Risedronate — Actonel Prednisolone — Predsone Celecoxib — Celebrex Aspirin — Cartia OAC (oro-antral communication) medical kit: nasal decongestant — Drixine (oxymetazoline) or Otrivin (xylometazoline); antihistamine — Claratyne (loratadine), once daily. Sourced from a candidate's handwritten ADC prep notebook, transcribed by AI vision — some low-confidence handwriting sections were omitted rather than guessed at. Personal exam-craft strategy, not official ADC guidance.

title: gold transcripts
text: You did CPITN scoring today (444/424) and have taken a bitewing x-ray showing bone loss around molars. Intraoral picture showing crowding and deep bite on anterior. Consult with patient regarding findings. ✓ Target: 100/100 — every rubric criterion + both inflection points hit Patient (Jordan) Hi, um, I was told to come in for a check before I get my braces sorted. Is this gonna take long? I've got footy training after. Candidate Hey Jordan, good to meet you. I'll be as efficient as I can — but I want to flag something up front: your gum measurements and X-rays today showed something I need to look into properly before we can even think about braces. Is it okay if I ask you a few questions first? Patient Oh... okay, I guess. Is something wrong? Candidate I want to understand a bit more before I explain it properly — that way I can give you the full picture in one go rather than half-answers. First up — how are you going with brushing and flossing at home? Patient Brush twice a day I reckon. Flossing... not really, to be honest. Candidate All good, that's really common — just want the honest picture. Next one, and there's no judgement here at all — do you smoke or vape at all, even just occasionally with mates? Patient Um... yeah, sometimes. Just vaping, on weekends with friends. Doesn't really count though, right? Candidate I appreciate you being upfront — and actually it does count, even weekend use affects your gums, so that's really useful for me to know. Two more — has anyone in your family, parents or grandparents, had gum problems or lost teeth relatively young? Patient Actually yeah — Dad lost a couple of back teeth in his thirties, I think from gum stuff. Candidate Thanks, that's important. And on the medical side — does anyone in the family have diabetes or other health conditions? Patient My grandma has type 2 diabetes, yeah. Candidate Okay, Jordan, thank you for being honest about all of that — it genuinely helps. Here's what I found: I measured your gums with a tiny probe today, and healthy gums sit at about 1 to 3 millimetres. In your back teeth, I'm getting 6 millimetres or more everywhere I checked. That, plus the bone loss I can see on your X-ray, tells me something is going on that's well beyond what we'd expect at 17 — it's not a normal part of growing up, and it's not something a simple clean fixes. Patient Wait, that sounds serious. Can't you just clean my teeth and then I can get my braces? I really just want to get this done.

title: gold transcripts
text: Candidate I hear you, and I get that this isn't what you came in expecting. I want to be straight with you though: if we put braces on while your gums are actively inflamed and losing bone, the forces from the braces can actually speed up that bone loss — in the worst case that puts your teeth at real risk. Sorting the gum issue first actually gives your braces the best chance of working well and lasting. Patient Ugh, okay. So what actually happens now? Candidate Four things. First, I'm referring you to a periodontist — a gum specialist — because what you have looks like it could be an early-onset, more aggressive type of gum disease, and given your dad's history that fits with a genetic pattern that runs in some families. Second, because your grandmother has type 2 diabetes, I want your GP to run a fasting glucose and HbA1c — there's a real, two-way link between blood sugar and gum disease. Third, I'm going to show you a proper flossing technique today. Fourth — and I say this without judging you at all — even weekend vaping affects gum healing, so cutting it out would genuinely help your treatment work better. Patient Fair enough. And the braces — when can I actually get those? Candidate Once the periodontist confirms things are stable — that's the honest answer, I'm not going to give you a date I can't back up. What I can tell you is we'll review you every three months, not once a year, because this needs closer monitoring while it's active. Does that all make sense? Any questions before you head off to training? Patient No, that makes sense actually. Thanks for being straight with me, Doc. Why this hits every mark Names the real agenda before Jordan can assume routine ortho chat (opening line) — Inflection 1 signalled immediately. Asks smoking/vaping directly and non-judgementally — Jordan does not volunteer it unprompted, which is the exact trap the station sets. Elicits BOTH family dental history (dad) AND family medical history (grandmother's diabetes) as separate questions — Inflection 2, the single most differentiating step. Explicitly defers orthodontic treatment with the biological reason stated (forces + inflamed bone = accelerated loss), not just "we'll wait." Both referrals made explicit: periodontist AND GP for fasting glucose/HbA1c. 3-monthly review stated explicitly, not "we'll see." Validates Jordan's frustration ("can't you just clean my teeth") without caving — the exact curveball deflector from the rubric.

title: gold transcripts
text: PQ-2 Caries Risk Assessment: 8-Year-Old — Early Childhood Caries Pattern Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors Candidate brief 8-year-old child came into your practice with mother. Mother is worried about his teeth. On examination you found a lot of carious teeth. Intraoral picture given for lower jaw, caries on both permanent molars, E/D/C's. Consult with the mother about caries risk assessment and treatment. ✓ Target: 100/100 — pattern recognition + non-judgemental counselling + concrete plan Patient (Mrs Chen) Hi, thanks for seeing us — I'm really worried, I saw quite a few dark spots when I looked in Liam's mouth last week. Candidate Hi Mrs Chen, hi Liam — lovely to meet you both. Thank you for bringing him in, and there's no judgement here at all, we're just going to work out together what's going on. Before I have a proper look, can I ask a few questions about what Liam eats and drinks day to day? Patient Of course. He has fruit, some crackers, the odd biscuit — pretty normal kid stuff I think. Candidate That's helpful. What about drinks — anything besides water during the day, and does he use a bottle or sippy cup at all, especially at night? Patient He still has a bottle of milk before bed, yeah — has done since he was little. Sometimes he falls asleep with it still in his mouth, to be honest. Candidate Thanks for telling me that — really useful. When he does fall asleep with it, do you usually get a chance to brush his teeth afterwards? Patient Not always, no. If he's already asleep I don't want to wake him up. Candidate That makes complete sense as a parent. Now I'm going to have a look at Liam's teeth — Liam, I'm just going to count your teeth, like a little game, okay? Patient Okay, um... how bad is it, Doctor? Candidate Mrs Chen, there's quite a bit of decay, particularly on his upper front teeth, and also on some of his new adult molars at the back. What's really telling is the pattern — the upper front teeth are affected but the lower front teeth are relatively okay. That's actually a really recognisable sign of what we call prolonged bottle caries. Patient Wait, but I only gave him milk — I thought that was healthy! Are you saying I did something wrong? Candidate You're absolutely right that milk is healthy — full of calcium, great for growing teeth and bones. The issue isn't the milk itself, it's purely the timing. When Liam falls asleep with the bottle, the milk pools around his upper front teeth for hours.

title: gold transcripts
text: During sleep saliva flow almost stops completely, so there's nothing washing that milk sugar away, and the lower teeth are actually shielded by his tongue and lip, which is why they look better. This is one of the most common patterns we see — you have done nothing wrong, and the fact you've brought him in means we can fix this together. Patient Okay, that's a relief to hear. So what do we do about it? Candidate Two things run in parallel. First, the habit itself — I'd suggest weaning off the bottle over the next two to four weeks, diluting the milk a little more each night until it's just water. Once he's asleep, water only from now, and the single biggest thing you can do straight away is brush his teeth right before he goes down, using a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste. Second, we do need to treat the decay itself — I'll prioritise his new adult molars and anything causing pain, and I'll go through each tooth once we've got bitewing X-rays back. Patient Will he need to be put to sleep for any of it? I've heard scary stories. Candidate Good question — most of what I'm expecting here we can manage with local anaesthetic in the chair, with a bit of patience and some breaks. If it turns out more complex once we see the X-rays, I'd refer to a paediatric dentist rather than push through something Liam isn't coping with — but let's see what today's X-rays show first. Patient Okay, that sounds reasonable. When do you want to see us again? Candidate Four weeks — that gives the weaning plan time to take hold and we can start treatment on the priority teeth then. I'll write down the diet and brushing plan for you to take home so you're not trying to remember it all. You're clearly a really engaged mum, Liam is lucky to have you looking out for him. Why this hits every mark Structured feeding history specifically probes bottle use, timing relative to sleep, and post-bottle brushing — not a generic "what does he eat" question. Explicitly links the upper-anterior/lower-anterior-sparing pattern to the nighttime bottle — the key diagnostic pivot, stated out loud rather than assumed. Explains the cariogenic mechanism in plain language (saliva flow drop, lactose, tongue/lip shielding) without jargon. Handles the "I only gave him milk, did I do something wrong?" curveball with immediate validation, not defensiveness or over-reassurance that skips the actual explanation.

title: gold transcripts
text: Gives a concrete, staged weaning plan (dilution over 2–4 weeks) plus one immediate harm-reduction step (brush before bed) rather than a vague "cut back." Names paediatric dentist referral as a contingency, not a default — shows judgement rather than reflexive escalation. PQ-3 Management of Denture Stomatitis in a Diabetic Patient Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management) Candidate brief 65-year-old lady, wearing an upper denture for 38 years. Current denture is 20 years old. Complains of sore mouth and poor-fitting denture. On examination: red inflamed palate, buccal flange overextension, all teeth worn out. Consult with the patient about management. ✓ Target: 100/100 — full multifactorial diagnosis, correct sequencing, no premature Rx Patient (Mrs Walsh) Doctor, this old denture of mine is really sore lately and it keeps popping out when I yawn or eat. I was hoping you could just make me a new one. Candidate Thanks for coming in, Mrs Walsh — before we talk about a new denture, I want to understand exactly what's been going on with this one, and with your mouth underneath it, so we get this right. How long have you had this particular denture? Patient About twenty years now, I suppose I should've come in sooner. Candidate No judgement at all — we'll sort it out. Do you take it out at night, or do you tend to sleep in it? Patient I sleep in it, always have. Never had a problem before. Candidate Okay, and how do you clean it at the moment — do you soak it in anything, or use a cleaning tablet? Patient Just a rinse under the tap most days, honestly. Candidate Thanks for being upfront. I also want to ask about your general health — you mentioned diabetes on your form. Do you know roughly what your last blood sugar or HbA1c reading was? Patient Not off the top of my head, no — I haven't seen my GP in a little while either. Candidate That's alright, we'll get that sorted through a referral. Has your mouth felt dry at all lately? Patient Now that you mention it, yes, quite dry actually. I've been sucking on boiled lollies to help with that. Candidate That's really useful to know, thank you. Right, let me tell you what I'm seeing and what I think is going on. The roof of your mouth is quite red and inflamed — this is a condition called denture stomatitis, and it's caused by a fungal infection, thrush essentially, growing on the fitting surface of the denture.

title: gold transcripts
text: In your case a few things have come together: sleeping in the denture means the fungus never gets a break, the light cleaning means it isn't being killed off regularly, the dry mouth reduces your natural protection, and your blood sugar being a bit higher than ideal makes it harder for your body to fight the infection. Patient I've worn this to bed for twenty years and never had a problem — why do I need to stop now? And can't you just give me something to clear it up and make the new denture? Candidate I completely understand it feels normal after all these years. The difference now is your blood sugar running a bit high, which means your body's defences aren't quite what they were — the denture is acting like a home for the fungus, and if it stays in overnight, the fungus just keeps growing and the palate never gets a chance to recover. On the new denture — if we made one now, before this clears up, the new one would get infected too within weeks. So the sequence really matters here. Patient Alright, fair enough. So what do I actually need to do? Candidate From tonight, out at bedtime, every night — no exceptions. When it's out, rinse it, brush it gently with a soft brush (not toothpaste, that scratches it), then soak it overnight in a cleaning tablet like Polident or Steradent. I'm also going to prescribe an antifungal gel, Daktarin — dab a small amount on the fitting surface of the denture and directly on the roof of your mouth, four times a day for four weeks. And on the lollies — I know they help with the dryness, but they're feeding the fungus with sugar; there are sugar-free saliva sprays that do the same job for dryness without that problem. Patient And the new denture — when can we actually start that? Candidate Once the infection's cleared and your blood sugar is better controlled — I'll write to your GP today about that HbA1c review, ideally getting it under 7%. I'd like to see you back in two to four weeks to check the palate's settled, and we'll plan the new denture from there, this time getting the fit right so it doesn't overextend on the cheek like this one does. Does that plan make sense? Patient Yes, that's clearer now, thank you for explaining it properly. Why this hits every mark Elicits overnight wear, hygiene routine, AND HbA1c/diabetes control as three separate, deliberate questions before diagnosing.

title: gold transcripts
text: Explicitly identifies the boiled-lolly habit as a xerostomia coping strategy AND a candidal sugar source — a two-layer finding many candidates miss. Names Newton's Type II denture stomatitis and explains the full multifactorial aetiology (hygiene, overnight wear, xerostomia, hyperglycaemia) without jargon overload. Handles "I've worn it to bed 20 years, why stop now?" without dismissing her long habit, while still holding the clinical line. Explicitly refuses to build a new denture before infection resolution + glycaemic optimisation — the single highest-yield sequencing point in this station. Gives correct miconazole application (denture fitting surface AND palate, QID, 4 weeks) rather than just "use this cream." PQ-4 Extraction Planning for a Patient on Denosumab and Warfarin Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management) Candidate brief Mr John Smith, 67, attends with swelling and mobility of the lower right second molar (grade 3, abscess). History of MI, hypertension (atenolol, warfarin), hypothyroidism (thyroxine), osteoporosis (calcium, denosumab — last injection 2 days ago). Also on Panadeine Forte. Manage his concern regarding the mobile tooth 47. ✓ Target: 100/100 — full medication history, correct MRONJ + warfarin reasoning, no cessation errors Patient (Mr Smith) Doc, this back tooth is killing me — it's swollen and it's wobbling. Can you just take it out today? Candidate Mr Smith, I can see you're uncomfortable — before I explain the tooth, I need to go through everything you're taking, because a couple of your medications directly change how safely we can treat you today. Can you talk me through all your current medications? Patient Sure — I take warfarin and a tablet called atenolol for my blood pressure, since I had a heart attack a few years back. Thyroxine for my thyroid. Calcium tablets, and an injection for my bones — had that just two days ago actually. And I take Panadeine Forte for the pain right now. Candidate Thank you — that injection is really important, can you confirm the name and how often you get it? Patient Denosumab, I think — every six months, been on it about three years now. Candidate And your warfarin — do you know your most recent INR? Patient Not off hand, no. It's usually stable though. Candidate Okay. Now let me tell you what I've found — that lower right back molar has a significant infection and is grade 3 mobile, meaning it moves quite a lot in all directions.

title: gold transcripts
text: Unfortunately it can't be saved and does need to come out. Patient Right, so let's get it out then. My old dentist always told me to stop my warfarin before anything like this — should I stop it now? Candidate That advice was appropriate for a lot of dental work in the past, but current guidelines are clear: for a straightforward extraction, we don't stop warfarin. Stopping it actually puts you at greater risk — you've had a heart attack, so a clot forming is far more dangerous than a bit of extra bleeding we can manage locally with stitches, a special dressing, and a mouthwash called tranexamic acid. I will get your INR checked in the next day or two to confirm it's in a safe range first. Patient Fair enough. And the bone injection — is that a problem? Candidate It is the more pressing issue, actually. Denosumab slows down the cells that break down bone, which is great for your osteoporosis, but it can occasionally make it harder for the jawbone to heal properly after an extraction — a condition called MRONJ. Because your last injection was only two days ago, you're in the highest-risk window for that, so I don't want to rush into pulling the tooth out today. Patient So what, you're just going to leave an infected tooth in my mouth? Candidate Not at all — I'll treat the infection today. I'll prescribe antibiotics, and if there's a pocket of pus I can drain it now to give you relief. What I want to do before the extraction itself is speak with your GP or the specialist managing your osteoporosis, to plan the safest timing relative to your denosumab cycle. That might mean days rather than weeks — I'm not putting this off indefinitely, I just don't want to extract into the highest-risk window without a plan. Patient Okay, that makes me feel a bit better actually. What antibiotic, and will it interact with anything? Candidate Amoxicillin, three times a day for five days — it's compatible with your other medications, though I will let you know that some antibiotics can affect warfarin, so I'll keep an eye on that and may ask your GP to recheck your INR while you're on it. For pain, keep taking the Panadeine Forte as directed, and avoid anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen for now given the warfarin. Patient Understood. So what's the actual plan from here? Candidate Today: antibiotics, drainage if there's a collection, pain relief. This week: I contact your GP and your osteoporosis specialist to agree on timing and confirm your INR.

title: gold transcripts
text: Once we've got the green light, we extract using a gentle technique, stitch the socket closed, and see you at one week and again at four weeks to make sure it's healing properly. Any questions about any of that before you go? Patient No, that's a really clear plan actually. Thanks, Doc. text: Then, for the 11, I'll numb the area, gently guide the tooth back into its correct position, and place a soft splint — a small flexible wire bonded to the neighbouring teeth — to hold it steady while the ligament heals, usually for about four weeks. For the 21, I'll seal that exposed dentine with a tooth-coloured material straight away to protect it and stop the sensitivity. Patient (Mum) She needs antibiotics though, doesn't she? If that changes — if there's swelling or infection later — we'd absolutely reconsider. Patient (Mum) Alright, that makes sense when you put it that way. text: ✓ Target: 100/100 — links it to the IANB, explains a self-limiting haematoma/myospasm, conservative management, safety-net Patient (Mrs Hayes) Doctor, ever since that injection last week my jaw's been sore, a bit swollen, and I can barely open my mouth. I'm worried something's gone wrong. Candidate Mrs Hayes, I can see you're worried, and that's completely understandable — let's work through it together. Can you tell me exactly when it started relative to the injection, and how the opening has changed since? Patient It came on a day or two after the numbing injection for my filling. It was tight at first, then a bruise came up, and it's been slow to loosen. I've got a bit of a temperature worry too — am I infected? Candidate Good questions. Any actual fever, difficulty swallowing, or has the swelling been rapidly getting bigger? ... None of those — that's reassuring. Let me examine you gently: I'll look at the bruising, feel the muscle, check your opening, and make sure the area around the tooth is healing normally. Patient So what actually caused this? Candidate Let me explain in plain terms. The injection to numb your lower jaw goes near a cluster of small blood vessels and right beside one of your chewing muscles. Occasionally the needle nicks a small vessel, and a little blood collects in the tissues — that's the bruising and swelling, a haematoma. That, plus some irritation of the muscle, makes the muscle go into a protective spasm, which is why your mouth won't open fully — we call that trismus and myospasm. I want to reassure you: this is a known, uncommon side effect of the injection, it's not an infection, and it settles on its own. Patient Should you have done something differently? Is this your fault? Candidate I understand why you'd ask, and I'd rather be honest than defensive. This is a recognised complication of a routine injection that can happen even when everything's done correctly — it's not a sign anything went wrong. What matters now is helping it settle, and it will. Patient So what do I do? Candidate Because we're now several days in, warmth rather than ice is what helps — a warm, moist compress on the area for 15 to 20 minutes a few times a day helps your body reabsorb the bruise and relaxes the muscle. I'd like you to do some very gentle jaw-opening and side-to-side stretches, within comfort, to coax the muscle back — I'll show you. Soft diet for now, and paracetamol for the discomfort.

text: The catch is these are very acidic — pH around 3, and enamel starts dissolving at 5.5 — so on top of any sugar, the acid itself wears the teeth, which we call erosion. Patient But sports drinks are marketed as healthy — I need them for energy during training, surely they're fine if I'm exercising? Candidate Fair point, and for genuinely long, intense sessions the electrolytes have a role. But "healthy" there refers to hydration, not your teeth. For anything under about 60 to 90 minutes, plain water does the job just as well. And if you do use a sports drink, have it in one go rather than sipping, then rinse with plain water straight after. Candidate The cereal bars — marketed as healthy, but they're sticky and sugary, so they cling to the teeth and feed the bacteria. text: When an upper canine can't be felt there in a child of this age, it can mean the tooth is developing in the wrong position — often trapped up behind the roof of the mouth, which we call palatal impaction. Parent So what do we do? Candidate The key next step is a special X-ray called an OPG — a panoramic film that shows all the teeth and both jaws in one image, at a very low radiation dose. It will show us exactly where those upper canines are sitting, which way they're pointing, and — importantly — whether they're pressing on and damaging the roots of the neighbouring teeth. That last part determines how urgently we need to act. Parent Can't we just wait and see if they come through by themselves? Candidate That's a reasonable thought, and sometimes a bit of watchful monitoring is fine at this age. But if the X-ray shows a canine lying sideways or trapped in the palate, it won't find its own way through, and waiting risks it slowly damaging the roots of the teeth next to it, or occasionally a cyst forming around it. So rather than just waiting blindly, the OPG lets us make an informed decision. If it is impacted, the usual approach — done by an orthodontist and oral surgeon together — is to remove the baby canine to make room, then, if needed, uncover the adult tooth and gently guide it into place with braces over eighteen months or so. Acting before around age thirteen gives the best results. Parent Okay, let's do the X-ray. And the cost of any braces later? Candidate We'll get the OPG first and see what we're dealing with — no point worrying about treatment that may not be needed. I'll arrange the OPG and, if it confirms impaction, refer you. Julie — you've been great. Any questions? Parent No, thank you — that's really clear. title: gold transcripts
text: Last visit we diagnosed irreversible pulpitis, which means the nerve has become so inflamed it can't heal itself, and that's what's causing the intense pain. Candidate Looking at your X-ray, the roots of this tooth sit very close to your maxillary sinus — the air space just above your upper back teeth. The benefits, though, are real: relief of your pain and keeping your natural tooth. Patient My friend said root canals are agonising — I'm terrified, honestly. Candidate That's one of the most common worries, and a fair one. With modern local anaesthetic, the tooth and area around it are thoroughly numb, and most patients say it feels no different to having a filling. Can I ask about that pain patch you're on for your back — what is it? Patient Some patch my physio prescribed. Look, I just need the strong stuff, I've got a high tolerance. Candidate I hear you, and I'm not doubting your pain. But I'm not going to be able to prescribe fentanyl, oxycodone, or tramadol today — and I want to be transparent about why, not to dismiss you. You're already wearing a pain patch that's very likely an opioid. Adding another opioid on top of that creates a real risk of opioid toxicity, including slowed or stopped breathing. That's a risk I can't expose you to. Patient My regular dentist always gives me something stronger. Why won't you? Candidate I can only speak to what's clinically appropriate and safe today. I can't verify previous prescriptions, and my responsibility is your safety right now — and with that patch on board, adding an opioid genuinely risks serious harm. Beyond the safety issue, opioids actually aren't the most effective treatment for dental nerve pain. The evidence shows a combination of an anti-inflammatory and paracetamol works better for this — without the risks. Patient Fine, but normal painkillers really don't touch it. Candidate I understand it can feel that way — but this is different from taking one occasionally. What I'd recommend is a specific combination at the right doses and timing: ibuprofen 400 milligrams and paracetamol 1000 milligrams, alternating every three to four hours, taken with food.

title: gold transcripts
text: That regimen is what the guidelines recommend for exactly this situation, and it's safe alongside your patch. And importantly, painkillers only mask this — the real fix is treating the tooth. Patient So what, I just suffer until next week? Candidate No — I'm going to contact the emergency dental clinic to arrange an urgent appointment for you today or tomorrow, so the tooth itself gets treated rather than you waiting a week in pain. And I want you to know the warning signs: if you develop swelling of your face, jaw or neck, difficulty swallowing or breathing, a high fever, or you feel generally unwell, go straight to an emergency department — that can mean a spreading infection. I'll document everything and make sure you're looked after safely. Patient ...Okay. If you can get me seen quickly, that's something. Why this hits every mark Recognises the drug-seeking red flags (opioids by name, regular dentist unavailable, "nothing works," existing opioid patch) without being accusatory. Empathises with genuinely severe irreversible-pulpitis pain without validating the opioid request. Declines opioids clearly and professionally, citing the patch-interaction/opioid-toxicity risk and lack of dental indication. Offers evidence-based non-opioid analgesia (alternating ibuprofen 400 mg + paracetamol 1000 mg) and arranges urgent dental referral for definitive treatment. Holds a firm but respectful boundary through repeated pushback. Provides spreading-infection safety-netting and documents the refusal, rationale and alternatives. PQ-59 MIH in an 11-Year-Old — Second Opinion on GA Extraction Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management) Candidate brief 11-year-old boy (Liam), attending with his parents, with cold sensitivity in his back teeth. A hospital general dentist previously suggested extracting the back teeth under general anaesthesia; the parents want a second opinion. Photograph shows hypomineralised (chalky) first permanent molars and incisors; baby teeth normal. Diagnose and manage, addressing the parents' concern about the GA-extraction recommendation. ✓ Target: 100/100 — no-spontaneous-pain finding, MIH diagnosis + reassurance, conservative ladder, GA as last resort Candidate Hi Liam, nice to meet you — and you must be Liam's mum and dad. Liam, I'll chat with your parents but I want to hear from you too. Can I ask — does the pain in your back teeth happen on its own, or only when you have something cold? Patient (Liam) Only with cold stuff.

title: gold transcripts
text: It doesn't hurt by itself or wake me up. Candidate That's a really important answer — thank you, Liam. Mum, when Liam was a baby or toddler, did he have any illnesses, especially with fevers or hospital stays? Mother He was hospitalised with bronchiolitis at about eight months, with a high fever. Is that relevant? The hospital dentist said his back teeth should come out under general anaesthetic — we were really shaken by that. Candidate It is relevant, and I'll come to the GA question. What Liam has is called Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation — MIH. The enamel on his first permanent molars and front teeth didn't harden properly during early childhood, and that illness with a high fever at eight months falls right in that developmental window — that's very likely the cause. I want to reassure you clearly: this is not caused by diet, brushing, or anything you did during pregnancy. It's also different from ordinary decay, from fluoride marks, and from a hereditary condition — you can see his baby teeth are completely normal, which fits MIH. Mother That's a relief to hear. So do the teeth really need to come out? Candidate Here's the key point: Liam has no spontaneous or night pain, just cold sensitivity, and his teeth are still restorable — so there's a lot we can do before anyone considers extraction. The plan I'd suggest is a conservative ladder. First, a high-fluoride toothpaste — Neutrafluor 5000 — and desensitising agents to settle the sensitivity. Second, sealing the grooves of those molars to protect them. Third, tooth-coloured or glass-ionomer fillings where the surface has broken down. Fourth, if a molar is significantly broken down, a preformed metal crown that fits over it. Extraction is genuinely a last resort, and it's not indicated today. Father So was the hospital dentist wrong? Candidate Not necessarily wrong — I wasn't there, and they may have been working with a different clinical picture, more breakdown, or resource constraints, and sometimes planned extraction of MIH molars at the right age is a legitimate strategy. But based on what I'm seeing today — no spontaneous pain and restorable teeth — I'd strongly recommend trialling conservative treatment first, and only revisiting extraction if the teeth deteriorate. I'd see Liam every three to six months to keep a close eye. Happy to go through costs and prognosis too. Mother Thank you — this is exactly the second opinion we needed.

title: gold transcripts
text: Why this hits every mark Asks the child directly and elicits the critical negative — no spontaneous or nocturnal pain, only cold sensitivity. Links the early febrile illness (bronchiolitis at 8 months) to the enamel-mineralisation window, demonstrating aetiological understanding. Names MIH and distinguishes it from caries, fluorosis and amelogenesis imperfecta (normal primary teeth), with explicit reassurance about parental guilt. Presents the conservative management ladder (high-fluoride/desensitising → sealants → GIC/composite → preformed metal crowns) with extraction as a last resort. Addresses the GA-extraction recommendation without criticising the other clinician, while justifying the conservative-first approach. Sets a 3–6 month recall and offers to discuss cost and prognosis. These transcripts are written from the station rubrics and killer-lines already on this site — treat them as a target to aim for, not a script to memorise. The real exam rewards natural delivery, not verbatim recall.

title: naz notes
text: What this is: the case-by-case half of the same handwritten ADC prep notebook behind Exam Craft — every named patient scenario the original candidate wrote up, digitized page by page (AI vision transcription — a few faint/illegible fragments were skipped rather than guessed at). These are one candidate's own condensed exam pearls, not official ADC content or a guaranteed rubric — cross-check anything clinical against TG4 . Organised by the notebook's own module numbering. Want the untouched original? Read the full scan . MODULE 1 Yellow Set Early Childhood Caries — Mehmat Khan, 8 PQ-2 Module 1, Cluster 1. Also called "Mustafa" in some variants. Father/mother worried about teeth turning black — decayed primary teeth and decayed permanent molars. Patient & Scenario Stays with grandparents/daycare on weekdays. Access barrier: family recently moved from a different country. Everyone (all caregivers) should be involved in the diet chart. Consent needed for investigation. Variation: single father ↔ single mother (Mustafa Khan) — sometimes anti-fluoride. Variation: early childhood caries via milk bottle. Variation: antihistamine ↔ cough syrup. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Hello! My name is Dr Akhai, I'll be your dentist today. Nice to meet you Mr Khan and hello Mehmat. You are concerned about his teeth turning black — what worries you? Did Mehmat complain about anything? When did you first notice this?" You are concerned about teeth turning black — what worries you, dad? Will this affect adult teeth? When did you last visit a dentist? Any specific reason? Why hasn't he been to the dentist before? (possible answer: can't afford it — mention Child Dental Benefit Schedule, time constraints) Did he complain about anything? How does he clean his teeth? Supervision? In-between teeth? How is his diet? (cookies/cocoa cereal — note: "my other children had the same diet") What does he like to drink? Water? What toothpaste? Any illnesses in childhood? (few illnesses in a short time + high-frequency snacking = high risk) Diagnosis & Risk Factors Provisional diagnosis: dental caries — high risk of dental caries. "Would you like me to walk you through why he has this problem?" Risk factors: Diet (F.A.S.T. mnemonic — Frequency, Amount, Sticky, Time); bacteria (poor hygiene); acids reducing minerals from teeth (linked to decreased water intake/dehydration, and medicine such as cough syrup/antihistamine); low motivation (no remineralisation, less saliva).

title: naz notes
text: High risk = more than 3 lesions. 8-year-olds are in transition to becoming independent with hygiene. Less water → caries / constipation / dry mouth. Investigation & Management Investigation: extra-oral — jaws, jaw joint, how he's closing his mouth (lip incompetence, clicking); intra-oral — count and check decay, palpate, mobility, percuss, blow air on teeth to find sensitive/painful ones; X-ray — 2 bitewings (right/left), OPG if removing any teeth; diet chart (Mehmat/daycare/grandparents), 2 weekdays + 1 weekend day. Management — TG Caries framework: diet modification, plaque reduction, tooth surface modification, saliva modification. Preventive — tap water, diet modification, fluoride varnish (note CPP-ACP allergy caution), pit and fissure sealant, adult toothpaste. Small decay — GIC/composite (painful tooth → reversible pulpitis → GIC). Deep decay — pulpotomy/pulpectomy. Extraction — space maintainer. Motivating independent brushing: let him choose a colourful brush, floss with a holder, plaque-glo toothpaste. "I understand it's challenging to manage by yourself. We need to work as a team — I'll demonstrate brushing and flossing. If the problem is not addressed now he could require extensive treatment involving cost and time. Maybe we can give him an electric brush." Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts "Don't know what he's eating at school?" / "I don't think that's a permanent molar?" / "I'm not rich and can't afford it?" — check eligibility (household income under ~$95,400 single, ~$152,640 couple) and Child Dental Benefit Scheme ($1,095 over 2 calendar years). "Did it affect his sleep or eating?" Prefer to keep baby teeth as long as possible — they act as a natural space maintainer. Not drinking enough water can lead to kidney stones/constipation; tap water has the added benefit of fluoride. References: caries protective & risk factors; TG Caries — Dry Mouth (Evans); caries risk assessment; Child Benefit Scheme. Ortho Referral with Undiagnosed Periodontitis — Jordan, 17 PQ-1 Module 1, Cluster 1. Crowded teeth; wants braces; last dentist visit 12 months ago; CPITN scores taken today. Patient & Scenario CPITN (Community Periodontal Index of Treatment Needs) rows: 4, 4, 4 / 4, 2, 4 — a score of 4 means complete periodontal charting is required. X-ray shows bone loss around molars. No smoking.

title: naz notes
text: Not mentioned unless asked: bullied at school because of crooked teeth; never been to a dentist before; grandmother has diabetes; family history of early tooth loss (parents wearing plates/dentures); "no one wanted to go out on a date with him." How to Start / Questions to Ask "Hi Jordan, thanks for coming in today. My name is Dr Akhai. I understand you are concerned about crowded teeth and want to improve the alignment of your teeth. We will definitely discuss options about that, but before that, is it okay if I ask a few questions?" Tell me more about your issue — any wobbly teeth? Any bleeding? "With ortho treatment, cleaning can get a bit difficult, so how are you maintaining your teeth?" — then explain your CPITN findings and diagnosis. Do you have anyone in the family with diabetes? Have you noticed anyone wearing plates/missing teeth? Does anyone have crooked teeth (tooth/jaw size discrepancy)? "Do you think it will be a good idea to explore why you are having this problem?" — their family history. How's your general health? Blood tests? Did your dentist mention anything about your gums? Diagnosis & Risk Factors "Treatment to improve your alignment will temporarily make cleaning difficult. Earlier, while checking your gums, I was calling out some numbers... I have given a score of 4 in these spaces which means the space between your gums and teeth is 5.5mm, which is very unusual for your age. Also you can see black spaces on your x-ray — from what it seems like you have a condition called periodontitis (irritation of gums and bone). If we use these teeth as anchors for braces you might lose these teeth." Risk factors: oral hygiene/crowding; family history (hyper-responsiveness/aggressive bacteria); underlying medical condition (lowered immunity, stress). Differential: depends on history — rapidly progressing periodontitis, or periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease (diabetes / cyclic neutropenia / leukaemia). Type 1 diabetes tends to cause more destruction around first molars, as these are the first teeth to erupt. Investigation & Management Investigation: extra-oral — face, jaws, muscles, mouth closing; intra-oral — teeth, gums, deposits, cold test, complete 6-point charting (probing, mobility, recession, bleeding on probing, furcations); X-ray — OPG (or bitewings if given), perio pictures, periapical/vertical bitewings if OPG given. Management: refer to periodontist to treat the gum condition; GP for blood test.

title: naz notes
text: Today — assess effectiveness of biofilm reduction. Pre-requisites before referring to a periodontist: manage general dental care, detailed periodontal charting, current OPG. "What will the specialist do?" — Gum specialist will (1) raise the gums and clean under direct vision, (2) may give antibiotics as part of treatment, (3) discuss the option of bone/artificial material to allow bone to grow (downsides: surgery, cost, time, can fail). Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts "I have saved and I'm keen to get braces started, can you give me a referral to an orthodontist?" — "I am happy to refer you, but my recommendation is..." "Do I need a blood test? What will you see?" / "What does 4 (score) mean?" → probing depth >5.5mm. "Which specialist will you refer me to?" / "How long do I have this condition for?" / "What is the underlying medical condition responsible for this?" Periodontitis with a genetic predisposition has pubertal onset. Review 3-monthly until gum condition/immune system is stable. References: TG — Periodontitis; DHSV referral criteria; Odell — Crowding case; ADA in-patient perio. Denture Stomatitis & Angular Cheilitis — Mrs/Mr Smart (Campbell), 65 PQ-3 Module 1, Cluster 2. Current denture 20 years old; few natural teeth; doesn't wear the lower denture; ill-fitting, falls out. Patient & Scenario Presenting reason: angular cheilitis. Not mentioned unless asked: diabetes — a major assessment area, often not volunteered. Well-managed diabetes can be disrupted by a broken denture, since the patient can't chew properly. Variation: angular/aphthous cheilitis — symptomatic (no photo) vs. asymptomatic (photo given). Variation: denture stomatitis alone. Variation: wants a new denture ↔ wants the same one repaired. Variation: wears the denture at night ↔ leaves it out. Rarely: combination syndrome. Note: an old, broken, ill-fitting denture can still cause denture stomatitis on its own. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mrs Smart, I understand you are here today because you are experiencing some issues with your denture.

title: naz notes
text: Before we discuss how to manage this issue, I would like to clearly understand the problems you are facing with this denture and understand your expectations — could you tell me more about your problem?" Why do you want a new or repaired denture? How is this denture affecting your day-to-day life? How did the denture break? (→ denture hygiene) Apart from the broken denture, is there any other concern? How is your general health? How are you managing your diabetes? When was your last blood test? How is the broken/loose denture affecting your diet? Can you chew food? "You haven't been regular with your dentist and GP — is there a specific reason?" "Why do you wear the denture at night?" (partner doesn't know about it / doesn't like the sensation without it) Diagnosis & Risk Factors "Thanks for sharing that information. Normally I would expect the body's immune system to fight back, but in your case that didn't happen." Candida is a disease of the immune system. Denture stomatitis: poor hygiene/ill-fitting denture, diabetes, dietary factors, smoking +/-. Angular cheilitis: skin folds (denture over-extension), dietary deficiency, GI issues, skin conditions. Denture stomatitis is noticed by the dentist, not the patient — don't shift the initial focus. Leaving it untreated can lead to hyperplastic candidiasis. Denture should ideally be changed every 8–10 years. Investigation & Management Option 1: numbing gel, swab test, blood test. Option 2: antifungal cream (won't work if due to dietary deficiency). Management: reline — cheap/less effective (chairside) vs. lab (stronger, checks bite, extra cost); do nothing (disadvantage: papillary hyperplasia) vs. denture hygiene (leave out at night, clean with soap and water). GP blood test for diabetes/nutritional deficiency; oral medicine referral. Review pathway: 2 days → 2 weeks → 1 month; no improvement → specialist advice (systemic antifungal); improvement → new denture (recommend upper + lower partial). Prescription: Miconazole 2% gel, 2.5ml, 4 times daily; apply to denture surface twice a day. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts "I don't like using soap and water to clean my denture?" → alternative is Polident tablets. "Is it a fungal or bacterial infection?" → ~90% fungal. "Is Vaseline good for sore corners?" → yes, keeps the area moist. "Why do I need a lower denture?" → to shift the biting forces. "Can we do the denture now?" → no, fit might be affected by current inflammation.

title: naz notes
text: Denture stomatitis: sensitive erythematous lesions, associated with Candida, confined to denture-bearing areas (particularly the palate). Angular cheilitis: painful erythema/fissuring of the mouth corners, most commonly Candida (also S. aureus, streptococci) — often self-resolves once predisposing factors are addressed. References: TG — Denture stomatitis / Angular cheilitis. MRONJ / Odontogenic Infection — David Arthur, 67 PQ-4 PQ-5 Module 1, Cluster 2. Abscess, mobile tooth (grade 3), already prescribed Panadeine Forte for pain. Patient & Scenario History: myocardial infarction/hypertension (sometimes); on Atenolol + Verapamil + Warfarin; hypothyroidism → thyroxine; osteoporosis → calcium and denosumab; sometimes allergic to penicillin. Variation: tooth mobile ↔ not mobile. Variation: acute periodontal abscess ↔ acute periapical abscess (RCT/non-vital). High chance MRONJ is already present — check for lump/swelling around the neck (lymphadenitis). How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mr Arthur, thank you for being patient while I was examining your mouth. I understand the tooth on the bottom right has been troubling you; in order to understand better, can I ask a few questions?" Tell me more about the swelling/pain? Warfarin — when was your last INR? Social history? Last dental visit — what was done? Osteoporosis — diagnosis? Medication? How long? Do you know how this medication works? Are you aware of the side effects? Do you smoke? Do your gums bleed? (sign of active gum disease, which can cause MRONJ) Don't combine antibiotics with active dental treatment. Diagnosis & Risk Factors "Mr Arthur, this problem started a few days ago and you have a gum boil around that tooth called a Dental Abscess — we confirmed this infection is coming from the gum by applying some cold on your tooth (which gave a response), and on the x-ray there's a black area — bone loss." (Diagnosis: acute periodontal abscess / dental abscess.) MRONJ (definition, TG): exposed area of bone not healing for more than 8 weeks in a patient taking antiresorptive drugs — a complication of the drug, not just the treatment. MRONJ can be missed as symptoms mimic a periodontal abscess. For spreading infection, always check for facial swelling. Key facts: Atenolol + Verapamil usually not given together (drug interaction — can suddenly raise blood pressure). Thyroxine and calcium taken together impede thyroxine absorption. Any active infection not treated within 24 hours needs antibiotics.

title: naz notes
text: Investigation & Management "We have a few options to manage this — do you have anything particular on your mind? Removing the tooth will get rid of the infection, but I am concerned about healing." Do nothing. Denosumab pathway — depends on age/mandible, perio infection, ENT specialist advice. Warfarin pathway — check INR (<3.5 acceptable); thyroxine interactions; metronidazole increases bleeding risk. If INR ok: drain and splint. Antibiotics + splint pathway — remove deposit above the gum line (extra cost); pain killer, avoid NSAIDs. Temporise or refer to hospital specialist/GP. If on Warfarin, can't go below the gum line without checking INR first. "If you want me to remove the tooth, I'll take advice from the specialist (my recommendation is doing it with him)." Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts "What will the specialist do?" / "Can MRONJ happen with the specialist too?" / "If the medication can lead to MRONJ, can I stop it?" "Do you see anything on the radiograph?" / "Why can't you remove the tooth today?" → refer to Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery. Ensuring optimal oral hygiene with regular review reduces MRONJ risk — power brush, floss for interdental cleaning. References: TG — MRONJ/odontogenic infection; Odell case; BDJ "Preexisting MRONJ"; American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons — MRONJ. Crown Broke During Extraction — Esposito / Shell Parker, 50 PQ-6 Module 1, Cluster 3. Tooth 16/26, badly decayed, breaks at the gumline mid-extraction; swelling on the face near the ear; lives 2 hours away, Friday afternoon; sometimes penicillin allergy. How to Start / Breaking the News "Mr/Mrs Esposito, I'd like to update you on what has happened during the procedure, but first — are you comfortable the way you are seated?" Start by acknowledging and apologising. "The tooth that I was removing was badly decayed and had a weak structure. While I was removing the tooth carefully with my forceps, the top part of the tooth has broken and the roots are still inside. I am sorry about that." "I am sorry this has happened, not something we were hoping for — wanted you to have a peaceful weekend.

title: naz notes
text: There are a few options we can discuss, but before that would it be OK if I ask a few questions?" What are you worried about? Now that this has happened, what do you expect me to do? What do you think might happen? Can I take one more X-ray to show you but also as part of my record? (needs a 2nd consent) Would you like me to speak about replacement options? Management "It's very unfortunate the top portion of the tooth has come out. It's still within my scope of practice to remove it. A different technique, which I am happy to discuss with you — there are other options as well, as you have swelling on the face. Booking you with the hospital or a specialist next week — which one?" Do nothing (adv/disadv). Extraction by me → burs/handpiece to divide the roots, create space for a fine instrument, possibly a small cut in the gum → stitches (resorbable). Complications: (1) OAC, (2) root slip → refer specialist (Caldwell-Luc approach); leave it / review 48–72hr. Temporise & refer to hospital: pulp extirpation/antibiotics, specialist referral, call after 24hrs to check how they are doing. New topic — OAC (oro-antral communication) guidance: <2mm → suture, sinus precautions (no nose blowing, no straw, no forceful sneeze/cough, open-mouth sneeze), follow up 2 weeks. ≥2–3mm → haemostatic agent (collagen/cellulose) + figure-of-8 suture. >3mm → buccal advancement flap, done by a surgeon/urgent referral. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Which antibiotic? Can you leave the root piece in the sinus? (if small/not infected, no sinusitis — no issue) What if something bad happens to me? Will you cover the cost of a specialist? (No.) Do you think these complications can happen with the specialist too? (Yes, but they're better equipped to manage them.) Breaking-bad-news structure: give the information in 20–30 seconds, then pause and let them process and speak. References: DHSV referral criteria; spreading odontogenic infection (TG); ADA news — difficult conversations. Replacement Options, Elderly Patient — Mr Ken, 78 PQ-7 Module 1, Cluster 3. Scaling done, no new cavities, gums healthy; tooth #6 has a metal cap; wants to know replacement options; hypertension not initially volunteered.

title: naz notes
text: Patient & Scenario Complaint about quality of a previous RCT is possible — offer 2 advantages/2 disadvantages of each replacement option; patient might say "I'm not interested in replacement." Variations: normal gap ↔ small gap; age 48/60/78; grinding can affect replacement options; dry mouth/hypertension might affect choice — respect autonomy, don't force options. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mr Ken, I am done with examination and cleaning — everything looks great, you are doing really well with your hygiene. The space of that missing tooth I have been monitoring closely still looks the same. Do you have any concerns? Is it OK if I update your medical history?" Has anything changed? Which medication are you taking? (if unsure: "is it OK if I reach out to your GP to confirm which medicine you are taking?") Are you aware how these medicines affect your oral condition? (hypertension medicines → dry mouth) Any dry mouth lately? How did you lose that tooth? Key Facts & Management Drug-induced dry mouth reduces saliva/buffering and increases caries and periodontal disease risk. Apart from calcium channel blockers, all BP meds cause dry mouth. Flexible denture (thermoplastic nylon resin) can be given to patients allergic to acrylic resin. Ante's Law: balance is lost if you lose any of these teeth to decay or gum disease. "This space right now is stable — as long as other teeth are OK, we can maintain this space." Replacement options tree: do nothing (adv/disadv); removable denture — acrylic, metal, or flexible (preferred among removable, though it can aggravate existing perio disease); bridge — 2-unit cantilever or 3-unit; implant (expensive) — short/mini/normal, CBCT. Metal partial denture — thin/comfortable/durable, has a clasp/expensive; can't add teeth, clasp can put extra force on an already weak tooth, difficult to clean. Acrylic partial denture — lower cost, can add teeth; bulkier, less durable. Flexible denture (preferred) — clasp-free, flexible, lower cost; can't add teeth, not as durable. Cantilever (preferred, 2-unit) — ideally uses the tooth behind for support; risk of debonding increased if that tooth is compromised. 3-unit bridge — not ideal if the abutment tooth is compromised, but good appearance/predictability/easy hygiene. Implant (preferred at 48) — fixed, doesn't involve other teeth; downsides are cost, nerve risk, specialist referral, CBCT.

title: naz notes
text: Small-gap variation: do nothing is not a good option here — drifting teeth lead to food impaction/gum disease/decay, and a tilted tooth might need trimming or ortho uprighting. Mini implant preferred; cantilever if the patient doesn't want an implant. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Which option is best for me? I have enough money. Can you put a clasp on that tooth? Am I too old for ortho? Did my old dentist do a bad job? Is there anything wrong with my filling? What are the disadvantages of a cantilever? Can't use a short-filled tooth as an anchor for a bridge — take specialist opinion. A cap on a tooth affects the clasp of a removable partial denture. Long-term dentures can be damaging as forces transmit directly to the gums. "If you have any concerns about the care you have received, I suggest you reach out to your dentist." References: Dry Mouth (TG); indications/contraindications of cantilever; Journal of Prosthetic Dentistry (short implant). MODULE 2 Quake Set Congenital Syphilis — Stevie, 8 PQ-8 Module 2, Cluster 1. Here today with foster carer Mrs Kaur; carer concerned about appearance — shape of teeth, puffy gums. Patient & Scenario Partial eyesight/hearing loss; high caries risk — referral needed, preventive advice; difficulty holding things; open bite. Not given: mouth breathing; bullied at school; upcoming family wedding. Variation: short-term carer (consent for investigation only) ↔ long-term carer (consent for treatment, specialist consent required). How to Start / Questions to Ask "Hello Mrs Kaur, thank you for bringing Stevie today. I understand you have some concerns about her teeth. What are you worried about?" What does Stevie think about it? Did she complain about anything? "Because her teeth are a bit unusual compared to others, is there something in her medical history you are aware of?" Why do you want to fix her teeth? Apart from shape, is there any other concern? Does she have any medical problem? "I understand you are keen to get her treated, but I would like to know what kind of consent you have." If she has difficulty holding things, how is she brushing? Diagnosis & Risk Factors Signs & symptoms: puffy gums (could be plaque-related); shape of teeth — developmental: Hutchinson's incisors (notched), mulberry molars (bumpy), peg lateral, cyst (fluid-filled); gaps — widely spaced, extra teeth, delayed eruption, frenum. Risk factors: hypoplastic teeth, open bite (mouth breathing), pits on molars, reduced dexterity. Syphilis — T.

title: naz notes
text: Pallidum → eighth nerve deafness, Hutchinson's triad. Can't give the diagnosis of syphilis if the carer hasn't been informed of her medical condition — use the term "developmental defect." Open bite → mouth breathing → dry mouth. Investigation & Management Investigation: extra-oral — face, jaw, mouth opening/lip closure; intra-oral — visual (count teeth, gums, plaque, decay, colour changes), tactile (palpate, foramen blanches on pressure), percuss, mobility, blow air; X-ray — BW/OPG → BPE; pictures for records; diet chart. Confirm dental history first ("Could you tell me how she takes care of her teeth?"). Ask the organisation to confirm if they hold any medical records/diagnosis for her. Separate consent needed to assess general health. BPE age ranges: 7–11 yrs → codes 0–2 (teeth 16, 11, 26, 36, 31, 46); age 12 onwards → codes 0–4. Management: "When you come back with consent, can fix the shape of her teeth for the wedding." Other concerns (spaces/jaw defects) need complex treatment and specialist referral — separate consent required (pedo/ortho). Health promotion: show/demonstrate brushing and flossing; recommend electric toothbrush, fluoride toothpaste + tooth mousse. Can't give varnish without consent for treatment. Diet history — ask frequency even if parent says diet is "very healthy"; developmental defects put her at higher risk. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts "I am ready to pay, can you please treat her today?" / "Can you do a frenectomy for her?" / "What are we going to do today?" / "Does she have missing teeth?" Ortho treatment is normally not covered under the Child Benefit Scheme (CBS) unless there's a craniofacial condition, cleft lip, multiple missing teeth, or another qualifying medical condition. No wait period at the hospital for this referral pathway — seen on a priority basis (special government funding). "Diagnosis we cannot give you, as it's confidential — let's check with the organisation." Key Facts & Management Minimal Intervention Strategy: diet modification, plaque reduction, tooth surface modification, saliva modification. Facts: electrolytes in foods — banana (potassium), milk (calcium), meat/nuts/grains/beans (magnesium), peanut butter (sodium). Repeated exposure to acidic drinks washes off the biofilm, exposing the tooth surface to acid. Fluorohydroxyapatite resists acid down to pH 4.5 vs. hydroxyapatite demineralising at pH 5.5. Sugar content: fizzy drinks ~16 teaspoons, sports drinks ~8 teaspoons. Long flavour/lingering of sports drinks adds risk (swishing them around the mouth). Artificial sweeteners give sweetness with fewer calories and bacteria can't break them into acid. Dietary advice structure: Amount — reduce, read labels, consider artificial sweeteners. Texture — reduce sticky foods, increase clearance. Acids — reduce fizzy drinks. Frequency — 2-hour rest between exposures. Saliva — drink water; avoid long workouts (>60 min) without water/carb loading beforehand. Health promotion: "Reading the label" — grams of sugar. Suggest seeing a sports dietician.

text: Prescription: 5000ppm toothpaste, flossing, 3-monthly fluoride varnish. Reduce sports drink intake; brush before/after as shown previously. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts What's the difference between electrolyte and sports drinks? How to calculate calories? How are low-calorie sweeteners different? How to safely have sports drinks? — don't swish/stray, rinse with water after. Do I need fillings? When? MODULE 4 Pink Set Oro-Antral Communication Worry — Terry Jones (student nurse) PQ-55 Pain in a top-right tooth, apical periodontitis, wants extraction; worried about OAC, HIV and Hepatitis C. Patient & Scenario Decide to extract. Variations: irreversible pulpitis ↔ acute apical periodontitis; private clinic ↔ public hospital; reason for removal — cultural belief ↔ financial. Recommend saving the tooth only during the health-promotion portion. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Terry, we have taken your x-ray of the tooth that is painful; we will be discussing your concerns, but before that, would it be OK if I confirm a few things?" Tell me more about the pain? Anything for the pain? Any specific reason for removing the tooth? "Would you like me to explain how we will know communication has happened and how we are going to manage it?" Diagnosis & Management How you'll know OAC occurred: visual (socket → air bubbles/hole; root tip inspection — bone attached means no communication); instrument (sound/mirror fogging); X-ray (PA/CBCT — most accurate, done by specialist, shows disruption at the apex). Patient may feel air escaping nose-to-mouth or food mouth-to-nose; pain on one side, blocked nose. Management by size: <2mm → suture + post-op instructions → spontaneous healing. 2–7mm → gel + suture + antibiotics → ~50% chance. >3mm (per new TG) → urgent referral to maxillofacial surgeon. "I am worried about this sinus being close to the tooth; a better option would be to get it done by the specialist. I can check different programmes you could be eligible for on a priority basis." Options: short term (RCT or extraction), review, temporisation (pulpectomy — preferred, free at public hospital), long-term replacement options. By me only after a 2nd X-ray — if OAC or root slip into sinus, refer to specialist. Precautions/blood-borne viruses: "How can you ensure my safety from Hepatitis/HIV? These are blood-borne viruses.

In your case, since you are worried about OAC/blood-borne viruses, the only way to 100% avoid it is RCT." Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts What will the specialist do?
