Missing/Peg Lateral Incisors, Diastema & Family History of Missing Teeth PQ-21 Mum brings her daughter in worried about a midline gap and possible missing lateral incisors; family history of missing wisdom teeth. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mum, could you tell me more about your concerns?" "Since you have a few concerns, what bothers you the most? What do you want me to talk about first?" — options: gap/large front teeth/crowding. How long has the gap been there? How did she lose her milk teeth? Anyone in family with gaps/missing teeth? Diagnosis & Risk Factors Reason for the gap: this is called a midline diastema — up to 2mm is self-correcting, but in her case it's a bit more. Causes: mesiodens/cyst/erupting canines/frenum. Usually the lateral incisors come by age 8–9, so there's still a year to go, but concern remains as there may not be enough space visible, or the teeth could be missing given her family history. Risk factors: genetically she could have a smaller jaw and bigger teeth ("weaker expression of genes"). Differential: diastema ← frenum/thumb sucking, cyst/mesiodens (extra tooth), missing lateral. Lateral incisor ← present by 8–9 years / stuck (family history/tooth-jaw discrepancy) / missing. Investigation & Management Extra-oral — face, jaw, lips; intra-oral — visual (count/extra or missing), tactile (palpate for bulge/blanch), instrument (measure space); X-ray — PA/occlusal; study models; photos. Referring criteria: diastema >2mm / deep bite. X-ray justified by family history of missing teeth.

text: Let the patient choose between PA and occlusal X-rays. No OPG right now as the issue isn't clear yet. What does she think about it?" "That's why orthodontic treatment is recommended — to correct teeth position and the way they meet." Family history is good justification for taking a radiograph now. She needs to be regular with hygiene and check-ups, as orthodontic treatment will increase her risk. Demonstrate; brochures. Would you be giving an appliance to wear? If we don't do anything, will the space close on its own? Will the laterals come on their own? Is it a serious genetic condition? Can we take an OPG? Congenitally-missing-teeth ranking: #1 third molars, #2 second premolars (5|5), #3 lateral incisors (2|2). Normal eruption timeline: canines/premolars ~8–9yrs; 3rd molar formation begins 7–9yrs, erupts 8–10yrs. Early interceptive orthodontics (9–12yrs) can reduce later fixed-ortho treatment time, with complete resolution in ~15% of cases. If only one lateral is missing, wait up to 6 months; if both missing, wait longer then take a radiograph (IOPA/occlusal), OPG to assess for other missing/ectopic teeth. References: BDJ — ortho treatment planning/appliance choice; management of missing lateral incisor; conservative interdisciplinary management of 2|2; restorative management of deep overbite. Tongue Ulcer — Possible Oral Cancer Concern (Smoker, Teacher) PQ-20 Ulcer on the lateral border of the tongue, noticed a month ago; last dental visit 2 years ago; smoker, school teacher. Patient & Scenario Name varies (Jane Highlands / Cooper Matthew) across variants. Variations: cough ↔ no cough (changes referral urgency); biopsy (traumatic cause) ↔ chest x-ray; reduced smoking recently ↔ quit smoking. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mrs Cooper, you are here today for check-up and cleaning; we can do that today, but other than that, any other concerns?" → ulcer.

text: Can I ask a few questions to understand what might be happening and when it started? Any idea what might have caused this? Does the tooth feel sharp in that area? Did you bite in that area? Any ulcers in the past? With this ulcer, have you noticed any restriction in tongue movement/numbness/difficulty swallowing? Any swelling/lumps around your neck? What do you do? Do you like your work? Work hours? On days when things get harder, what do you do? Smoking — how many? How long? Any changes lately? If cough — are you doing anything about it? Alcohol — how often? How is your diet? Weight loss? Diagnosis, Risk Factors & Investigation "I understand life can be busy/stressful since you are a teacher, but we also need to ensure we prioritise our health. Today I'm happy to clean also — do you want me to explain what could be causing the ulcer?" Possible causes: traumatic ulcer (sharp tooth, bit accidentally, stress/trauma); deficiency (diet); sinister (smoking & drinking, location). Key facts: after quitting smoking, cancer risk reduces but doesn't go away. Smoking causes DNA alteration in exposed areas (mouth/lungs/larynx/pharynx). Nicotine has dopaminergic effects similar to cocaine. Alcohol increases oral cancer risk 6x (direct damage + increased permeability to other carcinogens). Alcohol guideline: not more than 10 units weekly / 4 units daily (a small glass ≈ 1.6 units). Only ~3% quit smoking by willpower alone. Investigation: extra-oral — swelling/lumps around neck, jaw joints; intra-oral — measure ulcer size, check margins, check tongue movement, check teeth/broken fillings; picture; x-ray of the tooth with the broken filling. OMDR (Oral Medicine/Diagnostic Radiology) referral for biopsy. GP → chest x-ray, blood test. 2-week urgent referral pathway noted. "If you notice any difficulty swallowing/if the ulcer gets worse, get in touch." Health promotion: offer quitline referral if the patient allows; healthy diet is important to boost immunity. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Is this cancer? Why are we doing a biopsy? I don't want to give up smoking / don't talk about it. What will you check outside my mouth? References: TG — Ulcer; quitting smoking article; smoking/alcohol brochures. Acute Periodontal Abscess — Jane Highlands, 55 PQ-22 Sore tooth #1 (upper central incisor); extruded, probing 7mm mesially, generalized 4–5mm; smokes 25 cigarettes (sometimes); food lodgement is a sometime primary concern. Patient & Scenario Medically fit.

title: naz notes
text: Variations: concerns — extrusion/diastema/both; on examination, no developmental groove noted (variation). How to Start / Questions to Ask "Jane Highlands, you are here today for a painful tooth — could you tell me more about it?" Do you know how it started? How is this affecting you? Did you try anything for the pain? Any boil/discharge/fever/swelling of face/gums? Any other concerns? "Has it always been like that?" Diagnosis & Risk Factors Signs & symptoms: extrusion, pus may or may not drain back (pus could be pushing the tooth). Diagnosis: because food was stuck causing infection, and the tooth responded to cold test — acute periodontal abscess with generalized moderate periodontitis. Explain plaque/calculus; generalized wide gum-tooth spaces (normally 2–3mm, here 4–5mm); localized 7mm pocket. "Do you want me to explain what might have caused this?" — false pocket, food impaction, developmental groove, local trauma. Risk factors: pre-existing gum disease; hygiene (no flossing, no professional cleaning); smoking (reduces blood flow to gums by making blood sticky, lowers immunity, dries mouth); developmental grooves trap food. "How do you clean your teeth? Previous dental treatment?" Management "We can go about managing this with a few options — do you have anything on your mind?" Do nothing — infection can spread, tooth loss, can become life-threatening. Today: numb the area, drain pus through the pocket (incision & drainage), +/- splint if wobbly; clean/debride with saline; pain killer (paracetamol/ibuprofen) — per new TG can use chlorhexidine. Manage the gum condition first, then later manage diastema. GP — blood test for diabetes; review after 2 days. Review outcomes: improvement → extruded tooth (splint/refer), diastema (close/fill once gum improves), generalized perio 4–5mm → specialist. No improvement → specialist. Health promotion: "Our management will address the acute problem, but my concern is why it happened in the first place — smoking also played a big role in this. What do you think we can do?" "It's good you are trying to quit, but it's very difficult to do it just by yourself — if you allow me, I can connect you with quit line." Regular oral review (3-monthly), cleaning between teeth; brochure.

text: Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts How will you drain the pus? (Gracey curette) Will you give me antibiotics? Can you do ortho treatment to close the gap? Can you put a filling to close the gap? Why is there a deep pocket on that tooth? Active treatment for localized infection doesn't need antibiotics. Periodontal abscess is common in people with pre-existing gum disease. Extrusion/flaring of front teeth indicates bone loss. References: TG — Periodontitis; DHSV — Perio article. Traveller with Acute Irreversible Pulpitis — Mr Fitz-Patrick Mckenzie PQ-23 Emergency appointment for pain from a broken tooth, going interstate shortly. Patient & Scenario Variation: generally healthy, no meds ↔ taking OTC/Cartia (low-dose aspirin) to prevent stroke. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mr Patrick, I'll try my best to get you out of pain — since you are in a hurry, where are you headed? How long will you be away?" What are you worried about? Anything that triggers the pain? Have you tried anything for it? Can't eat — because it's sensitive or painful to bite? "Before I recommend any pain meds, I need to know about your medical history — anything to add?" Are you taking any medication, prescribed or OTC? (Cartia — blood thinner, increases bleeding risk) How often were you taking Panadol? "I can give you an injection to numb the area." Diagnosis & Management Diagnosis: irreversible pulpitis (no apical involvement) — pain on biting/hot/cold. Since the tooth still responds to hot/sweet, the nerve is alive — inflamed to the point it can't repair itself. Option 1: remove the top part of the nerve (pulpotomy) — takes about 15 minutes. Option 2: give pain medicines now; do the definitive treatment when the patient is back. Options overall: do nothing (↑pressure/pain on the flight) → RCT/pulpotomy/pulpectomy/pain killer → referral (GP → dentist). Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Can you give me antibiotics? What are you going to do today? Why does hot make it worse? Why does cold relieve it? Is the tooth infected now? A-fibres respond to cold/sweet; C-fibres respond to hot. Late-stage irreversible pulpitis: cold can relieve pain (reduces pressure). Cartia = low-dose aspirin; NSAIDs (ibuprofen) contraindicated with it. Dosing: Paracetamol 1000mg 4–6 hourly (max 4000mg/day); Ibuprofen 400mg 6–8 hourly (max 2400mg/day); Oxycodone 5mg max 3 days (driving/alcohol restriction); Tapentadol 50mg 6 hourly (max 3 days).

title: naz notes
text: Codeine — not effective for dental pain, no longer prescribed for it. Irreversible pulpitis pulp is usually free of bacteria (infection often confined to the coronal pulp). References: TG — analgesics, pain chapter, endodontic emergencies; NPS Medicinewise. Consent for Extraction — Badly Broken Molar Near Sinus (Mackenzie) PQ-25 Removing a badly broken molar; palatal root close to the sinus; smoker. Patient & Scenario Variations: diagnosis irreversible pulpitis ↔ spreading odontogenic infection; root close to sinus ↔ inside sinus; moderate decay ↔ badly broken. How to Start / Diagnosis "I have taken your x-ray and the pain you are experiencing is coming from this tooth as it has a hole inside it. There are a few ways to manage this so that you can get back to work — is it OK if I confirm a few details?" Diagnosis: acute irreversible pulpitis (hot & cold worsen the pain; nerve exposed by decay, irreversibly damaged). "If you want to try and save this tooth, I can refer you. But to help with the pain, I or the specialist can remove this tooth." "I'll walk you through the steps to remove the tooth, but at any point if you feel it's too much for you, we have an option of giving you sedation." Procedure & Complications Patient has a choice between the general dentist or a specialist for the extraction. Procedure: numbing/injection; hold tooth with instrument and wobble it out; if broken, may need to section and remove roots individually. Common complications: dry socket (5%), temporary nerve damage (2%), permanent nerve damage (0.5%), bleeding (managed with gauze), pain (paracetamol/ibuprofen), post-surgical infection. Dry socket: clot might get dislodged; dry heat/suction are contributing factors. Uncommon: damage to a neighbouring tooth, tooth breaking, OAC (management by size: <2mm / 2–3mm / >3mm per new TG), root slipping into the sinus. Slipped root: try suction first; if not out, leave it (if not infected) or refer to specialist (Caldwell-Luc approach preferred). Post-op instructions given; review in 2 days. Replacement options discussed briefly (dentures/bridges/implant, detailed next time).

text: Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Why can't we save this tooth? Will the tooth come out easily? How long should I quit smoking? (at least 2 days) Can I cover the area and smoke? Can you give me a bridge? Why should I replace it? How did my tooth get decayed? How long will complete healing take? Can you give me nitrous oxide? Ask-Advise-Assist: brief chairside intervention for smoking, even when the patient isn't ready to quit. Smoking affects healing by reducing blood supply and immunity. Complaint / Pain After RCT by Another Dentist — Burke PQ-24 RCT done 3 days ago; pain with that tooth on biting; band and GIC filling placed; took Panadol. Patient & Scenario Flare-up vs. normal post-op pain: flare-up — severe pain 8/10, most things cause pain, since RCT day; normal post-op — mild pain 3/10, pain only on biting, starts when eating from that side. Onset differentiates the two. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mr Burke, thank you for being patient while I was examining. I have taken this x-ray of the tooth that is troubling you after treatment — is it OK if I ask a few questions to have some understanding about this pain you are having, so that we can come up with a plan?" Tell me more about the pain? When did it start? What were you doing when it started? What causes it? Were you given any instructions? Told not to eat from that side? Have you tried anything for the pain — hot or cold? Any swelling/puffiness? Fever? Unwell? Any updates in your medical history? How many sittings for the RCT? (single sitting can cause a flare-up with periapical infection) Differential & Management Differentials: normal post-op pain; high spot (extra biting force); band impinging (difficulty cleaning that area); food impaction; RCT-related complication (over-instrumentation, short filling, irrigants pushed beyond apex, debris/bacteria pushed beyond apex). "Would it be OK if I get your records here?" "Why was root canal done for that tooth? How long did it take?" Management — short term: articulating paper to check high points/band; ibuprofen 400mg 6–8 hourly; avoid eating from that side ~2 weeks (add oxycodone if already on ibuprofen properly). Long term: cap/replacement; review in 3 days. Outcome — pain subsides → cap/further treatment; pain persists → re-RCT (specialist), cap/further treatment, or endodontic evaluation. Ask for consent to access previous records to compare radiolucency.

title: naz notes
text: "Can you remove the tooth today?" → "I would recommend continuing for 3 days, give it another chance." Health promotion: regular reviews avoid decay reaching the nerve; brushing twice daily, flossing, fluoridated toothpaste. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Do you think my dentist did a bad job? Should I go see a specialist today? How can I complain? Is there something wrong with the filling? Why is the filling short? Why is there a shadow (furcation)? — not unusual to have accessory canals directing infection into that area. Flare-up = severe pain and/or swelling after endodontic treatment. Palatal Swelling — Mr Smith PQ-26 Large palatal swelling; last dental visit 6 years ago; colour changes red → pink/bluish; BP sometimes noted. Note in the notebook: "Don't emphasise the swelling if swelling is not a primary concern." Patient & Scenario Variations: swelling comes and goes ↔ constant; previous treatment filling ↔ incomplete RCT; presenting complaint mobility ↔ swelling → tender, daughter concerned. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mr Smith, I am your treating dentist today. What bothers you?" Tell me more about it? Has it happened before? Anything that causes this, can you recall? How long has the swelling been there? "You said it comes and goes — does it completely go away or reduce in size?" When it pops, did you notice fluid/bad taste? Is the swelling painful, in any other area? Any other problems — numbness/fever (sinus issues)? Any medical conditions? Differential Diagnosis & Management "There could be a few reasons for pain in your tooth. Since you had a filling/incomplete RCT (leakage causing infection), it could find an alternate pathway towards the roof of your mouth" — a dental abscess (appeared after filling but painful). Cyst (chronic infection, doesn't come and go). Could be unrelated to the tooth. Abnormal growth differentials: salivary gland (mucocele — comes and goes, painless); lymph node (lymphoma); salivary gland (adenoma); haemangioma (blood vessel); sinus tumour. Swelling pattern → cause → referral: comes & goes → abscess → manage yourself (GDP); comes & goes → mucocele → OMS; constant → cyst → maxillofacial specialist; constant → abnormal growth → OMS (haemangioma) or maxillofacial specialist (adenoma, sinus tumour, lymphoma).

title: naz notes
text: Investigation: extraoral — swelling, lumps, fever; intraoral — teeth, gums, feel the swelling (shape/size/texture + photos), bite test; radiograph — occlusal (can't take IOPA due to swelling), OPG, sinus view if no dental cause found; specialist imaging — ultrasound (haemangioma), CT (cyst/tumour), MRI (salivary). Management: dental cause → treat the tooth, clear infection, incise & drain. Non-dental → refer to specialist. FNAC (fine needle aspiration cytology) differentiates benign vs malignant. A cyst can resorb the root, making a tooth mobile — recent-onset mobility is a red flag. Health promotion: uncontrolled BP raises stroke risk; regular oral review prevents tooth loss; oral hygiene/flossing brochure. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts What is FNAC? What are the biopsy types (incisional/excisional/punch) — can I do it after 6 months? Can we save the tooth? Is it cancer? Will I lose the tooth? What are the names of these cysts (for my own research)? Which specialist will you refer me to? BP medication side effects worth knowing: calcium channel blockers → gingival enlargement; ACE inhibitors (captopril, ramipril, lisinopril) → delayed-onset recurrent angioedema of the head/neck. Dental Implants — John Edward, 70 PQ-27 Wants implants to replace missing teeth; heart valve replaced 2 years ago; barriers — old age/dexterity, brushing efficiency, forgetfulness. Patient & Scenario Variations: missing teeth (all posterior / upper back / 3 lower-right); medication (regular blood tests / none); smoking history not given → ex-smoker. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mr Edward, you're here to know about implants to replace your teeth — is it OK if I ask a few questions so I understand your expectations?" Why do you need implants? How long ago were these teeth removed, and why? Was it fillings chipping or teeth getting shorter? Any sensitivity? Do you grind your teeth? Sore muscles? Anything a partner's noticed? Have you worn replacement teeth since — for how long, any issues? Last dental visit — why not regular? Tell me about the heart valve replacement. Any medication? OK to confirm with your doctor? Any regular blood tests? How do you manage oral hygiene, given age/dexterity? Fitness for Implants & Risk Factors "With your permission I'll run preliminary investigations to confirm implants are suitable — if you don't mind me asking, why is it important to you that it's specifically implants?" Tests: INR / CTX / CBCT / HbA1c.

title: naz notes
text: Missing back teeth shift biting forces → chipping/wear (physiological vs pathological tooth wear). 3 implant risk factors: no abnormal forces; gum health; bone remaining. Patient-related risk factors: peri-implantitis, excessive forces/tooth wear, bone quality & quantity (denture use, time since extraction, smoking), sinus proximity (upper)/nerve proximity (lower) → CBCT scan → possible bone augmentation → maxillofacial/oral surgeon + prosthodontist. Procedure-related risk factors (cost roughly $5–6k): heart valve → antibiotic prophylaxis; warfarin → INR; alcohol/hypertension → bleeding, dry mouth; explain bacterial endocarditis risk. Investigation & Closing Extraoral — jaw joints, closing pattern, muscle activity, facial height at rest/closing; intraoral — all teeth, decay, photos, missing teeth, occlusion; gum health/BPE/bleeding since the patient hasn't attended recently; OPG as a general survey → CBCT with specialist. Closing (teamwork framing): general health matters because heart valve replacement raises endocarditis risk from daily-hygiene bacteraemia if oral hygiene lapses (recommend a power brush); implants need the same ongoing review as natural teeth; will liaise with specialist and send a brochure. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts OPG vs CBCT? "I brush but forget to floss" (possible cognitive concern)? What is INR? Am I fit for implants? Can implants join to a natural tooth? Will you stop my blood thinner? MODULE 5 Orange Set 4-Year-Old with Multiple Caries / Anti-Fluoride Parent — Shaun PQ-29 Module 5, Cluster 2. Mum: Mrs McConnell. Pain in lower left area; uncooperative — two bitewings taken; mum brought a diet chart. Patient & Scenario Not initially given: doesn't use fluoridated toothpaste. Variations: first vs second appointment; diet chart brought as a 2-day online chart vs a 3-day chart given by the dentist; anti-fluoride due to religious belief vs no particular personal issue.

title: naz notes
text: How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mum, it was difficult to make Shaun sit, but we managed to take his bitewing radiographs which will give us a fair idea and help us understand what is causing this pain — tell me more about it." (Pain occurs when sultanas get stuck, or when removed.) Did the pain affect his sleep/playing? Has he been to the dentist before, why? How does he clean his teeth, between teeth, what toothpaste? Why herbal toothpaste? (variation) Explain why we're asking these questions — to understand why he has holes in his teeth; explain how food/bacteria cause decay. Diagnosis, Risk Factors & Management Diagnosis: dental caries; reversible pulpitis (pain relieved on cleaning); high risk of caries given multiple holes; concerned the other decayed tooth (deep) could be dead/necrotic. Risk factors: hygiene; diet; irregular review; lack of fluoride toothpaste. Cultural sensitivity: avoid all fluoride (including GIC — filling/luting material) and toothpaste if anti-fluoride due to religious belief. Two behaviour-management tries recommended before qualifying for general anaesthesia (GA). Do nothing. Behaviour management: Tell-Show-Do, distraction, modelling. If successful → proceed with inhalation sedation/tablet. If unsuccessful → refer to specialist, try again next time, or hospital under GA. X-ray 1 → temporary filling (GIC or ZOE) → Hall crown (long-term; GIC filling replaced after ~3 months; Hall crown more expensive but longer term). X-ray 2 → RCT via specialist (temporise if painful); if the nerve is dead — space maintainer. Fluoride rebuilds weak enamel, prevents decay, reduces bacterial growth; GIC has fluoride release. Recommend children's fluoride toothpaste. Health promotion: "We need to work as a team to help Shaun and make sure he doesn't have a similar problem again." Supervise brushing, reduce exposure time so saliva can neutralise acids, reduce dietary sugars. Review every 3 months until risk is lowered; telehealth for some reviews.

title: naz notes
text: Questions Parents Ask & Key Facts Will fluoride cause autism? Is it safe to give inhalation sedation at this age? Is diet the only reason? Fluoride is used to kill rats? (myth to address) Why does he need to floss? What is the pathway to see a specialist? Hospital? "We will try various techniques to get him to cooperate — is there anything you can suggest?" References: fluoride benefits; oral health in rural communities; teledentistry; Hall crown article/technique; TG — sedation/anxiety management/fluoride. Uncontrolled Diabetes Patient with Cellulitis — Mr Heiss, 47 PQ-28 Module 5, Cluster 2. Pain/swelling around the upper 1st molar for about a week; diabetic, immunocompromised; grossly decayed tooth with roots close to the sinus; pulpitis symptoms. Patient & Scenario Variations: diabetes medication taken vs not; meal had vs missed; Augmentin prescribed by GP taken 1 week ago / 4 days ago / 2 days ago. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mr Heiss, you have a swelling on your face; I also had a look inside your mouth. Tell me more about the issue you are having." Which antibiotic? How many days? Do you think the swelling is increasing in size? "Normally we would expect the antibiotics to work and reduce the swelling — that takes us to a question about your general health. If your immune system is weak, antibiotics wouldn't work alone. How are you managing your diabetes?" When was the last HbA1c test? Reason for not being regular with medication/GP visits? Dental visits? Any difficulty opening your mouth/breathing/swallowing? Feeling unwell? Fever? Diagnosis & Key Facts "Do you want me to walk you through what might be going on and why the medication didn't work?" — source of infection is tooth decay: bacteria caused the nerve to die; infection is now spreading beyond the jaw (spreading odontogenic infection) — no severe swelling/breathing difficulty/trismus currently, but since the patient is unwell, systemic features are starting to appear. Rule of thumb (corrected in notebook): controlled diabetes → can extract; uncontrolled → extirpate (pulp removal) instead. HbA1c testing: uncontrolled → every 3 months; controlled → every 6 months (covered by Medicare). Increased stress (pain/injection) → increased cortisol → increased blood sugar. HbA1c 6.5–7 = borderline diabetes → lifestyle changes, testing every 12 months. Point-of-care device gives HbA1c in ~6 minutes vs ~4 hours for a standard test.

title: naz notes
text: Management Ideally remove the tooth to address the source of infection. No medication/no prescription for diabetes → refer to hospital (medical-emergency pathway). If the patient has eaten, wait before proceeding; if alcohol involved, metronidazole cannot be given. "Would it be okay if I check with your GP to arrange an HbA1c test?" Decision pathways: normal HbA1c, result available today → refer to ENT/specialist for LA/RCT referral or extraction. High HbA1c, no result today → pulp extirpation, refer for infection advice. No medication for diabetes → refer to hospital. Controlled diabetes → check with glucometer → proceed with endodontics. Borderline diabetes with no recent follow-up → refer to hospital. Antibiotic timeline: Augmentin 3 days ago → continue 2 more days; 4 days ago → add metronidazole; 5 days ago → same; 1 week ago → amoxicillin + metronidazole. Can't prescribe antibiotics alone — risk of sepsis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, Ludwig's angina if source untreated. Health promotion: regular diabetes management is important as uncontrolled diabetes affects immunity; recommend regular hygiene review. Review after 2 days; brochures. Complaint — Amalgam Filling Done by a Colleague (Chipped Filling / Pain) — Harry PQ-30 Module 5, Cluster 3. Filling done 2 weeks ago by a colleague; chipped after 2 days; X-ray shows radiolucency. Patient & Scenario Scenario: save the tooth vs. patient wants it removed. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Harry, I'm sorry that this has happened to you. It's very unusual to have pain after a filling — what do you think is causing this?" ("It's possible that if you were feeling odd, my colleague could have left the filling slightly high, leading to more biting forces in that area (high spot) — this is a reason it could have chipped.") "Would you like me to explain what I can see on the X-ray? This tooth has a shadow which usually shows up around 3 weeks after treatment, even though you didn't have pain — but this indicates some kind of infection beginning (acute apical periodontitis/necrosis of the pulp).

text: How to Start / Questions to Ask "Thomas, tell me more about what's going on." "Who has taken this X-ray, wanted to show you what was going on inside your mouth — your last tooth is decayed, as the area can be difficult to clean and harbours bacteria, causing infection which has spread to surrounding areas; as you have a swelling and fever, we call this a spreading odontogenic infection. Are you with me so far?" Anything trigger the pain? Did you do anything about it? What about the swelling — only in the middle of the day? Has it increased in the last hour? Is it affecting your swallowing/breathing/mouth opening? Are you able to eat/drink? Any fever? Diagnosis, Referral Criteria & Management Diagnosis: spreading odontogenic infection from the carious/cracked tooth #8. Referral criteria for facial swelling (plus fever): dyspnoea/dysphagia/stridor; trismus <2cm; swelling closing the eye; unstable (worsened in the last hour). "There are a few ways we can address this, as this infection needs to be treated. What do you think — anything you expect today?" Extraction removes the source of infection and the swelling will improve. Options: hospital medical team (check airway, blood culture, IV antibiotics — 2-day stay disadvantage) vs. dentist (extraction, place drain). Cannot give antibiotics right now if unstable — the preferred plan. Penicillin allergy not severe (unconfirmed): Cephalexin 500mg 6-hourly + Metronidazole; recommend confirming allergy with GP. If severe/rapidly worsening → Clindamycin 300mg 8-hourly. New/worsening respiratory symptoms → COX-2 selective NSAID (Celecoxib 100mg 12-hourly), avoid non-selective NSAIDs. Asthma itself is not a contraindication to NSAIDs unless there's a history of NSAID-triggered exacerbation. Health promotion: repeated inappropriate antibiotic switching risks resistance — worth raising gently given the patient is only 21. Provide brochures; confirm allergy; review regularly. Questions Patients Ask How does Clindamycin work? How is it different from Amoxicillin? Can I delay it? What will they do at the hospital? Which hospital? How long do I stay? Antibiotics will localise the infection and arrest growth of the swelling; by the time of the specialist appointment the patient should be ready. Differential Diagnosis & Investigation TG note: persistent pain and swelling after extraction could be dry socket or infection — fever is never seen in dry socket. Referred pain; normal post-op pain (only 2–3 days); nerve injury (with numbness). "Have you ever done any blood test — diabetes/deficiency can reduce immunity." "How long did the tooth removal take?" Dry socket: clean with saline, Alvogyl dressing, review in 24–48 hours per pain severity — dressing frequency: severe → daily, mild/moderate → alternate days. Nerve injury: 2-point discrimination test both sides; review at 2 weeks/1 month/3 months.

text: "The reason I was asking is to understand the reason for the sore spot — would you like me to explain? It is concerning as the location is on the lower jaw, duration more than 2 weeks." You have been through a lot lately, and as a result of that emotional toll, diet was not the best, and smoking increased." Risk factors: "Do you know how smoking and alcohol affect your oral health? They have chemicals that make abnormal changes in your body and increase absorption of harmful substances." Also stress/unhealthy diet affecting the immune system. Giant cell granuloma from constant irritation is painless, growing, whitish. Increased oral cancer risk: smoking ×2, alcohol ×6. Investigation & Management "By just looking, it's hard for me to say if this is cancer, but it has been around for this long — it's concerning. Would you like me to explain what I'm doing today?" text: Sometimes a step-father helps examine Max. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Hello, you are here due to Max's injury — what are your concerns? How did it happen?" You mentioned it happened a week ago, you brought him in today — any reason why? Was there any other injury? Bleeding around the tooth? Does he frequently injure himself? (indicates suspecting abuse) Was he supervised by an adult when he got injured? Is there any other concern besides the discolouration? Note: toddler bumps and minor injuries are common. Diagnosis & Management Diagnosis: dental concussion (injury to supporting structures) — no X-ray needed for concussion alone. "Because there's a difference in size of the teeth, I'm worried this one has gone slightly inwards — we call this intrusion." How did the cut to the lip happen? Any mobility/bite interference? With intrusion: can poke the adult tooth (dilaceration possible, review needed). Can take an X-ray to confirm intrusion. Discolouration: could be blood/bruising (colour change), or a sign of infection. Do nothing (recommended for concussion, monitor). Tooth-coloured filling — tooth-coloured but costly/bulky. X-ray only if there's intrusion. If nerve injury: pulpectomy/extraction (specialist)/space maintainer. Key facts: dentists are in a position to recognise and report abuse — sexual, physical, neglect, emotional/social. Minimum age for OPG → 3 years old, only if tracheal/fracture suspected. Mouthguard can be given once children play contact sports. Tetanus immunisation indicated if the last dose was more than 5 years ago. Review: concussion — 1 week up to 6–8 weeks; intrusion — immediate review, then check for missed injury. Maintenance for 1 week + 0.2% CHX mouthwash topically on cotton (per TG). Health promotion: "From a general health point of view, it's important to monitor the child at this age when they are playing." Recommend monitored brushing / mouthguard for contact sports. Why do I have to see a specialist? Can you give him a mouthguard? (not now, only for contact sports) Why can't you do RCT? Difference between kids' and adults' RCT? Can we do teeth whitening? (intrinsic issue) Which X-ray, and why? Amalgam Replacement (Mercury Toxicity Concern) — Mr Chen PQ-35 Module 6, Cluster 2. Worried about mercury toxicity from 8–10 year old silver fillings.

text: Not initially given: smoking/grinding/vaping. Patient & Scenario Variations: RCT on front tooth ↔ RCT on molar ↔ no RCT; smoking ↔ vaping; primary concern mercury toxicity ↔ aesthetics ↔ both. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mr/Mrs Chen, you have concerns about those fillings — could you tell me more about your concerns?" How are those fillings affecting you? Where did you read that? Diagnosis & Management There could be some secondary decay/overhanging margins present. "Which one do you want to talk about first?" (aesthetic vs health concern). "Since you are worried about health effects of mercury..." — amalgam replacement with informed consent about concerns re: mercury and the environment (being phased out). Mercury hazard concern → discuss FDA/TG guidance, environmental issue, mercury vapour, SMART protocol (Safer/Selective Amalgam Removal Technique), patient safety, environmental safety. Aesthetic concern → options: do nothing/composite/ceramic inlay-onlay/cap (gold, metal, zirconia — more aggressive prep). Composite: weaker (grinding risk), staining risk (smoker/alcohol), shorter lifespan. Grinding → recommend a splint. "Fillings that are already inside the mouth are not recommended to remove — they have good strength. Silver fillings don't have a connection with the problem you are having; when inside your tooth, a very small fraction of mercury is released, which is poorly absorbed. My concern is if we remove these fillings — that's when vapours are released. We use the SMART protocol to prevent exposure." Key Facts & References ADA guideline: no justification for removal of amalgam fillings based on health concerns alone. Amalgam fillings release a nanogram of mercury, within safe limits — the major concern is when patients inhale mercury vapours released during removal/placement. Peri-Implantitis in a Smoker (Bleeding Gums) — Mr/Mrs Dubey PQ-37 Module 6, Cluster 3. Chief complaint: bleeding gums. Peri-implantitis: 6–7mm pockets around implants; generalised 4mm pockets elsewhere; smokes 18/day. Case notes describe the patient as "resistant to quitting," "cold and non-compliant." Patient & Scenario Variations: reason for tooth loss — accident ↔ perio; blood pressure recent ↔ healthy; LGBT/undergoing hormonal treatment (variation). How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mr Dubey, you are here today as your bleeding gums are bothering you, tell me more about it." Any other concerns — pain/discomfort/bad taste/breath? "You have an implant-supported bridge in the front part, how did you lose those teeth?" Last dental visit? Oral hygiene? (interdental brush/floss — "Piksters") Last GP visit? Any medication? "Because you have bleeding gums and spaces between your implant/teeth and gums, is it OK if I ask a few questions about your social life? Do you smoke? How many? How does smoking fit into your life?" "There are a few things that might be causing this — before I come to that, what do you think might be happening?" Do you feel your implants are moving? Diagnosis & Risk Factors "Mr Dubey, there are spaces around your implant. You mentioned earlier that your dentist told you implants are for life, but in reality nothing is for life; we can never guarantee, but implants do have a good survival rate — you have to keep them well maintained." Diagnosis: peri-implantitis — destruction of bone supporting the implant. Risk factors: poor oral hygiene, no professional clean; previous gum disease (linked to earlier tooth loss); traumatic bite + grinding; smoking (lowers immunity, ↓ blood flow, dry mouth → bacteria build up and irritate gums).

text: How to Start / Questions to Ask "I'd like you to have a look inside your mouth and take this photo." "Mr Gamage, could you tell me a bit more about your pain? Pain on releasing (biting)?" Investigation & Management Extraoral — muscles, temperature, jaw movement, tension; intraoral — all teeth, wear/grinding signs; cold test, bite test (cotton roll), Fracfinder to locate the part of the tooth, probing for spaces. Post-Op Instructions for Patient on Anticoagulant (Eliquis) — Amaro, 70 Module 7, Cluster 3.

title: naz notes
text: Just had a mobile tooth #13 extracted; taking Eliquis (apixaban); anxious; smoking has caused this patient's gum disease. Notebook flags "high mortality" as a note. How to Start / Conversation "Mr Amaro, I have removed your tooth, and I am going to be discussing some of the instructions you are supposed to follow to take care of the wound. Are you comfortable the way you are sitting?" "You had some concerns — is there anything you are worried about?" "We proceeded without stopping the medication as the risk of stroke is much higher than the bleeding risk." What worries you the most? Bleeding/bruising — instructions to minimise it. "What if Panadol doesn't work? If it didn't work, we might be looking at some other cause — smoking, tell me about it?" (can cause dry socket) Management / Post-op Explanation "Eliquis makes your blood thin so that blood runs smoothly, and that's not helpful in your case as we have removed the tooth and we want the blood to fill that space and form a clot. In your case it might not happen, so we have placed a gel (haemostatic) which provides a meshwork to promote blood clotting, which eventually becomes part of your bone like normal healing." Resorbable stitches placed to hold it, will come out on their own. "Would like you to wait in the waiting room; I'll check if the bleeding has completely stopped before you go — with written instructions." Today: (1) bleeding → gel + sutures + pressure/gauze + written instructions, contact us or go to hospital if persistent; (2) numbness + Paracetamol; (3) swelling/bruising — cold pack wrapped in a towel (cannot give Ibuprofen given the anticoagulant); (4) no alcohol/smoking for the first 24 hours; (5) GP — will replace blood volume/cauterize the wound if required. Complications: dry socket (from ↓ blood flow + negative pressure from smoking — avoid anything creating heat in the mouth for the first 24–48 hours); infection. Health promotion: "Mr Amaro, you are smoking — tell me more about it? What do you like about smoking?" Written instructions provided. Smoking is a documented cause of stroke/tooth loss/dry socket — offer quitting connection, nicotine replacement, electric brush, regular hygiene review. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Which tea bag to stop bleeding? (black/green tea contains tannins) Ice pack for how long? — 20 minutes on/off, first 24 hours. How long do I stop smoking? — 48–72 hours.

title: naz notes
text: Why did you remove the tooth / why didn't you stop that medication? How will I know it's dry socket? Will I bleed to death? (no — cauterize) What is tranexamic acid? Patient & Scenario Note: patient tends to emphasise bleeding over sensitivity; previous treatment involved numbing (a complaint point). Variations: diabetes controlled ↔ uncontrolled; recently relocated; supervised neglect — possible; why is a specialist the preferred option? How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mrs Lima, we have done your examination and I'll explain the findings to you in a bit, but before that is it OK if I confirm a few things?" Can you tell me a bit more about your issue? Any specific areas? What triggers it (brushing)? Any other concerns? Tell me about your previous dental visit — what was done? Why was cleaning done? Any numbing injection? Have you been regular with dental visits? What do you do in general? Diagnosis, Risk Factors & Key Facts "Earlier we were measuring spaces between your gums and teeth — normally 2–3mm, but in your case some teeth are 4/5mm which is more than usual; some areas have shrunk away exposing the root, involving >30% of your mouth." → Generalized moderate periodontitis. "I understand it might be shocking to you, but I also want to find out what might be causing this." Risk factors: periodontitis — poor oral hygiene, irregular visits, diabetes, smoking/stress. Sensitivity — gum disease, previous scaling, aggressive brushing. Key facts: bone loss/year in high-risk cases is normally ~1mm, here 3mm in 6 months. Periodontitis affects glycaemic control bidirectionally: gram-negative perio infection → increased insulin resistance → poor glycaemic control. Always address the acute condition (bleeding) first, not the milder symptom. Gum disease usually takes years to develop but can be faster with diabetes + smoking compounding. Management "Gum disease starts between your teeth.

title: naz notes
text: Since you don't floss it can lead to build-up, and your previous dentist did a good job, but since no numbing injections were given, some areas under the gums might have been missed; any bacteria left behind can irritate your gums and bone. And you also have diabetes and smoke." "Do you know how diabetes and smoking affect your oral health?" — smoking: heat, ↓ blood flow, sticky plaque; diabetes: affects immunity, saliva, gum disease. Superficial clean today (concern: uncontrolled diabetes). Deep clean: 4–5mm pockets → me/numb, 4–6 week appointment; 5–6mm pockets → specialist (preferred), extra cost, especially at 10 cigarettes/day (Grade C). GP — for current sugar levels. Health promotion: "Me/specialist will do the treatment but you need to be part of this — oral hygiene instruction, regular review, and since you're worried about long-term teeth, quit smoking." Review 3-monthly; brochure. Questions Patients Ask Why did this happen to me? Did my dentist do a bad job? How do I raise a complaint? What will the specialist do? How can you save my teeth? Can periodontitis develop this fast? Will I lose teeth? MODULE 8 Red Set Aphthous Ulcer & Coeliac Disease — Charlette, 20 PQ-43 Module 8, Cluster 1. Ulcers inside the lips for 3 days; stress due to exams; sister has coeliac disease. Smoking mentioned recently — "came out coeliac test." Patient & Scenario Variations: 1st episode ↔ 2nd/3rd episode; minor ↔ major (fever, swelling around neck/lymph nodes); family history of ulcers positive sometimes; quit smoking recently, sometimes. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Charlette, having these ulcers could be related to your general health, or sometimes genetic factors.

title: naz notes
text: Does anybody in your family have a similar problem?" Tell me more about it — how is it affecting you? Did you do anything for the pain? How did it start? Any injury? Any vesicle (to rule out herpes)? Has it happened before? Last time, how long did it take to heal? Same place? Left scarring? Fever/swelling? Any pattern to when these happen? (oestrogen thins oral mucosa — contraceptive pills/hormonal treatment) "Because you have these ulcers and we are trying to find a cause, sometimes it can be due to hormonal changes which impact the lining of the oral cavity — is it OK if I ask a few questions?" Any medications/contraceptive pills? Any tummy issues, as your sister has coeliac? "You mentioned you are under a lot of stress due to exams — what are you doing about it?" Differential Diagnosis & Key Facts Differential (rule out, give only 2 in the exam): traumatic ulcer; recurrent aphthous ulcer; herpetic gingivostomatitis; aphthous major; cancer. Key facts: aphthous ulcers are recurrent, non-infectious, non-vesicular, immunologically-mediated; more common in females. Herpes lesions recur at the same spot each time (along a nerve distribution) — aphthous ulcers don't follow this pattern. Coeliac disease can be asymptomatic and clusters with other autoimmune diseases. Stress → increased salivary cortisol → suppresses leucocytic activity. Quitting smoking can itself cause ulcers via mucosal thinning as keratinisation reverses. Investigation & Management Extraoral — swelling (neck), fever, cheek muscles; intraoral — ulcer size/shape/texture, neighbouring teeth; photos for records; blood tests — vitamin B12/folate/zinc deficiency, coeliac antibody test (small bowel biopsy later if needed). Today: Benzydamine gel 1% (apply 2x hourly); warm saline mouthwash; GP referral; check diet (takeaway foods often implicated); check recent blood tests. Review: heals in 7–10 days; minor ulcers heal on their own, persistent ones need specialist review/biopsy; hydrocortisone 1% works in the pre-ulcer stage; major aphthous ulcers → specialist advice. Preventive: stress management, healthy diet.

title: naz notes
text: "Thanks for giving all the information, I have an idea about what could be causing this ulcer (a breach in the lining of the mucosa) — most commonly trauma (traumatic ulcer), sometimes your immune system reacting abnormally to trauma (genetic or triggered by stress/diet)." Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Why are you doing an intraoral exam? (checking for enlarged lymph nodes) Is coeliac disease contagious? Can you give me supplements? Will it go away completely? What is coeliac disease? Can I use the ointment my sister uses? Reference: aphthous ulcers article; note in the notebook on "how to handle burnout" (personal aside). Missing or Impacted Canine — Julie, 10 PQ-44 Module 8. Worried about appearance; feels her front teeth are big. Concerns: splayed teeth, missing (canine) tooth. Patient & Scenario Notebook note: "Don't say 'ugly duckling stage.'" Variation: gap increasing vs same/unchanged. Mum is sensitive about Julie being bullied — approach carefully. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mum, thanks for bringing in Julie. I have taken this photo which we will discuss." Mum, could you tell me more about the concerns Julie has? Has the gap increased recently? Does she have or had a thumb-sucking habit? How and when did she lose those baby teeth? Any history of trauma? Any other concerns? "Because you are worried about how her teeth are looking, sometimes the cause could be genetic as well — does anyone in the family have missing teeth or blocked-out teeth? What treatment was done?" There are a couple of concerns here — which one do you want me to talk about first? Gap / canine. Diagnosis, Investigation & Management Diagnosis: the gap between the centre teeth is called a midline diastema — as long as it's small (<2mm), it corrects itself when the canine comes in; other causes may apply here. Risk factors/investigation: frenum (blanch test); extra tooth; eye tooth (canine) missing or pressing against roots. Canines usually erupt around 11–12yrs — she's still within range, but a bulge should still be visible. Canine differential: impacted (stuck, genetically coded in the wrong place); ectopic (pressing laterally against roots); smaller jaw/bigger teeth (not enough space); missing completely. 3 things on OPG to determine impaction: overlap with the lateral root, vertical height, angulation. Active treatment postponed until canines erupt — this can cause spontaneous closure of the gap. Normal gap ≤2mm; >2mm might not resolve on its own.

title: naz notes
text: Investigation: extraoral — developing jaws, bones, face symmetry, lips closing, photos; intraoral — teeth, missing/spaces, bulges, decay, gums (important pre-ortho). No bulge means the tooth could be missing or stuck. X-ray needed ("not directed towards organs") — OPG gives a bigger perspective on location, angulation, height. Management: a gap <2mm is okay at this stage. If stuck, refer to an orthodontist — sometimes removing the baby tooth allows the permanent tooth to descend; specialist decides on CBCT. Health promotion: how is she maintaining hygiene (not regular with a dentist)? Future ortho treatment raises decay risk, so good hygiene habits matter now. Brochure. Questions Patients Ask I am worried about the X-ray, is it necessary? (not many X-rays required) Are we going to treat anything at this stage? What is CBCT and why is it needed? Why are teeth splayed in front? Do we need to go to the orthodontist now? What will the orthodontist do? Is this gap normal? ANUG (Acute Necrotising Ulcerative Gingivitis) — John Smith, 25 PQ-45 Module 8, Cluster 2. Very painful, bleeding gums; smokes 10/day; ulcers around the gum margins. Scenario: exam ↔ lost job (life stressor variant). How to Start / Questions to Ask "John, I have taken this photo so we can discuss it — tell me more about the pain you are experiencing, also bad taste and smell, and bleeding. Is it okay if I ask a few questions to understand your condition?" I am sorry to hear you're not able to clean/eat — how is it impacting you? Anything for the pain? Has it happened before? Onset? Fever? Swelling? Bleeding gums? How do you clean your teeth in between? Previous dental visit — why? Any changes in your routine lately (smoking/alcohol)? How's your diet? General health? Diagnosis & Pathophysiology "If you look at this photo your gums are looking red (inflamed), ulcers in between your teeth." "You have an acute condition going on called necrotising ulcerative gingivitis, and this kind of infection happens when you have a pre-existing gum disease. Are we clear so far?" Starts with bacteria already present in your mouth (fusospirochetal complex); anything that tips the balance of the immune system lets them cause damage. "Do you want me to explain what might have caused this? Even though these bacteria are present, your body is usually able to fight them." Risk factors: viral infection (immune system down); diet, smoking, stress, alcohol (dry mouth), reduced immunity masking gum disease.

title: naz notes
text: Management Today (do not notify): Debridement — removal of bacteria/pseudomembrane deposits/damaged gum tissue. Topical numbing gel → clean with cotton + mouthwash → ultrasonic instrument → irrigate with CHX/H2O2. Antibiotic — Metronidazole 400mg every 12 hourly (avoid alcohol). Pain killer — Ibuprofen + Paracetamol. Mouthwash — CHX or H2O2. Review app. (after 2 days): thorough cleaning, detailed gum exam. Specialist referral criteria: severe, immunocompromised, no response within 2 weeks, aesthetic concern, or risk of progressing to necrotising periodontitis. Health promotion: good opportunity to discuss quitting smoking; balanced diet, avoid alcohol; brochure/coping strategy for stress. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Why metronidazole and not amoxicillin? Will the gums go back to normal position? (as long as confined to the gums) Is it contagious? I've already started GP antibiotics — should I stop it? Can I use chlorhexidine regularly? Chlorhexidine kills bacteria/prevents plaque build-up; H2O2 is oxygenating, kills anaerobic bacteria. Generalized Periodontitis (ADC Handbook Case) — Mrs Wilson, 45 PQ-46 PQ-47 Module 8, Cluster 2. Ms Hawkins is her regular dentist; recently moved from Sydney; smokes 10/day; heavy plaque and calculus; generalized probing 4–3mm; regular attendee. Patient & Scenario Variations: recession vs no recession; old OPG vs newly arranged OPG; smoking vs no smoking; 4–5mm vs 5–6mm pocket depths. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mrs Wilson, I am done with examination, there are a few findings I would like to discuss with you shortly, but wanted to know your concerns first." Just need to ask a few questions related to my findings — any sensitivity/pain? Bleeding? What causes it? How do you clean your teeth in between? "Asking these questions as I am seeing something unusual here — do you want me to explain my findings and X-ray?" Diagnosis & Risk Factors Findings: normally 2–3mm between teeth and gums, here 4–5mm; deposits on X-ray, pockets. Diagnosis: affecting >30% of teeth → generalized moderate periodontitis , Stage 2, Grade C. "Mrs Wilson, it's very unlikely to have happened in the last 1 year. Gum disease generally spans over years — but I can see you are smoking, which can speed up the process. Can I ask a few questions about it?" Risk factors: smoking; family history; oral hygiene; incomplete cleaning; stress (due to recent move).

title: naz notes
text: "Do you know how smoking affects your oral health?" (dry mouth, allows bad bacteria to grow, reduces immunity). Key facts: rate of bone loss ~1mm/year in high-risk patients. Diabetes check-up recommended every 3 years in non-diabetics. "Supervised neglect" — a patient regularly attending but not correctly assessed/treated by a previous dentist. Management First step: remove deposits irritating the gums. Below-gum cleaning requires numbing, 2–4 sittings, blind procedure (may miss spots). Do nothing / scaling (superficial today) / deep cleaning (below gum). 4–5mm pockets → manage myself; no improvement → specialist referral. 5–6mm pockets → specialist (preferred, especially Grade C, >10 cigarettes/day, >2mm loss in 5 years). Review: 3 months. "Complaint response" if the old dentist retired: "If you have doubts about the care you have received, do you think you can speak to your dentist? If you allow, I can ask for your records and guide you, and you can raise your concerns." Health promotion: "I understand you are worried about losing teeth — do you know smoking can affect the outcome of any treatment we do? People who smoke have fewer chances of successful treatment." Quit line, brochure. Questions Patients Ask Is it possible gum disease developed in 1 year? What will the specialist do? How do I raise a complaint? Why did my dentist not clean back teeth? Are you guys after my money? Why should I do a blood test? Apical Root Broken While Extraction — Mr/Mrs Singh PQ-49 Module 8, Cluster 3. Pain in an upper molar (badly decayed); agreed to extraction. Apical root broke during extraction, close to the sinus. Patient & Scenario Variations: periapical shadow in broken root vs shadow on removed root; mesiobuccal root (less risk, can attempt) vs palatal root (more risk, refer to specialist). Note: avoid talking about the X-ray initially — it's for record, not to decide if you can remove the fragment. Breaking the News / 2nd Consent "Mr Singh, I would like to pause here to discuss something important with you — are you comfortable in the way you are seated? Anything I can get you?" "We had this conversation about this tooth being badly broken and about possible complications. Unfortunately, Mr Singh, while I was removing your tooth, one of the three roots has broken while removing the tooth.

title: naz notes
text: I am really sorry about it." (Let them speak and vent.) "Now I need your permission to take a new x-ray to see how the broken piece looks, so that we can discuss how to manage this and it becomes part of my records." Explanation & Management Risk factors for the fracture: decay (difficult to hold), pre-existing fracture, palatal forces, curved root. "There's a few ways we can manage this, but what are you worried about?" (weekend plans etc.) "Are you generally fit and healthy? Any medical conditions? It is very unlikely for this infection to spread." To remove: check if the root is mobile, clean and suction to see if it comes out; may need a root tip elevator. Key facts: never put RCT files in the mouth without a rubber dam. Closed extraction technique = root tip elevator/suction; open extraction technique = surgical extraction. Problems a leftover root can cause: cyst, infection, implant complications. Options: do nothing/monitor if not infected. Extraction by me — manage OAC/root-in-sinus by size (<2mm suture, >3mm buccal advancement flap/surgeon). Extraction by specialist (preferred) — antibiotics usually not needed, pain killer, post-op instructions. "Can we leave the root behind?" — if infected, must remove (preferred by specialist); if not infected, specialist advises whether it can be left; if diagnosis is necrosis, no antibiotic needed. Health promotion: nasal decongestant (oxymetazoline 0.05%) 1–2 sprays 8-hourly for 5 days; new X-ray for record; post-op instructions and review after 2 weeks. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Why did you break my root? What if the pain/infection gets worse? How will you remove the tooth? How will the specialist remove it? For an implant, will the broken fragment interfere? Will you give me antibiotics? You expect me to pay you and also the specialist? Reference: socket shield article (case selection criteria). RCT (Root Canal Treatment) Consent — Jonathan, 27 PQ-48 Module 8, Cluster 3. Irreversible pulpitis, tooth 6 (upper first molar), pain, doesn't want extraction. Patient & Scenario Variations: apical periodontitis vs spreading odontogenic infection (quick, sometimes); pulp stone vs no pulp stone (blocked canal not visible on X-ray). How to Start / Explanation "Jonathan, you are here again due to that tooth troubling you? How are you doing? I have this x-ray of your tooth...

title: naz notes
text: Tell me about your pain, have you taken anything for it?" Explain the X-ray: hole in the tooth → bacteria irritating the nerve → nerve still alive, responding to hot/cold (tooth has lost its capacity to heal). Diagnosis: acute irreversible pulpitis. Management & Consent "Have you heard about RCT? Want me to explain? In root canal treatment we remove the nerves in the tooth that are dying and replace them with filling material — gutta percha. The good thing about this procedure is more than 90% success and nothing like having your own natural teeth. But because this tooth has multiple roots, might not be possible to finish in one appointment because there are multiple canals; x-rays may be needed." Success of treatment also depends on the cap on top (separate cost), which seals the tooth. Informed consent covers: diagnosis/pathophysiology, cost, procedure, complications. Complications: if a pulp stone or blocked canal is seen on X-ray, take another radiograph to confirm. Common: pain (Ibuprofen 400mg 6–8hrly; Paracetamol 1000mg 4–6hrly); broken/fractured tooth; discolouration. Uncommon: broken/separated files; perforation/ledge; short RCT, missed/extra canals; instrumentation beyond the apex; extra/blocked canal; hypochlorite extrusion; infection spread into sinus; re-infection. "Based on the 2nd radiograph I will decide if I can do it or refer you to a specialist." If there's no pulp stone, only a blocked canal, add pulpotomy to pain management; refer after Stage 2. Procedure detail: 1st step — numb, rubber dam to isolate the tooth, remove decay, expose/remove the nerve, place medication, temporary filling. 2nd step — clean and shape the canal for obturation, then permanent filling/cap in the future (wait 3–6 weeks — risk of breakage/recontamination in the meantime). Health promotion: the only way to prevent future pain is regular review and maintaining oral hygiene. "Now that you are aware of the procedure and risks, would you like to go ahead?" Questions Patients Ask What is odontopaste? What can we do today for the pain? Is it a very painful procedure? Why do I need a cap? Are you doing the RCT yourself? Why can't it be done in one appointment? Is there any other way than RCT to save this tooth? MODULE 9 New Cases / Brown Set Denture Broke — Mr/Mrs Cooper Module 9. Denture teeth broke (made by a colleague 6 months ago); angry patient/complaint. Exam findings not given to the student: reduced vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO) and angular cheilitis.

title: naz notes
text: Lost natural teeth in an accident 30 years ago. Patient & Scenario Variations: occupation — sales vs commissioner; photo — 2/3 teeth fractured vs 6 teeth fractured (canine always fractured); sometimes grinds day and night. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mr Cooper, I can see you are upset as your denture teeth are broken and you're having constant trouble with your denture. How about we find out what may have caused this?" "Mr Cooper, do you remember what happened when these teeth chipped? (You were sleeping with your denture) — is this something you do always?" Is there a specific reason you sleep with the denture on? (don't like the sensation of teeth/gums touching) Did you have a similar problem with your previous denture? "Why did my teeth chip? I may have an answer, but what do you think happened here? First — how are we going to fix this now?" Diagnosis & Risk Factors Diagnosis: (1) reduced vertical dimension (over-closure, excessive joint pressure); (2) angular cheilitis. Broken denture risk factors: grinding, stress (busy schedule/burnout), wearing the denture at night. Angular cheilitis risk factors: reduced VDO, night wearing, nutritional deficiency. "Mr Cooper, you have had a history of dentures that keep breaking, and you had high hopes with what my colleague made for you. This one didn't fracture as it has a metal frame, but teeth are still plastic. The height of your teeth has been reduced; we call this reduced vertical dimension (additionally, you are grinding). I reached this conclusion as you have wrinkles at the corner of your lips — this is called angular cheilitis. When we make a denture we also record how your jaws meet, giving teeth a comfortable position called centric relation. If there's any discrepancy, it can lead to excessive forces and cause chipping or breakage — at night the jaws relax, and if teeth aren't set for that, there could be forces causing breakage." Management "What we can do today is fix this denture for you, so you can go back to work, but I can't guarantee a new one won't break, especially working in a stressful environment and wearing the dentures at night." For the bite issue: short term — chairside (here/low cost/today, but less strength/temporary, can't check interference) vs lab (stronger, checks bite, extra cost/time). Long term (loss of VDO, lip wrinkling) — refer to prosthodontist for overlay denture/increased bite height/implants/bridge. Instead of denture at night, recommend a Michigan splint.

title: naz notes
text: Complaint handling: "My colleague may have overlooked correcting the bite issue or not removing interferences. I am happy to have a chat with my colleague — would you be interested if I arrange a meeting with him?" Health promotion: stress management alongside denture care; practice manager route → complaint → reimburse the cost of this denture. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Can you modify my current denture? Can't afford implants — is there any other option? Natural teeth → canine guidance; denture teeth → group function. Consider sleep apnoea (oral appliance therapy) if there's no obvious cause of stress/snoring. Denture life is normally 8–10 years. MIH (Molar Incisor Hypomineralization/Hypoplasia) — Nick Henderson, 11 PQ-59 Module 9, Cluster 2. Advised extraction and GA elsewhere; sensitivity on back teeth. (Referenced age 8 as the ideal extraction age for tooth 6 to allow tooth 7 to passively take its place.) Patient & Scenario Not given: front teeth not aligned properly. Photo given: deep bite/crowding vs occlusal view. Sometimes concerns are sensitivity vs front teeth. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mrs Henderson, I have had a look inside Nick's mouth, I have some x-rays/photos — tell me about your concerns? Would it be okay for Nick to sit aside while we are having a conversation?" "Just to understand, you are concerned about tooth removal or general anaesthesia?" If teeth removal — why are we removing these teeth? "We wouldn't remove these teeth just because of sensitivity — did they tell you why?" If we were to remove his teeth, what worries you? Any major illness or medication he took while these teeth were developing? What was his age at the time (toddler)? Diagnosis & Risk Factors "Thank you for sharing this vital information. If you see this photo, front teeth (incisors) and back teeth (molars) are affected — something we call molar incisor hypomineralization (MIH). It is a time-related chronological developmental defect due to bouts of ear infection when these teeth were forming, so these teeth have compromised/less minerals and are weak in structure, making them high risk and more prone to decay." Risk factors: oral hygiene (brushing, flossing); diet — frequent snacking; irregular attendance; ear infection history; previous dental visits. Because these teeth are structurally weak and difficult to clean, they trap food and break down faster.

title: naz notes
text: Management Class II malocclusion also noted: upper jaw fully developed, lower jaw not — deep bite can be a problem later; advised orthodontic treatment around age 12 (may need to remove some teeth to create space). Wisdom teeth will take their place. Do nothing. Save and restore (GIC/composite/cap). Extract → specialist (preferred under GA rather than multiple injections). Contralateral/balancing extraction decided by specialist (paed + ortho team). Health promotion: electric brush, fluoride toothpaste and tooth mousse; diet advice; demonstrate technique. Orthodontic treatment later raises decay risk further. Questions Patients Ask & Key Facts Why GA? (multiple teeth requiring multiple injections) Does he need orthodontic treatment? Can you remove this tooth/do RCT? Should all 4 teeth be removed? Can you give white crowns? Age groups referenced: infant (1 month–1yr), toddler (1–3yrs), preschool (3–6yrs). Ideal extraction age for a compromised molar: 8.5–9.5yrs. Reference: DHSV referral criteria (Pedo/ADJ). Combination Syndrome — Mr Cavalli Module 9, Cluster 2. Wants an upper complete denture / lower removable partial denture; Grade II mobility on teeth 33/43; old denture 10 years old. Diagnosed with osteoporosis, referred for clearance; prefers to travel overseas for a 2nd opinion and treatment. Patient & Scenario Variations: OPG sometimes given; clearance needed vs not asked. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Could you tell me more about your existing dentures? 10 years old, loose, affecting diet — don't wear the lower one, can chew with lower front teeth." "I did notice you have a few remaining teeth in your lower jaw — any concerns with those?" How do you maintain your teeth and denture in general? "You have been diagnosed with osteoporosis — did your GP mention their treatment plan for you? Do you know how the medicine used to treat osteoporosis affects you?" "You mentioned your denture is loose — how long has it been like this? Do you know why it might have happened? Do you want me to explain?" Diagnosis Dentures normally last 8–10 years as they sit on bone that slowly wears away; osteoporosis (which also weakens bone) compounds this. Combination syndrome — lower front teeth against the upper complete denture exert a lot of force in the front upper jaw, causing more bone loss there, and gums become loose/flabby; as the jaw closes forward, the front part of the denture tilts upward, and lower teeth become mobile/supra-erupt. Denture stomatitis.

title: naz notes
text: Risk factors — combination syndrome: lower anterior teeth against an upper complete denture; osteoporosis; old dentures. Denture stomatitis: ill-fitting denture, poor hygiene, nutritional deficiency, periodontal disease. Related reference: MRONJ. Signs of combination syndrome: loss of bone in the anterior maxilla; overgrowth of the tuberosities; lower anterior teeth over-erupt/intrude into the opposing arch; loss of bone under the lower denture. Overseas Treatment Discussion & Management Overseas elective treatment is not recommended — treatment may be compromised, records/details may not be available, oral health can't be achieved in a single episode and needs regular maintenance; insurance won't cover it (including the treating dentist's own indemnity if issues arise). "Any questions so far? Do you have a preference in terms of treatment option? [If patient wants only a top-jaw solution] I can give you a denture for your top jaw with a special technique because those gums are loose/mobile. If you continue using only an upper denture, the bone underneath will get worse and you might need surgery to correct it. I recommend you think about replacing those back teeth, as we need to shift biting forces backwards." Keep lower teeth / upper complete denture — "can't give you clearance as this puts you at risk of MRONJ." Extract lower teeth (recommended) — RPD (less expensive, teeth can be added, but loose teeth aren't good support) vs overdenture/implant-supported (preferred, but cost) vs complete denture. Refer to: GP, prosthodontist (if emotionally attached to teeth, forces transferred, or cost is a factor). Health promotion: clean new dentures with soap and water (toothpaste is abrasive, causes scratches); don't leave dentures soaking in water overnight (fungi thrive); check with GP for nutritional deficiency (can cause denture stomatitis). Questions Patients Ask What is the special impression technique for the upper jaw? Is combination syndrome a disease? Is there another name for it? Concern about overseas treatment being expensive long-term due to repeated travel for maintenance. Mr/Mrs Caldarin — Patient Wants a 3rd Opinion (RCT Tooth, MRONJ Risk, Smoking) Module 9, Cluster 2. Tooth 25: RCT with voids present; on Fosamax 10mg for osteoporosis. Smoking/diabetes status not given — to be elicited. Patient & Scenario Scenario: post & core removed → RCT + core again (re-treatment cycle). Patient's concern today: chipped tooth, food impaction.

title: naz notes
text: Long-term prognosis of the tooth is questionable — removal is worth considering. "Do nothing" is one option. How to Start / Questions to Ask "Mrs Caldarin, I have taken the X-ray of the tooth troubling you and I also had a brief look inside your mouth — would it be OK if I go through your concerns, and we can then explore together what is best for you?" "If I may ask, what is the reason for getting so many opinions for this tooth?" — patient felt something chipped off this morning. Any pain or discomfort? Was this the reason for seeking advice? Food getting stuck there? How do you clean your teeth, especially that area? Generally, are you regular with your dentist? You mentioned you have osteoporosis and are taking medication for it — tell me more? Any other medical condition I should be aware of? Diagnosis & Risk Factors "Thanks for providing all the information. We have some answers to why you have that issue — would you like me to explain what is causing this, or what I suggest for managing this tooth first?" Radiograph: "You can see a black shadow on this tooth" → diagnosis: secondary dental decay (coronal seal breakdown). Risk factors: no cap/leakage around the filling (coronal seal failure); not cleaning between teeth; irregular oral hygiene review; MRONJ risk, diabetes, smoking duration (modifying/associated factors). Patient autonomy note flagged in the margin: "Why can't you remove it if you want me to?" / "If you take advice, if you remove it" — patient concern about removing teeth/implants and worry about health. Management (also covers a follow-on MRONJ/restorative-failure page in the same notebook section) "We have some options to go about this — do you have any preference? Option 1: save the tooth; Option 2: remove it. Which one do you want me to talk about first?" Option 1 (save the tooth): re-RCT by a specialist (endodontist), possibly + crown lengthening if the decay/voids require redesigning gum and bone for the new cap margin.

title: naz notes
text: Disadvantage: cost, lower success rate, and surgery for crown lengthening — "You are taking Fosamax — this medication prevents your bone from breaking down, but when we do any surgery you might end up with an exposed area of bone for longer than 8 weeks, which we call MRONJ." Option 2 (remove the tooth): by the dentist or specialist (recommended, atraumatic extraction) — "Talk to your GP about the best time to do it, or temporarily stop the medication (GP decides)." A drug holiday, or timing the procedure with a low serum concentration of the drug, is suggested to reduce MRONJ risk. Health promotion: regular review; smoking cessation; brochure on caring for teeth while on this medication. Key Facts Learn to differentiate "at risk" from "Stage 0" MRONJ. Smoking delays healing (reduces blood supply); diabetes lowers immunity; RCT-treated teeth are more prone to decay. Reference: Odell Table 68.2 (MRONJ/restorative failure). Sourced from the same candidate's handwritten ADC prep notebook as Exam Craft , transcribed by AI vision. A handful of faint or water-damaged pages (e.g. an RPD/flabby-ridge case in Module 9) couldn't be transcribed reliably and were left out rather than guessed at. Personal exam prep, not official ADC content — always verify anything clinical against TG4 or a current reference.

title: odell pearls
text: Clinical Problem Solving, cross-referenced to what you'll actually be asked. Odell's Clinical Problem Solving in Dentistry (4th ed., Elsevier) is 75 worked cases of real clinical reasoning — history, examination, differential, investigation, management, all laid out the way an examiner thinks. We went through it looking specifically for cases that sharpen a station in this bank, and pulled out the facts, thresholds, and quotable lines that are genuinely worth knowing cold — not a chapter summary, a distillation of what would actually move your mark. Each section below names the Odell case it's drawn from and the OSCE Coach station(s) it sharpens, so you can go read the original if you want the full worked reasoning. 🦷 Caries risk & restorative High caries risk & diet counselling Odell Case 1 — A High-Caries-Rate/High-Risk Patient · PQ-2, PQ-60 (Caries Risk Assessment, 8-Year-Old) "High caries risk" has a working definition worth quoting: more than 2 new/active lesions in 2 years. The gold-standard diet history is a 4-day written diary — 2 weekdays + 2 weekend days — not a 24-hour verbal recall (memory is unreliable, and weekday/weekend patterns differ). WHO guidance: free sugars should be <10% of total energy , roughly 50g/day (18kg/year) . Frequency of exposure matters as much as total amount. Watch for hidden-sugar foods parents don't think to mention: baked beans, breakfast cereal, tomato ketchup, "plain" biscuits. A genuinely useful patient-facing line: damage to enamel continues for up to an hour after a sugary food or drink (the Stephan curve, without needing the jargon). Treatment sequencing that examiners like to hear stated explicitly: immediate (pain/drainage) → stabilisation (temporary restorations, all quadrants) → prevention → definitive restoration → recall , in that order — prevention starts alongside stabilisation, not after. If a sinus is present and the source tooth is ambiguous, a gutta percha point traced into the sinus tract on radiograph identifies the offending tooth.

title: odell pearls
text: For diet counselling framing: COM-B (capability, opportunity, motivation, behaviour) and GPS (goal-setting, planning, self-reflection) are named behaviour-change models — dropping the name shows structure, not just "eat less sugar." Deep caries, pulpitis, and minimally invasive excavation Odell Case 9 — A Deep Carious Lesion · PQ-52 (Vague Pain, Interproximal Caries), any station with a pulpitis differential Classic reversible pulpitis : brief pain episodes triggered by hot/cold/sweet, fading slowly, no pain on biting, no tenderness to percussion . Pain on biting or percussion tenderness points toward periapical involvement instead. Strong line for a management explanation: pulpitis does not respond to analgesics — the treatment is removing the cause (caries), not painkillers. Useful when a patient asks "can't you just give me something for the pain." Eugenol-containing temporary materials are obtundent (genuinely pain-relieving) but must not be used if the definitive restoration will be bonded composite — eugenol inhibits resin polymerisation/bonding. Caries dentine has two zones: infected (superficial + bacterial penetration — must be removed) and affected/demineralised (deeper, structurally intact, can remineralise — can be left over a vital pulp). Clinical excavation endpoint is a texture, not a colour: dentine that is "scratchy and sticky" (leathery) to a sharp probe . Caries detector dyes are unreliable — they overstain and drive unnecessary excavation; largely superseded. Stepwise excavation (removing caries in two stages 6–9 months apart) is now considered unnecessary by current evidence — one-stage selective/minimally-invasive removal with a well-sealed adhesive restoration is preferred. Rubber dam is not just moisture control — it's infection control that protects a possible future RCT's prognosis if the pulp is exposed. Medico-legal pearl worth remembering generally: when a minimally-invasive approach is used, document that it was discussed and offered as an alternative to full excavation — "ignorance of the technique is not a defence." Cracked tooth syndrome — pain on biting Odell Case 11 — Pain On Biting · PQ-52 (Vague Pain, Interproximal Caries), any "sharp pain on biting only" presentation The signature history: sharp, electric-shock pain, poorly localized, only on biting or releasing biting pressure — not triggered by hot/cold.

title: odell pearls
text: This pattern alone should move a cracked cusp/tooth to the top of the differential over pulpitis or periodontal pain. Differential to state out loud: cracked cusp, electro-galvanic pain (dissimilar occluding metals), acute periodontitis from a high spot, and — rarely — trigeminal neuralgia if no dental cause is found. Always ask about bruxism/clenching — nocturnal parafunction is the classic predisposing factor, and partners often know about it when the patient doesn't .
