text: KEY POINTS ✅ Identifies overnight denture wear and poor hygiene as primary local risk factors for denture stomatitis ✅ Asks about and correctly interprets HbA1c 8.2% as poorly controlled diabetes contributing to candidal susceptibility ✅ Diagnoses Newton's Type II denture stomatitis and explains the multifactorial aetiology including xerostomia and hyperglycaemia ✅ Prescribes miconazole oromucosal gel 2% with correct instructions for application to both denture fitting surface and palatal mucosa ✅ Recommends GP liaison for diabetes optimisation and explains that a new denture should only be constructed after infection resolution and improved glycaemic control KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "Mrs Walsh, thank you for coming in — before we talk about a new denture, I want to understand exactly what's been going on with this one, and with your mouth underneath it." Why it works: Signals you won't just reflexively remake the denture — sets up the real diagnostic agenda (hygiene, candida) immediately. Clinical Authority An HbA1c of 8.2% indicates poorly controlled diabetes — this impairs neutrophil function and cell-mediated immunity, significantly increasing susceptibility to oral candidal infection. This is Newton's Type II denture stomatitis — diffuse erythema of the denture-bearing mucosa — most commonly caused by Candida albicans proliferating in the biofilm on the fitting surface of the denture. Miconazole oromucosal gel 2% should be applied to the fitting surface of the denture before insertion and directly to the palatal mucosa four times daily for a minimum of four weeks, continuing for two weeks after symptoms resolve. Wearing a denture overnight prevents the palatal mucosa from recovering and maintains continuous contact with the fungal reservoir — cessation of overnight wear is non-negotiable as part of treatment. A new denture should not be constructed until the infection has fully resolved and glycaemic control has improved — ideally HbA1c below 7% — otherwise the new denture will become reinfected and treatment will fail. Curveball Deflectors Patient says: 'I have worn my denture to bed for 20 years and never had a problem before — why do I need to take it out now?' → Acknowledge her long habit without dismissing it, then explain: 'I completely understand it feels normal to you after all these years.

text: The difference now is that your blood sugar levels are higher than ideal, which means your body's defences against infection are not as strong as they used to be. The denture is acting like a home for the fungus — if it stays in overnight, the fungus keeps growing and the palate never gets a chance to recover. Taking it out at night is one of the most important things we can do to help this heal.' Candidate prescribes antifungal medication without addressing denture hygiene or overnight wear → This is a red flag. The examiner expects the candidate to recognise that antifungal therapy alone will fail if the denture remains a fungal reservoir. The correct approach is to address denture hygiene and overnight wear first, then layer in pharmacological treatment. I can see you are having some discomfort and I want to make sure I understand everything that is going on so we can sort this out together. Can I ask you a few questions first? How do you clean your denture at the moment — do you soak it in anything overnight, or use a denture cleaning tablet? I also want to ask about your general health — I understand you have diabetes. Are you taking any medication for that, and do you know what your last blood sugar reading or HbA1c result was? Have you noticed your mouth feeling dry at all? I noticed you mentioned using boiled lollies — can you tell me a bit more about that?' Candidate listens actively and notes: denture worn 24 hours a day, cleaned only occasionally with toothpaste, never soaked. HbA1c 8.2% three months ago — poorly controlled. Dry mouth present. Boiled lollies used as a coping strategy for xerostomia — a significant candidal risk factor due to sucrose exposure. No drug allergies. STAGE 2: Diagnosis and Explanation 'Mrs Walsh, based on what you have told me and what I can see in your mouth, I believe you have a fungal infection called oral thrush — or more specifically, something called denture stomatitis. It is causing the redness and soreness on the roof of your mouth.

title: index
text: This is actually quite common, but in your case several things have come together to cause it. The denture is acting like a home for the fungus — especially because it stays in overnight and is not being soaked regularly. Your blood sugar levels being a little higher than ideal at the moment also means your body is not fighting off infections as easily as it normally would. And the dry mouth you have been experiencing reduces the natural protection your saliva provides. The good news is that this is very treatable, and I am going to go through everything we need to do step by step.' Candidate clearly names Newton's Type II denture stomatitis and explains the multifactorial aetiology — linking HbA1c 8.2%, xerostomia, overnight denture wear, and poor hygiene — without using jargon. This demonstrates the systemic-oral link the examiner is looking for. STAGE 3: Non-Pharmacological Management 'The first and most important thing I need you to do is to stop sleeping with your denture in from tonight. I know that might feel strange at first, but it is essential — the palate needs time to breathe and recover. When you take it out at night, please rinse it under water, brush it gently with a soft brush — not toothpaste, as that can scratch the surface — and then soak it overnight in a denture cleaning solution, like Polident or Steradent tablets dissolved in water. This will kill the fungus on the denture itself. I also want to gently suggest that the boiled lollies, while I understand they help with the dry mouth, are feeding the fungus with sugar. I would like to suggest some sugar-free alternatives — there are also saliva substitute sprays and gels available from the pharmacy that can help with the dryness without the sugar.' Candidate addresses all local risk factors: overnight wear cessation, correct denture cleaning technique, soaking regimen, and dietary modification. Recommends sugar-free saliva substitutes as a TGA-available alternative to boiled lollies. STAGE 4: Pharmacological and Long-Term Management 'I am also going to prescribe you a gel called Daktarin Oral Gel — it is an antifungal medication. I would like you to apply a small amount to the inside surface of your denture — the part that sits against your palate — before you put it in each morning, and also dab a little directly onto the roof of your mouth. You will do this four times a day for four weeks. It is important to keep going for the full course even if things feel better sooner.

I would also strongly recommend you make an appointment with your GP to discuss your blood sugar levels — getting your HbA1c closer to the target range, ideally below seven percent, will make a real difference to how well your mouth heals and how well any future dental treatment goes. I would like to see you back in two to four weeks to check how things are improving.' PQ-4 Extraction Planning for a Patient on Denosumab and Warfarin Station 4 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management) CANDIDATE BRIEF Mr John Smith is a 67 year old patient, attended your surgery today complaining of a swelling and tooth mobility in the lower right side. After examination, you have noticed that the lower right second molar has grade 3 mobility and abscess related to that tooth. The patient has a past medical history of Myocardial infarction, he also has Hypertension for which he is taking atenolol and warfarin. The patient also complains of hypothyroidism for which he is taking thyroxine, and osteoporosis for which he is taking calcium and denosumab iv injection only two days ago. He has also been taking panadeine forte. Manage patients concern regarding the swelling and mobile 45. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Introduction and History (0–3 min) Greet Mr Smith, acknowledge his pain and anxiety. Take a structured medication history: confirm denosumab dose (60 mg SC), frequency (6-monthly), duration (3 years), and that the last injection was only two days ago . Ask about warfarin — indication, dose, and most recent INR. Ask about all other medications (atenolol, thyroxine, Panadeine Forte).

title: index
text: INFLECTION 1 — The two-day interval since denosumab injection is the critical pivot: this dramatically elevates MRONJ risk and changes the management pathway from routine to specialist-liaison required. Stage 2 — Examination Findings and Diagnosis (3–5 min) Explain findings in plain language: the lower right back molar has a severe infection and is Grade 3 mobile — it cannot be saved and requires removal. Confirm periapical pathology on radiograph. Stage 3 — Risk Explanation and Consent (5–9 min) Explain MRONJ in patient-friendly terms: "Your bone injection helps keep your bones strong, but it can sometimes make it harder for the jawbone to heal after a tooth is removed — this is a rare but serious risk we need to discuss." Explain warfarin management: no need to stop, INR must be checked and confirmed ≤3.5–4.0; local haemostatic measures will be used. INFLECTION 2 — Incorrectly advising the patient to stop warfarin is a common and serious error that examiners will penalise. Stage 4 — Management Plan and Specialist Liaison (9–12 min) Given the very recent denosumab injection, discuss temporising: drain abscess acutely, prescribe antibiotics (amoxicillin 500 mg TDS or clindamycin if penicillin-allergic), and defer definitive extraction pending GP/specialist consultation. If extraction proceeds, outline atraumatic technique, primary closure, antimicrobial cover, and close follow-up. Document consent discussion thoroughly.

title: index
text: KEY POINTS ✅ Denosumab details must be elicited: 60 mg SC, 6-monthly, 3 years duration, last dose only 2 days ago — this is the highest-risk scenario for MRONJ ✅ Warfarin does NOT need to be ceased for simple extraction if INR ≤3.5–4.0; local haemostatic measures (sutures, Surgicel, tranexamic acid mouthwash) are sufficient ✅ MRONJ must be explained in plain language and documented as part of informed consent — patient must understand the risk before any extraction proceeds ✅ Given the 2-day post-injection window, specialist/GP liaison is mandatory before definitive extraction; temporising with drainage and antibiotics is the safer immediate step ✅ CTX testing is no longer recommended as a standalone risk-stratification tool in current Australian guidance and should not be used to clear or delay treatment in isolation KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "Mr Smith, I can see you're uncomfortable — before I explain the tooth, I need to run through everything you're taking, because two of your medications directly change how safely we can treat you today." Why it works: Flags medication-safety stakes before the exam even starts, rather than as an afterthought. Clinical Authority Warfarin does not need to be stopped for a simple dental extraction provided the INR is within the therapeutic range and confirmed at or below 3.5 to 4.0 — we manage bleeding risk locally with sutures, oxidised cellulose such as Surgicel, and tranexamic acid mouthwash. Denosumab — brand name Prolia — is a RANK-L inhibitor that suppresses osteoclast activity. Unlike bisphosphonates, it does not permanently bind to bone, but the risk of MRONJ is still clinically significant, particularly in the period immediately following an injection. With the last dose given only two days ago, this patient is at elevated risk and specialist liaison is required before we proceed with definitive extraction. Current Australian guidance, including position statements from the Australian Dental Association and relevant specialist bodies, no longer supports using CTX — the C-terminal telopeptide blood test — as a reliable standalone predictor of MRONJ risk. We do not use it in isolation to clear or delay treatment.

title: index
text: My immediate management would be to address the acute infection today — incision and drainage if fluctuant, and prescribe antibiotics such as amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for five days — and then liaise with the patient's GP or treating specialist before scheduling the definitive extraction, to discuss the timing relative to the denosumab injection cycle. If we do proceed to extraction, the MRONJ prevention protocol includes an atraumatic technique, primary closure of the socket, perioperative antimicrobial cover, avoidance of sharp bony edges, and close review at one week and four weeks post-operatively. Curveball Deflectors Patient says: 'My doctor told me to stop my warfarin before any dental work — should I stop it now?' → Reassure the patient clearly and confidently: 'That advice is outdated for simple dental procedures. Current guidelines recommend that we do not stop warfarin for a straightforward extraction, because stopping it actually increases your risk of a serious blood clot. Instead, we confirm your INR is in a safe range — ideally checked within 24 to 72 hours of the procedure — and we use local measures like stitches and a special dressing in the socket to control any bleeding. I will coordinate with your GP to confirm your INR before we proceed.' Examiner or simulated specialist asks: 'Did you consider ordering a CTX blood test to assess MRONJ risk before proceeding?' → Acknowledge the question and demonstrate current knowledge: 'CTX testing was previously used to help risk-stratify patients on antiresorptive therapy, but current Australian guidance no longer supports it as a reliable standalone predictor of MRONJ risk. A low CTX result should not be used to clear a patient for extraction, nor should a borderline result be used to indefinitely delay necessary treatment. My risk assessment is based on the clinical picture — the drug class, dose, duration, timing of the last injection, and the extent of the planned procedure — combined with specialist liaison where indicated, as in this case.' ✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ► STAGE 1: Introduction and Medication History "Good morning Mr Smith, I'm Dr [Name]. I can see you're in some discomfort today — I want to make sure we look after you properly. Before I explain what's happening with that tooth, I'd like to ask you a few questions about your health and the medications you're taking, if that's okay.

text: Can you tell me all the medications you're currently on?" Listen as patient volunteers medications. Specifically probe: "You mentioned a bone injection — can you tell me the name of it? Then ask: "You're also on warfarin — do you know what dose you take, and have you had a recent blood test to check your INR level?" Confirm INR result and therapeutic range. Document all medications: atenolol, warfarin, thyroxine, calcium, denosumab, Panadeine Forte. STAGE 2: Explain Findings and Diagnosis "Mr Smith, I've had a look at your tooth and the X-ray. The lower right back molar has a significant infection around the root — you can see this dark shadow on the X-ray — and the tooth is very loose, what we call Grade 3 mobility. Unfortunately, this tooth is not saveable. The infection is the cause of your swelling and pain, and the tooth will need to come out. I want to be upfront with you about that." Show radiograph to patient. Confirm periapical radiolucency. Explain that the tooth cannot be root-treated or restored due to the degree of mobility and infection. Transition to risk discussion. STAGE 3: Informed Consent — MRONJ and Bleeding Risk "Before we go ahead, I need to explain two important risks specific to you. The first relates to your bone injection — Prolia. This medication works by slowing down the cells that break down bone, which is great for your osteoporosis, but it can sometimes make it harder for the jawbone to heal after a tooth is removed. This is called medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw — a rare but serious condition where the bone doesn't heal properly. Because your last injection was only two days ago, your risk is higher than usual, and I want to speak with your GP or specialist before we proceed with the extraction, to make sure we're doing this at the safest possible time and in the safest possible way." "The second risk is related to your warfarin. I want to reassure you — you do not need to stop your warfarin before this procedure. Stopping it could actually put you at risk of a blood clot, which is far more dangerous. Instead, we'll confirm your INR is in a safe range, and we'll use stitches and a special dressing in the socket to control any bleeding. We can also give you a mouthwash called tranexamic acid to help with clotting." Document consent discussion in notes.

Arrange GP/specialist liaison letter today. Schedule extraction appointment with MRONJ prevention protocol: atraumatic technique, primary closure, perioperative antimicrobial cover, review at 1 week and 4 weeks. text: STAGE 2: Explaining the Risks — MRONJ and Bleeding "Mr Smith, I want to be honest with you about two things we need to think carefully about. The first is your denosumab. Because warfarin thins your blood, there is a risk of increased bleeding after the extraction. However, the good news is that current guidelines actually recommend we keep you on your warfarin — stopping it could put you at risk of a clot or a stroke, which is far more dangerous. As long as your INR is within a safe range on the day, we can proceed safely with some extra precautions." Explain MRONJ in lay terms. Address 'jaw bone rot' fear directly and empathetically. PQ-9 Patient Mid-RCT Requesting Extraction Instead Station 8 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors CANDIDATE BRIEF Mr Argenti is attending your clinic today and complaining of severe pain coming from one of the tooth on the top left side. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Acknowledge Before You Assess (0–1 min) This station looks like an endodontic case and is not one — the pain is non-odontogenic maxillary sinusitis driven by untreated hay fever, and everything the station rewards flows from the candidate resisting the pull toward the tooth. text: INFLECTION 1 — Agreeing to extract, or even conceding the tooth is the likely source, at this stage is an immediate fail regardless of how the rest of the station is handled. Here it is unchanged — the RCT made no difference at all. INFLECTION 2 — This single question is the discriminator the whole case is built on; candidates who never ask it default toward extraction. Stage 3 — Draw Out the Hidden Sinus History (3–5 min) He will not volunteer it. Stage 4 — Investigate and Interpret Correctly (5–7 min) Percussion is diffusely tender across several upper left teeth, not one localised offender — that non-localisation is itself the finding. PQ-10 Peg Lateral Incisor — Explain and Plan Station 9 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management) CANDIDATE BRIEF Miss Nguyen is a new patient at your clinic, attending today complaining about the appearance of her front tooth. She works in the pub and her partner thinks she has vampire tooth. MH; patient has anxiety in general and taking diazepam 10mg twice/day. Diagnose and manage patient concern. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Rapport and Concern Elicitation (0–2 min) Greet Miss Nguyen warmly. Ask open-ended questions: "Can you tell me in your own words what's been bothering you about your smile?" Acknowledge her self-consciousness without minimising it. Stage 3 — Treatment Options (4–8 min) Present three options in order of invasiveness: (1) Composite resin build-up — conservative, reversible, minimal preparation, ~$200–$400/tooth; (2) Porcelain veneers — superior aesthetics, 10–15 year longevity, minimal irreversible enamel reduction, ~$1,500–$2,500/tooth; (3) Crowns — not indicated here due to excessive tooth reduction required. INFLECTION 2 — Recommending crowns for peg laterals is a common error; examiners will penalise this. Stage 4 — Shared Decision-Making and Safety Netting (8–10 min) Address her concern about damaging teeth directly. Recommend composite as a reversible first step. Acknowledge her insurance may assist. Offer a written treatment plan and a follow-up appointment. Given her diazepam use, note that anxiolysis is already managed medically but ensure she has support attending appointments.

text: KEY POINTS ✅ Identifies bilateral peg lateral incisors (12 and 22) as a developmental anomaly — not disease or neglect ✅ Notes diazepam 10mg BD for anxiety and adapts communication style accordingly — calm, unhurried, non-alarmist ✅ Presents composite resin build-up as the conservative, reversible, first-line option with approximate Australian cost range ✅ Explains porcelain veneers accurately — minimal but irreversible enamel reduction, 10–15 year longevity — and correctly excludes full crowns as disproportionate ✅ Involves patient in shared decision-making, directly addresses fear of damaging natural teeth, and offers a follow-up treatment planning appointment KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "Thank you for coming in — before we look at anything, I'd love to hear in your own words what's been on your mind about your smile." Clinical Authority Peg lateral incisors result from a developmental anomaly of the permanent dentition — the tooth bud fails to fully differentiate, producing a conical or peg-shaped crown with normal root morphology. Composite resin build-up for peg laterals is considered additive and reversible — no enamel preparation is required in most cases, preserving the full biological width of the natural tooth. Porcelain veneers require approximately 0.3–0.5 mm of enamel reduction on the labial surface — this is irreversible but minimal, and the preparation is typically confined to enamel. Full coverage crowns are contraindicated as a primary treatment for peg lateral incisors in otherwise healthy dentitions due to the disproportionate sacrifice of sound tooth structure. Curveball Deflectors Patient asks: 'Will veneers ruin my teeth? I've heard they grind them down to nothing.' → Validate the concern: 'That's a really common worry and it's great you asked. For veneers, we remove a very thin layer — about the thickness of a contact lens — from the front surface only. We keep as much of your natural tooth as possible. Compare that to a crown, which we wouldn't recommend here, where we'd need to remove much more.

STAGE 2: Explaining the Condition "So what I can see — and what the X-rays confirm — is that the two teeth on either side of your front teeth, called your lateral incisors, didn't fully develop to their normal size. STAGE 3: Treatment Options "There are a few ways we can improve the appearance of these teeth, and I want to walk you through them so you can decide what feels right for you. The first option — and the one I'd suggest starting with — is a composite build-up.

text: That's where we use a tooth-coloured material, similar to a filling, and carefully shape it around your existing tooth to make it look like a full-sized tooth. The great thing is we don't need to drill or remove any of your natural tooth at all. It's completely reversible, and in Australia it typically costs around $200 to $400 per tooth. The result looks very natural and can last several years with good care. The second option is a porcelain veneer — a very thin ceramic shell that's custom-made and bonded to the front of the tooth. text: PQ-11 Generalised Periodontitis With Replacement Options Station 10 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management) CANDIDATE BRIEF Miss Luiz is a 55 yr old patient, attending your clinic today complaining of pain, bleeding gums and mobility of left lateral incisor (22). OPG given with boneless around most of the teeth and lateral has boneless up to 90%. Perio chart provided with probing depth of 7-8mm around some of the teeth. MH: she is taking thyroxine for hypothyroidism, bone pain and coeliac disease and taking calcium, vitamin D for bone. Patient wanted to know about replacement option and how we can prevent these long term. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Establish rapport and confirm concerns (0–2 min) Greet Miss Luiz, confirm her presenting complaints (pain, bleeding, mobile tooth 22), and acknowledge her concerns about keeping her teeth. Confirm medical history: hypothyroidism (thyroxine), coeliac disease, calcium and vitamin D supplementation. INFLECTION 1 — Recognise that coeliac disease and hypothyroidism can impair bone metabolism and healing; this affects prognosis and implant planning. Stage 2 — Explain diagnosis using OPG and perio chart (2–5 min) Use the OPG to show generalised bone loss. Explain that tooth 22 has 90% bone loss and Grade 3 mobility — it cannot be saved and must be extracted. Explain that several other teeth have 7–8 mm pockets indicating active, advanced disease. Use plain language: "The bone that holds your teeth like a fence post in the ground has been dissolving away." Stage 3 — Address smoking and disease control (5–8 min) Explain smoking is a major risk factor for periodontitis and implant failure. Offer Quitline referral (13 7848). Outline initial periodontal therapy: full-mouth debridement, oral hygiene instruction, and reassessment at 8–12 weeks. INFLECTION 2 — Candidates who skip disease stabilisation before discussing replacements will lose marks; disease must be controlled first. Stage 4 — Present replacement options with pros/cons (8–12 min) Present three options: (1) Removable partial denture — affordable (~$1,500–2,500), non-invasive, but less comfortable and aesthetic; (2) Dental implant — most functional, ~$4,000–6,000 per implant, requires bone volume, smoking cessation, and 6–12 month timeline; (3) No replacement for posterior teeth — acceptable short-term but risks drifting, over-eruption, and chewing difficulty.

text: Stage 5 — Staged treatment plan and follow-up (12–15 min) Summarise staged plan: initial therapy → extraction of tooth 22 → healing (8–12 weeks) → interim denture if needed → definitive replacement. Arrange next appointment. Provide written information and answer questions. KEY POINTS ✅ Explains generalised periodontitis in plain language using OPG and perio chart — bone loss described as loss of tooth support ✅ Identifies tooth 22 (and any other hopeless teeth) as non-restorable due to >90% bone loss and Grade 3 mobility, requiring extraction ✅ Addresses smoking as a critical modifiable risk factor for periodontal disease and implant failure, and offers Quitline referral (13 7848) ✅ Outlines staged treatment: initial periodontal therapy and disease stabilisation BEFORE any definitive replacement discussion ✅ Presents all three replacement options (RPD, implant, no replacement) with realistic pros, cons, and Australian cost estimates, involving patient in shared decision-making KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "I can see you're dealing with quite a bit of discomfort — before I explain what I've found, can I just confirm a couple of things about your health, since they may well be connected?" Why it works: Signals early that her medical history — not just her gums — is central to the diagnosis here. Clinical Authority Tooth 22 has approximately 90% bone loss with Grade 3 mobility — by definition this tooth is hopeless and extraction is indicated; there is no periodontal or restorative treatment that can predictably retain it. Smokers have a two- to three-fold increased risk of periodontal disease progression and implant failure rates are significantly higher — up to 20% higher than non-smokers — which is why smoking cessation is not optional, it is a prerequisite for implant success. We must stabilise the periodontal disease first — placing an implant into an uncontrolled periodontal environment risks peri-implantitis, which is essentially periodontitis around the implant and can cause implant loss. Coeliac disease can impair calcium and vitamin D absorption, which affects bone density and healing — this is relevant to implant osseointegration and we may need to liaise with her physician before proceeding.

text: The reassessment appointment at 8–12 weeks after active periodontal therapy is critical — we need to see pocket depth reduction and resolution of bleeding on probing before we can classify the disease as stable and plan definitive replacements. Curveball Deflectors Patient says: 'Can't you just pull the wobbly tooth and put an implant in straight away? I don't want to wait months.' → Acknowledge her frustration and desire for a quick solution. Explain that placing an implant immediately into a mouth with active, uncontrolled periodontitis is like building a house on unstable ground — the infection around the remaining teeth can spread to the implant site and cause it to fail. The 8–12 week stabilisation phase protects her investment and dramatically improves the chance of long-term implant success. Offer an interim partial denture to address aesthetics during the healing phase so she is not without a tooth. Candidate jumps straight to implant discussion without addressing periodontal disease control or smoking first. → This is the most common error in this station. The examiner will likely prompt: 'Is there anything you would want to address before planning the implant?' The correct pivot is to return to disease stabilisation: 'Before we can consider any replacement option, we need to get the gum disease under control — otherwise any replacement we place is at high risk of failing. That means a course of deep cleaning, improving your home care routine, and ideally stopping smoking.' ✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ► STAGE 1: Rapport, History Confirmation, and Diagnosis Explanation "Miss Luiz, thank you for coming in today. I can see you're having quite a bit of discomfort, and I want to make sure we address everything properly. You've mentioned pain, bleeding gums, and that wobbly front tooth — those are all really important concerns and I'm glad you came in. Before I explain what's going on, can I just confirm a couple of things about your health? You're taking thyroxine for your thyroid, and calcium and vitamin D — is that right? text: "So I've had a good look at your X-ray and the measurements we took of your gum pockets today, and I want to explain what we're seeing. You have a condition called periodontitis — that's a serious gum infection where bacteria living under the gumline have been slowly dissolving the bone that holds your teeth in place. Think of your teeth like fence posts — the bone is the ground they sit in. When that ground erodes away, the posts become loose. On your X-ray, I can see that most of your teeth have lost a significant amount of that supporting bone. The wobbly tooth at the front here — your upper left lateral incisor — has lost about 90% of its bone support. I'm really sorry to tell you this, but that tooth cannot be saved. It will need to come out." Point to tooth 22 on the OPG. Allow the patient to process this. Acknowledge any emotional response before continuing. STAGE 2: Smoking, Risk Factors, and Disease Control "Now, one of the most important things I want to talk to you about is smoking. Smoking is one of the biggest risk factors for gum disease — it reduces the blood supply to your gums, which means your body can't fight the infection as well, and it actually masks the bleeding so the disease can progress silently. It also significantly reduces the success rate of dental implants, which I know you're interested in. I'm not here to lecture you, but I do want to be honest with you — if we're going to invest time and money into saving your teeth and replacing the ones we lose, quitting smoking gives us the best possible chance of that working long-term. There's a free service called Quitline — the number is 13 7848 — and I'd really encourage you to give them a call. I can also refer you to your GP for support." Document smoking status. Offer written Quitline information. Now explain the treatment sequence — disease control must come before replacement planning. If she asks "why did my GP not tell me about this side effect?" — acknowledge it plainly rather than getting defensive: it's a known but under-discussed risk, and the job now is managing it properly, not assigning blame. Useful diagnostic aside: pulpitis pain is never constant (it's triggered/episodic) — if a differential ever turns on this, constant dull pain points away from simple reversible pulpitis. text: KEY POINTS ✅ Elicit the spontaneously resolving toothache 4 months ago — this is the historical key to diagnosing pulp necrosis in a primary molar ✅ Explain the sinus tract (parulis) in parent-friendly terms as a 'drainage tunnel' and clarify that absence of pain does not mean absence of infection ✅ Correctly advise that antibiotics are NOT indicated for a chronic draining abscess without systemic signs — definitive treatment (extraction or pulpectomy) is required ✅ Address the parent's diet concern non-judgmentally: identify cordial at kindergarten as a caries risk factor and explain the multifactorial nature of early childhood caries ✅ Gain consent for examination using age-appropriate, positive language with the child; acknowledge Sarah's guilt empathetically without dismissing her concern KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "You must be Lily! Clinical Authority A toothache that resolves on its own in a child's baby tooth is actually a warning sign — it often means the nerve inside the tooth has died, so the tooth can no longer feel pain, but the infection continues silently at the root tip. The pimple you're seeing is called a sinus tract or parulis — it's a small channel the body has created to drain the infection away from the tooth root. Because it's draining, Lily isn't in acute pain right now, but the infection itself has not gone away. Antibiotics alone won't fix this. The source of the infection is inside the tooth, and until we treat the tooth itself — either by removing the nerve tissue or by taking the tooth out — the infection will keep coming back even if the pimple temporarily disappears. Early childhood caries is caused by how often teeth are exposed to fermentable carbohydrates, not just the total amount of sugar. Cordial — even diluted — contains sugars and acids that can cause decay if sipped frequently throughout the day, especially if teeth aren't brushed twice daily with fluoride toothpaste. Because Lily has no fever, no facial swelling, and no signs of spreading infection, this is classified as a chronic localised abscess.

STAGE 3: Addressing the Diet & Caries Concern "Sarah, I really appreciate you raising that — and I want you to know, you're clearly doing your best for Lily, and that matters enormously. So for example, if Lily is sipping cordial at kindy — even diluted cordial — over a long period of time, her teeth are being bathed in that liquid repeatedly, which can cause decay even if the overall sugar content seems low. text: Clinical Authority The bruising is tracking down toward the neck because blood follows gravity through the tissue planes — this is expected and does not by itself indicate a dangerous complication, but I will monitor it closely. Aspirin reduces platelet aggregation, which means the blood did not clot as quickly in the small vessels, allowing it to spread more widely into the surrounding tissues — this is why the bruising looks more extensive than you might expect. Cold compresses are most effective in the first 24 hours to limit bleeding; at this stage, warm compresses will help the body reabsorb the blood more quickly. I would be concerned and want you to go to emergency immediately if you develop any difficulty breathing, difficulty swallowing, a fever above 38 degrees, or if the swelling increases rapidly — these would suggest a more serious complication requiring urgent care. There is no indication for antibiotics or surgical drainage at this point — the socket is healing normally and there are no signs of infection. Curveball Deflectors Patient says: 'Should you have stopped my aspirin before the extraction? Is this your fault?' → Acknowledge the concern empathetically and explain clearly: current Australian and international guidelines recommend continuing low-dose aspirin for cardiovascular patients undergoing routine dental extractions because the risk of stopping it — including heart attack or stent thrombosis — outweighs the risk of increased bleeding. The haematoma is a known, manageable complication, not a result of clinical error. Avoid being defensive; be factual and reassuring. Candidate considers prescribing antibiotics or recommending incision and drainage for the haematoma → Resist this — there are no signs of infection (no fever, no pus, no worsening pain, normal socket healing). Antibiotics are not indicated for an uncomplicated haematoma. Incision and drainage would introduce infection risk and is not appropriate here. Management is conservative: warm compresses, analgesia, reassurance, and monitoring with clear safety-netting. ✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ► STAGE 1: Focused History "Mrs Hayes, thank you for coming in today. I can see you're worried about the swelling and bruising — that's completely understandable, and I want to make sure we go through everything carefully together.

I'll be gentle." Inspect extraoral ecchymosis and swelling — note distribution and tracking toward neck. Assess mouth opening — within acceptable limits, no significant trismus. This means the blood spread more widely into the surrounding soft tissues rather than clotting in one spot. That's what's causing the bruising you can see on your face and down toward your neck. I know it looks quite alarming, but I want to reassure you — this is called a haematoma, and in your situation, it is not dangerous. The bruising will change colour over the next one to two weeks, going from purple to green to yellow as your body reabsorbs it, and it will fully resolve. The socket itself is healing beautifully — there are no signs of infection." Deliver diagnosis clearly and in lay terms. Normalise the appearance of the bruising. text: STAGE 4: Management and Safety-Netting "Here's what I'd like you to do at home. Because it's been more than 24 hours since the extraction, cold packs won't help much now — instead, I'd like you to apply a warm, moist cloth to the area for about 15 to 20 minutes, three or four times a day. This helps your body reabsorb the blood more quickly. For any discomfort, regular paracetamol — two tablets every six hours as needed — should be enough. Please stick to soft foods for the next few days and keep the area clean with gentle rinsing after meals. I'd like to see you again in about five to seven days to check on your progress. Most importantly, I need you to know when to seek urgent help. Please go straight to the emergency department — or call triple zero — if you develop any difficulty breathing or swallowing, if the swelling increases rapidly, if you develop a fever above 38 degrees, or if you notice pus or worsening pain around the socket. These would be signs of a more serious complication that needs immediate attention. Do you have any questions about anything I've explained?" Confirm patient understanding. text: Stage 3 — Inhaler Advice (3–4 min) INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must connect asthma medication to oral health. Salbutamol (Ventolin) reliever is acidic; corticosteroid preventers (if applicable) increase candidiasis and caries risk. Advise: rinse mouth with water and spit after every inhaler use; do not eat or drink (except water) for 30 minutes post-use. Stage 4 — Practical Alternatives & Fluoride (4–5 min) Suggest plain water as primary drink; sports drinks only during intense training, followed by water rinse. Replace cereal bars with cheese, unsalted nuts, or fresh fruit. Reduce sugar in hot drinks. Recommend fluoride toothpaste twice daily; consider Tooth Mousse given thick saliva indicating possible reduced salivary flow. Wait 30 minutes after eating before brushing. Clinical Authority Sports drinks typically have a pH between 2.9 and 3.7 — well below the critical pH of 5.5 at which enamel begins to dissolve — and sipping them throughout a workout means the teeth are under continuous acid attack rather than a single brief exposure.

title: index
text: Salbutamol (Ventolin) reliever inhalers are themselves acidic, and the propellant can lower the oral pH directly; rinsing with plain water and spitting immediately after each puff is a simple but evidence-based step to reduce this risk. Thick, stringy saliva is a clinical indicator of reduced salivary flow — saliva is our primary natural defence against both acid erosion and caries because it buffers acids, remineralises enamel, and clears fermentable carbohydrates; when flow is reduced, all of these protective mechanisms are compromised. Cereal bars and dried fruit are particularly cariogenic because they combine high fermentable sugar content with a sticky, adhesive texture that prolongs contact time with tooth surfaces — the combination of substrate, frequency, and contact time drives the caries process. The recommended approach after eating is to wait at least 30 minutes before brushing, as the enamel is temporarily softened by acid and brushing during this window causes additional mechanical erosion of the softened surface. Curveball Deflectors Patient says: 'But sports drinks are marketed as healthy and I need them for energy during training — surely they're fine if I'm exercising?' → Validate his concern and acknowledge that electrolyte replacement has a role during prolonged intense exercise. However, clarify that the marketing of sports drinks as 'healthy' refers to hydration and electrolyte content, not dental safety. Explain that plain water is equally effective for sessions under 60–90 minutes, and that if he does use a sports drink, he should consume it in one sitting rather than sipping, then rinse with plain water immediately afterwards. Avoid being dismissive — frame it as a small, practical adjustment rather than eliminating something he values. Candidate focuses only on sugar and forgets to address the erosive/acidic component, or forgets to ask about inhaler use entirely → This is the most common error in this station. Caries and erosion have different aetiologies — sugar drives caries via bacterial fermentation, while acid (regardless of sugar content) drives erosion directly. A candidate who only says 'cut down on sugar' will miss the erosion diagnosis and the inhaler connection. Always ask: 'Do you use any inhalers or medications?' and always address pH/acid exposure separately from sugar content when discussing sports drinks and fizzy drinks.

STAGE 2: Explaining the Risk — Drinks "One of the things I noticed on your chart is that you're having quite a few sports drinks and fizzy drinks. Now I know these seem like a healthy choice, especially around training — but here's the thing: these drinks are actually very acidic. PQ-26 Assessment and Management of a Chronic Palatal Swelling Station 25 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors CANDIDATE BRIEF Mr Michael Jones, 52, is new to your practice and attends complaining of a painful tooth; his last check-up was four years ago. PQ-27 Implant Assessment and Counselling in a Patient with a Prosthetic Heart Valve Station 26 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors CANDIDATE BRIEF John Edward, 70, retired, is a new patient who wants to replace his missing back teeth with implants, having been recommended them by a friend. He is missing all his back teeth, and his front teeth are chipping away and have become short. He had prosthetic heart valve replacement surgery two years ago and takes regular medication for it. Gather information, explain the necessary investigations, and address his concerns. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Rapport and Chief Concern (0–2 min) Warmly introduce yourself and confirm John's chief concern — replacing his missing back teeth with implants because they feel natural and low-maintenance. Stage 4 — Procedure-Related Medical Risk (7–9 min) INFLECTION 2 Explain procedure-related risks tied to his history: antibiotic cover given his prosthetic valve, careful coordination of his warfarin and INR around surgery, the effect of alcohol on both bleeding and bruxism, and the effect of hypertension on bleeding and dry mouth — framing the overriding concern as avoiding bacteraemia and the small but serious risk of infective endocarditis. Stage 3 — Examination (4–6 min) Examine intraorally to identify the grossly carious upper right first molar as the likely odontogenic source and assess for vestibular swelling or discharge of pus. text: PQ-40 Diagnosis and Management of Dental Fluorosis in a Teenager Station 39 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management) CANDIDATE BRIEF Kim, 15, attends alone complaining of white and brown patches on all her teeth. Examination shows generalised white and brown/yellow mottled staining across all visible teeth. She lived in a rural area with fluoridated water until age 10 and took fluoride tablets until age 10. She doesn't want any drilling or local anaesthesia, wants her teeth fixed as soon as possible for her sister's wedding photoshoot in a few weeks, and is paying with her mother's credit card. Explain the diagnosis, treatment planning, and management. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Rapport and Understanding Her Concern (0–2 min) Warmly greet Kim and take time to understand her concerns about her smile and her upcoming photoshoot. Stage 2 — Fluoride Exposure History (2–4 min) Take a focused history exploring fluoride exposure during the critical period of tooth development, birth to age eight: the water source in the rural area where she lived until age ten, whether fluoride tablets were taken alongside fluoridated water, and whether she swallowed toothpaste as a young child. Ask about childhood illnesses, fevers, medications such as tetracyclines, or dental trauma to differentiate fluorosis from other enamel defects such as Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation or amelogenesis imperfecta. Stage 3 — Explaining the Diagnosis Sensitively (4–6 min) INFLECTION 1 Explain the diagnosis clearly and sensitively: the white and brown patches are dental fluorosis, caused by excess fluoride during enamel formation in early childhood, where fluoride intake in the range of roughly 1500–2000ppm before age six, while enamel was still forming, results in subsurface porosities from hypomineralisation. Reassure Kim that the enamel is structurally sound, the teeth are not weaker, and there is no increased risk of decay. Acknowledge that multiple fluoride sources — rural water, fluoride tablets, and toothpaste — likely contributed together, avoiding assigning blame and reassuring that this was not the result of negligence.

text: Stage 4 — Treatment Options and Timeframe (6–9 min) INFLECTION 2 Address her immediate concern about the photoshoot by explaining the realistic options: for mild fluorosis with intact enamel, microabrasion can reduce brown spots; resin infiltration (Icon) is a minimally invasive option that masks white spot lesions without drilling or anaesthesia, directly addressing her preference, and could potentially be completed before the wedding, though she should be warned that staining foods like berry juices may need occasional polishing visits afterwards; microabrasion combined with bleaching can be considered for a more even overall tone (bleaching would need specialist advice given her age); composite or porcelain veneers, or no-prep veneers, would be deferred until adulthood given her age, though no-prep options avoid drilling and anaesthesia if ever needed sooner. Stage 5 — Consent, Payment, and Health Promotion (9–11 min) Involve Kim in the decision, explain realistic timeframes, and recommend monitoring with reassessment around age eighteen for more definitive options if desired. Explore how she will be paying and explain that because payment is being made on her mother's card, parental consent is needed and important for record-keeping, particularly as some procedures carry a small risk of enamel damage. Provide health promotion advice on fluoride toothpaste use and GC Tooth Mousse to help remineralise, offer a brochure explaining all options, and emphasise the importance of involving a parent or guardian in this cosmetic decision-making process, offering to contact them directly.

text: KEY POINTS ✅ Explores fluoride exposure history systematically (rural fluoridated water, fluoride tablets, toothpaste swallowing) during the critical birth-to-age-eight enamel formation window ✅ Screens for alternative causes (childhood illness, tetracycline exposure, trauma) to differentiate fluorosis from MIH or amelogenesis imperfecta before settling on the diagnosis ✅ Explains the diagnosis sensitively without assigning blame to Kim or her family, and reassures her the enamel is structurally sound with no increased decay risk ✅ Presents treatment options tiered by invasiveness and timeframe, directly addressing her stated preferences (no drilling, no anaesthesia, fast turnaround before the wedding) with resin infiltration as the standout option, while appropriately deferring veneers to adulthood ✅ Recognises the consent and safeguarding issue given she is a minor paying on her mother's card, and insists on parental involvement in the decision before proceeding with any cosmetic procedure KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds ""Hi Kim, thanks for coming in — I can see these marks on your teeth have been bothering you, especially with the wedding coming up. Let's talk through exactly what's going on and what we can realistically do in the time you've got."" Why it works: Validates her cosmetic concern and time pressure immediately while setting up an honest conversation about realistic options. Clinical Authority What you're seeing is called dental fluorosis — it happens when there's a bit too much fluoride on board while your adult teeth were still forming their enamel, usually before around age six, and it looks like you had a few different fluoride sources together as a child, which is very common and nothing anyone did wrong. Importantly, this doesn't mean your teeth are weaker or more prone to decay — the enamel underneath is actually still quite sound, this is really about appearance rather than tooth strength. Given you don't want any drilling or numbing, and you're working to a tight timeframe, resin infiltration is a strong option for you — it's a minimally invasive treatment that soaks into the white patches and masks them without touching the tooth with a drill, and it's realistic to get done before the wedding.

text: PQ-41 Vertical Root Fracture in a Patient on Long-Term Prednisolone Station 40 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management) CANDIDATE BRIEF Mr Tiner, a new patient, complains of pain in an upper right first molar. There is a large MOD composite restoration and an 8mm pocket in one localised area of the tooth. You diagnose a vertical root fracture and decide the tooth should be extracted. He has a history of asthma and arthritis, taking Ventolin and prednisolone 15mg. Explain the diagnosis and management to the patient. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Rapport and Pain History (0–2 min) Introduce yourself and establish rapport with Mr Tiner before taking a focused history: onset, duration, and character of the pain, any previous dental treatment on the tooth, and specifically whether there has been any trauma. Elicit that root canal treatment was completed three years ago, and that he has been avoiding chewing on that side for about six weeks. Stage 2 — Examination Findings and Diagnosis (2–4 min) INFLECTION 1 Explain the diagnosis of vertical root fracture, noting the combination of a root-canal-treated tooth, a large MOD restoration, and an isolated, deep, narrow pocket as the classic diagnostic picture. Ask about risk factors — diet, grinding, the RCT history, and the large restoration — and explain how the fracture likely happened (a root-filled tooth with a large restoration and grinding load is more prone to fracture under biting forces). Stage 3 — Delivering the News (4–6 min) Communicate clearly and empathetically that the tooth cannot be saved and requires extraction, noting that a specialist could be consulted regarding whether hemisection is a viable alternative in some cases, though this tooth's fracture pattern makes that unlikely. Stage 4 — Medical History and Adrenal Crisis Risk (6–8 min) INFLECTION 2 Note his medical history — asthma and arthritis, on Ventolin and prednisolone 15mg for four weeks — as directly affecting management. Explain that his adrenal glands, suppressed by prolonged corticosteroid use, may not produce enough stress hormone during a surgical extraction, risking an adrenal crisis with a drop in blood sugar and blood pressure; guidelines for steroid cover are generally triggered at higher doses (around 20mg or more) sustained for more than two weeks, so his exact risk needs careful assessment before any extraction proceeds today.

text: Stage 5 — Interim Pain Management and Staged Plan (8–11 min) Explain that because the adrenal crisis risk thresholds are not clearly met today, and given the need for care, the tooth will not be removed today; the focus is on pain management. Take an X-ray today to help plan the eventual removal. Temporise with a band if needed, manage mild pain with paracetamol and oxycodone, adjust any high occlusal contact, and prescribe antibiotics only if infection is present. Plan the tooth removal as an action plan — ideally accompanied by an adult, in a morning appointment, with his asthma inhaler present — and arrange hospital referral if severe pain develops. Discuss long-term replacement options or a splint, and give health promotion advice on avoiding hard foods, managing grinding (night guard), and regular review. KEY POINTS ✅ Takes a focused pain history establishing the RCT three years ago, the large restoration, and six weeks of avoiding chewing on that side ✅ Reaches the correct diagnosis of vertical root fracture from the classic triad — root-treated tooth, large restoration, isolated deep narrow pocket — and explains risk factors (grinding, large restoration, RCT) clearly ✅ Delivers the news that the tooth cannot be saved empathetically, while appropriately mentioning hemisection as a specialist-only consideration rather than a realistic option here ✅ Identifies the adrenal suppression risk from his prednisolone use and correctly reasons that extraction should not proceed today until his corticosteroid risk is properly assessed ✅ Provides a safe interim pain-management plan and a clear staged action plan for eventual extraction (morning appointment, accompanied, inhaler present, hospital referral if severe pain) plus long-term replacement discussion KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds ""Mr Tiner, thanks for coming in — I can see you've been protecting that side of your mouth for a while now. I've had a good look, and I want to explain clearly what's going on and what we need to do about it, carefully and safely."" Why it works: Signals both clinical seriousness and a safety-conscious approach before revealing the extraction news, appropriate given the steroid complication ahead.

text: Clinical Authority The combination of a root-canal-treated tooth, a large filling, and this one deep, narrow pocket on just one side of the tooth is the classic picture of a vertical root fracture — unfortunately, once a root fractures this way, the tooth generally can't be saved. I need to ask about your prednisolone specifically — how long have you been taking it, and at what dose? Long-term steroid use can suppress your adrenal glands' ability to produce extra stress hormone when your body needs it, such as during a surgical procedure like an extraction. Because of that risk, I don't think it's safe to remove this tooth today without being confident about your adrenal function first — I'd rather take an X-ray today and focus on getting you comfortable, then plan the extraction properly once we've assessed that risk. In the meantime, I can help settle any high spot on the tooth, and manage your pain with paracetamol and, if needed, a short course of oxycodone — I wouldn't want to start antibiotics unless there are clear signs of infection. When we do go ahead with the extraction, I'd like to book it for the morning, have someone come with you, and make sure you bring your asthma inhaler — and if you develop severe pain before then, please don't wait, come back in or go to hospital if needed. Curveball Deflectors Patient says: 'Can we just take it out today? I'm so over avoiding chewing on this side.' → Explain the safety reasoning clearly and kindly: "I completely understand wanting this sorted today, and I'm sorry it's been going on for six weeks. But because of the steroid medication you're on for your arthritis, I need to make sure your body can cope safely with a surgical procedure like this before we go ahead — rushing into it today without checking that properly could put you at risk of a serious reaction. Let's get you comfortable now, and I'll organise the extraction properly and safely as soon as we can." Candidate proceeds to extract the tooth today without asking about his prednisolone dose or duration. → This is a significant safety omission. Any patient on long-term corticosteroids being considered for a surgical procedure must have their steroid history (dose and duration) clarified, since prolonged use above certain thresholds risks adrenal suppression and crisis under physiological stress — this must be assessed, and steroid cover or medical liaison arranged if indicated, before proceeding.

STAGE 2: Examination and Diagnosis "On examination, I'm finding one very deep, narrow pocket on just one side of this tooth, along with the large filling and the previous root canal treatment — together, that's a strong sign of a crack running down the root itself, called a vertical root fracture." STAGE 3: Delivering the News "I'm sorry to tell you that once a root fractures like this, the tooth can't be saved, and it will need to come out. PQ-42 Post-Operative Instructions for Patient on Liquid Diet Station 41 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning CANDIDATE BRIEF Mr Michael Sian, regular patient. Scenario: You have just extracted a mobile tooth 23. Haemostasis gel applied and suture placed. Medical History: Taking Eliquis to prevent stroke. Medication was NOT stopped prior to extraction (after consulting GP). Previous extraction done 3 years ago when patient was not taking Eliquis. Smokes 25 cigarettes/day. Clinical Image: No intraoral clinical photo — text-only slide on dark background. Task: Give post-extraction instructions to the patient and explain possible complications that may happen. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Confirm Procedure and Check Understanding (0:00–1:00) Greet the patient by name and confirm what was done: both lower wisdom teeth were surgically removed today, involving gum flaps, some bone removal, and dissolvable stitches placed on both sides. Check the patient understands and address any immediate anxiety. Note that the area is still numb and sensation will return over the next few hours. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must acknowledge the bilateral surgical nature; failing to do so underestimates recovery expectations and leads to poor advice about return to work and diet timeline. Stage 2 — Liquid Diet Rationale and Specifics (1:00–2:30) Explain that the surgical sites need protection while the blood clot forms and healing begins. Recommend a liquid diet for the first 24–48 hours: cool or lukewarm soups, smoothies, protein shakes, milk, yoghurt drinks. Avoid hot, cold, spicy, or crunchy foods. Progress to soft foods (mashed potato, scrambled eggs, soft pasta) from day two or three as tolerated, returning to a normal diet around day seven if comfortable. Stage 3 — Straw, Rinsing, and Swelling Advice (2:30–3:30) Explicitly advise no straws — suction dislodges the clot and causes dry socket. No rinsing for the first 24 hours.

text: From day two, gentle warm salt water rinses three times daily. Apply ice packs to the cheeks for 20 minutes on, 20 minutes off, for the first 24 hours to reduce swelling. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must explain the mechanism of dry socket, not just state the rule; examiners award marks for clinical reasoning. Stage 4 — Analgesia Plan (3:30–4:30) Confirm paracetamol 1g every six hours is at home. Recommend adding ibuprofen 400mg every eight hours with food, alternating with paracetamol for better pain control. Advise taking the first dose before the local anaesthetic wears off. Confirm two days off work is appropriate. Stage 5 — Safety-Net and Emergency Contact (4:30–5:00) Warn about signs requiring urgent review: uncontrolled bleeding, severe worsening pain after day two or three, fever, increasing swelling, or difficulty swallowing or breathing. Provide the practice emergency number and confirm the patient has safe transport home. KEY POINTS ✅ Confirms bilateral surgical extraction with flaps, bone removal, and sutures — sets accurate recovery expectations ✅ Liquid diet 24–48 hours with specific examples (cool/lukewarm soups, smoothies, protein shakes, yoghurt drinks), progressing to soft diet over 5–7 days ✅ No straws — explains suction mechanism causing clot dislodgement and dry socket risk ✅ Analgesia: paracetamol 1g 6-hourly alternating with ibuprofen 400mg 8-hourly with food; advise taking first dose before numbness wears off ✅ Safety-net: uncontrolled bleeding, worsening pain after day 2–3, fever, increasing swelling, difficulty swallowing/breathing — provide emergency contact KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "We've just finished today — before you go, I want to make sure you know exactly what to expect over the next few days, especially given you're on Eliquis." Why it works: Names the anticoagulant explicitly in the opening line, since bleeding risk is the whole point of this station. Clinical Authority Using a straw creates negative intraoral pressure that can physically dislodge the blood clot from the socket, exposing the underlying bone — this is called dry socket, or alveolar osteitis, and it typically presents as severe, throbbing pain starting around day two to four. Because both sides were done surgically — with bone removal and flaps — swelling will peak around 48 to 72 hours and then gradually improve; this is normal and expected, not a sign of infection.

title: index
text: I'd recommend taking paracetamol one gram and ibuprofen 400 milligrams in alternation — so one every three hours staggered — rather than together, as this gives more consistent pain coverage throughout the day. Take the first dose now, before the local wears off. No rinsing at all for the first 24 hours — even gentle rinsing can disturb the clot. From tomorrow, rinse gently with warm salt water — about half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water — three times a day, especially after meals. Two days off work is appropriate given the bilateral surgical nature of what was done today, but everyone heals differently — if you're feeling well and comfortable, you can return when you feel ready. Curveball Deflectors Patient asks: 'Can I drink coffee?' or 'Can I have a hot drink?' → Acknowledge the question positively, then explain that hot drinks should be avoided for the first 24 hours because heat increases blood flow to the area and can dissolve the clot, increasing bleeding risk. Lukewarm or cool drinks are fine. From day two, warm drinks are generally acceptable as long as they are comfortable. Candidate gives generic single-extraction post-op advice without accounting for the bilateral surgical nature of the procedure → This is the most common error. The examiner context specifies raised flaps, bone removal, and bilateral sutures — this is not a simple extraction. The candidate must explicitly mention that swelling will be more significant, recovery takes longer, the liquid and soft diet timeline is more important, and that bilateral numbness means the patient must be careful not to bite their cheeks or tongue while numb. Failing to address the bilateral surgical context will lose marks on multiple rubric criteria. ✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ► STAGE 1: Confirm Procedure and Acknowledge Anxiety "Hi Michael — sorry, I should say, hi David. So, we've just finished today and I want to make sure you're comfortable and that you know exactly what to expect over the next few days. Is that okay? Before I go through everything, can I just check — do you have a rough idea of what we did today?" Allow the patient to respond. Confirm and clarify: "That's right — we removed both of your lower wisdom teeth. Because of the way they were positioned, we had to make a small cut in the gum on each side, remove a little bit of bone, and then place some dissolving stitches to close everything up.

text: It's a bit more involved than a straightforward extraction, so I want to make sure you're well prepared for the next few days. The area is still numb right now from the local anaesthetic — that will wear off over the next one to three hours, so it's a good idea to take some pain relief before it does." STAGE 2: Diet Instructions — Liquids, Soft Foods, and Timeline "For the first 24 to 48 hours, I'd like you to stick to a liquid diet. That means things like cool or lukewarm soups — not hot — smoothies, protein shakes, milk, or yoghurt drinks. The reason is that the blood clot forming in each socket right now is really important for healing, and we want to protect it from any pressure or trauma. Hot foods and drinks can dissolve the clot, and anything hard or crunchy can physically disturb it. From around day two or three, you can move on to soft foods — things like mashed potato, scrambled eggs, soft pasta, or well-cooked vegetables. By about day seven, most people are comfortable returning to a more normal diet, but just listen to your body and go at your own pace." Address the patient's concern about returning to work: "You mentioned you've taken two days off — that's actually exactly right for what we've done today. Given that it was both sides and involved a bit of surgery, two days is appropriate. Most people feel well enough to return to an office job after that, though you might still have some swelling." STAGE 3: Straw, Rinsing, Ice Packs, and Swelling "One really important thing — please don't use a straw for at least the first week. When you suck through a straw, it creates a vacuum inside your mouth, and that suction can pull the blood clot right out of the socket. STAGE 3: Procedure, Specific Risks & Benefits "Let me walk you through what root canal treatment actually involves. First, we'll give you a local anaesthetic injection to completely numb the tooth and the area around it — so you won't feel pain during the procedure. Once you're numb, we make a small opening in the top of the tooth to access the nerve space inside. We then carefully remove the inflamed nerve tissue, clean and shape the canals using very fine instruments, and disinfect everything thoroughly. Once the canals are clean, we seal them with a special filling material. After that, we'll place a permanent restoration — usually a crown — to protect the tooth long-term. This typically takes two to three appointments. Now, I do need to go through some important risks with you. Looking at your X-ray, the roots of this tooth sit very close to your maxillary sinus — that's the air space just above your upper back teeth. There is a small risk that during treatment we could create a small communication between the tooth and the sinus. If that were to happen, we would manage it at the time and monitor it closely. Other risks include: the treatment not fully working — root canal treatment has a success rate of around 85 to 95 percent, so there is a 5 to 10 percent chance we may need to retreat the tooth or perform a small surgical procedure called an apicectomy. There is also a small risk of a fine instrument breaking inside the canal, a perforation of the root, or the tooth cracking over time. The benefits, though, are significant — relief of your pain, and keeping your natural tooth, which is always our preference." Frame the sinus proximity as changing the calculus in RCT's favour, not against it: because the roots sit close to the sinus, extraction is arguably the riskier of the two options here (surgical sinus complications), which is part of why saving the tooth via RCT is generally preferred in this specific case. The permanent cap/crown afterward is not optional — worth stating why explicitly: it seals the tooth coronally and prevents recontamination/fracture. Mention timing (ideally within about 6 weeks of completing RCT) — a longer gap raises the risk of the tooth breaking down or reinfecting before it's protected. PQ-49 Management of Apical Root Fragment Retained During Extraction Station 48 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning CANDIDATE BRIEF 50+ year-old male. Came to the surgery on a Friday afternoon. Lives 2 hours driving distance from the practice. Scenario: Patient presented with pain and swelling on upper right molar side which was badly decayed. Was advised for extraction and agreed.

title: index
text: During extraction, palatal root fractured and small apical 1/3 is left behind. Discovered that tooth had a vertical crack after extraction. On radiograph, root was in close proximity to maxillary sinus. Patient is taking blood pressure medication. Currently under control. Clinical Image: Periapical X-ray of the upper molar region showing retained root tip/fragment with a highlighted circle indicating its location close to the maxillary sinus floor. Task: Inform the patient about the broken root and explain further management. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Stop, Stabilise and Disclose (0–2 min) Pause the procedure. Ensure haemostasis and patient comfort. Calmly and honestly inform the patient: "I need to let you know that a small piece of the root tip has broken off and is still sitting in the bone. I want to explain exactly what that means and what we can do about it." INFLECTION 1 — Failure to disclose promptly or using evasive language here will cause patient anxiety to escalate and risks a duty-of-care failure. Stage 2 — Explain the Clinical Situation (2–5 min) Describe the fragment in plain terms: small (3–4 mm), located near the floor of the maxillary sinus, no visible infection, no sinus communication. Reference the X-ray. Explain the vertical crack found in the tooth as context for why the root fractured. Stage 3 — Present Options with Risks and Benefits (5–8 min) Option A — Surgical retrieval: risks include excessive bone removal, sinus perforation, nerve proximity, prolonged procedure. Option B — Conservative monitoring: evidence supports leaving small, asymptomatic apical fragments; they often encapsulate or resorb. INFLECTION 2 — Candidates who recommend immediate aggressive retrieval without weighing sinus proximity and fragment size will lose marks for clinical reasoning. Stage 4 — Shared Decision-Making and Consent (8–10 min) Recommend monitoring given fragment size, absence of infection, and sinus proximity. Invite patient questions. Gain verbal consent for the agreed plan. Document the discussion. Stage 5 — Post-Op Instructions and Follow-Up (10–12 min) Advise: no nose-blowing, watch for pain, swelling, discharge, or bad taste. Prescribe analgesia (e.g. ibuprofen 400 mg if no contraindication, or paracetamol given antihypertensive use). Review in 1–2 weeks; radiographic review at 3–6 months. Provide written instructions and emergency contact details given 2-hour travel distance.

text: KEY POINTS ✅ Honest, timely disclosure of the retained root fragment using plain language — this is a duty-of-care and open disclosure obligation under Australian standards ✅ Accurate clinical assessment: fragment ~3–4 mm, close to maxillary sinus floor, no infection, no sinus communication — these factors directly drive the management recommendation ✅ Evidence-based recommendation: small, asymptomatic apical fragments without infection or sinus involvement may be safely monitored — immediate retrieval is NOT always indicated ✅ Shared decision-making: patient is informed of both options with risks and benefits, her questions are answered, and verbal consent is obtained for the chosen plan ✅ Safety-netting and follow-up: written post-op instructions, signs of complications clearly explained, review appointment booked, and radiographic monitoring planned at 3–6 months — with written contact details given the 2-hour travel distance KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "Marion, I need to pause and be completely honest with you about something that happened during the extraction." Why it works: Direct, unhedged disclosure with no euphemism — the model way to open a complication conversation. Clinical Authority Small apical root fragments of 3–4 mm that are asymptomatic, free of infection, and not communicating with the maxillary sinus may be safely left in situ and monitored — this is consistent with current evidence and accepted Australian oral surgery practice. Attempting retrieval of a fragment in close proximity to the maxillary sinus floor carries a real risk of iatrogenic sinus perforation, which would convert a minor complication into a significantly more complex one requiring specialist referral. The presence of a vertical root fracture in the extracted tooth explains the apical fracture and is relevant clinical context — it does not change the management of the retained fragment but should be documented. Post-operative analgesia should be selected with awareness of the patient's antihypertensive medication — NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can interact with antihypertensives and elevate blood pressure; paracetamol 500–1000 mg up to four times daily is a safer first-line choice in this patient. Open disclosure of a procedural complication is a professional and ethical obligation under the Australian Dental Council's professional competencies and the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care open disclosure framework.

PQ-50 Incidental White Lesion — Differential Diagnosis & Biopsy Decision Module 10 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors CANDIDATE BRIEF Hanna, 45-year-old, new patient. Attending for the first time requesting a routine check-up and clean. Incidental Finding: On intraoral examination, you notice a white patch on the right side of the mouth (buccal mucosa / lateral tongue region adjacent to an amalgam restoration on the right side). Patient is not aware of it. History: Smokes occasionally. Currently under a lot of stress. No other significant medical history mentioned. Clinical Image: Intraoral photo showing a white lesion on the buccal mucosa/lateral border — requires differential diagnosis. Task: Gather information. Determine what special investigations are required. Explain findings and provide a differential diagnosis. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Lesion Description & Initial Disclosure (0–2 min) Systematically describe the white lesion: site (right buccal mucosa adjacent to amalgam), size, colour, surface texture, border definition, and confirm non-removability with gauze — this single step rules out pseudomembranous candidiasis and anchors the differential. Disclose the finding to Hanna calmly: "I've noticed a small white area on the inside of your right cheek — you may not have been aware of it. I'd like to ask you a few questions about it." Stage 2 — Targeted History (2–6 min) Elicit smoking quantity and duration (do not accept 'social smoker' — press for cigarettes per day and years smoked). Ask about alcohol use, oral symptoms (pain, bleeding, dysphagia), trauma or cheek-biting habit, duration of current lesion, and medications.

title: index
text: INFLECTION 1 — Ask specifically: "Have you ever noticed anything similar in your mouth before — any white patches or ulcers that came and went?" This unlocks the prior left buccal mucosa episode, elevating the risk profile significantly via field cancerisation. Stage 3 — Differential Diagnosis (6–9 min) Present differentials in weighted order: (1) contact lichenoid reaction to amalgam — most anatomically plausible; (2) frictional keratosis from cheek biting; (3) leukoplakia — diagnosis of exclusion; (4) oral squamous cell carcinoma — must be named as a condition to exclude, not a likely diagnosis. Mention candidiasis as less likely given non-removability. INFLECTION 2 — Failure to name OSCC, or naming it without appropriate framing, both lose marks. Stage 4 — Management & Communication (9–12 min) Immediate steps: clinical photography and measurement for baseline documentation; toluidine blue staining if available. Referral to oral medicine or OMFS for biopsy within two weeks — non-negotiable given non-removable lesion, 20+ pack-year smoking history, age over 45, and prior lesion at a separate site. Discuss amalgam replacement as a supplementary diagnostic manoeuvre only. Mention importance of cervical lymph node assessment. Reassure Hanna honestly: most white patches are benign, but investigation is the right and responsible step.

title: index
text: KEY POINTS ✅ Confirm non-removability with gauze before forming any differential — this is the single most important clinical observation that separates this lesion from candidiasis ✅ Quantify smoking accurately: 5–10 cigarettes/day for 20+ years — 'social smoker' is not an acceptable endpoint; the true history materially changes the risk profile ✅ Ask specifically about previous oral white patches or ulcers to uncover the prior left buccal mucosa episode — this is the hidden inflection point and signals field cancerisation ✅ Name oral squamous cell carcinoma in the differential without catastrophising — frame it as a condition that must be excluded, not a likely diagnosis, and hold the tension between honesty and reassurance ✅ Refer to oral medicine or OMFS for biopsy within two weeks — advising 'come back in a few months' without a referral plan is a failing response for a non-removable white lesion in a smoker over 45 KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "While I was having a look around your mouth today, I noticed something I want to tell you about — you may not have been aware of it at all."
