Clinical Authority A non-removable white lesion in a patient over 45 with a 20-plus pack-year smoking history must be referred for specialist assessment and biopsy within two weeks — observation alone is not appropriate. The prior white patch on the contralateral buccal mucosa two years ago raises the possibility of field cancerisation — a process where the entire oral mucosa has been exposed to carcinogens and may harbour dysplastic change at multiple sites simultaneously. Non-removability with gauze is the key clinical feature that distinguishes true leukoplakia and its differentials from pseudomembranous candidiasis, which wipes off to leave an erythematous base. Toluidine blue vital staining can be used as an adjunct to identify areas of increased nuclear activity within a white lesion, helping to guide biopsy site selection, though it is not a substitute for histopathological diagnosis. title: index
text: Do we really need to do anything about it?' → Acknowledge her explanation as entirely plausible — cheek biting and frictional trauma are genuine causes of white patches and her stress history supports this. You may not have been aware of it at all, and that's completely fine — these things are often picked up incidentally. I'd like to ask you a few questions about it, if that's okay?" Clinically: the lesion is located on the right buccal mucosa adjacent to the amalgam restoration. It appears as a homogeneous white patch, approximately [estimated size] in diameter, with a slightly raised or flat surface, well-defined borders, and — critically — it does not wipe off when tested with gauze. This non-removability rules out pseudomembranous candidiasis and confirms the lesion warrants further investigation. Document with clinical photography and measure for baseline records immediately.

title: index
text: STAGE 2: Targeted History "I'd like to ask you a few questions to help me understand this better. Firstly, have you noticed any soreness, bleeding, or difficulty eating or swallowing? ... And do you sometimes bite the inside of your cheek — particularly when you're stressed? ... You mentioned you smoke occasionally — can I ask roughly how many cigarettes a day, and how long you've been smoking? ... And do you drink alcohol at all — even just socially? ... Now, this is an important one: have you ever noticed anything similar in your mouth before — any white patches, ulcers, or areas that looked a bit different and then went away?" Key findings to elicit: no pain, bleeding, or dysphagia; cheek-biting habit under stress acknowledged; smoking accurately quantified at 5–10 cigarettes per day for over 20 years — do not accept 'social smoker' without pressing for specifics; alcohol approximately 6–8 standard drinks per week. Most critically: direct questioning about previous oral changes reveals a prior white patch on the LEFT buccal mucosa approximately two years ago that resolved spontaneously. This is a significant red flag for field cancerisation and escalates the urgency of specialist referral. No medications, no allergies, no family history of oral cancer. STAGE 3: Differential Diagnosis "Let me explain what this patch could be — there are a few possibilities and I want to be straightforward with you. The most likely explanation, given how close it is to that silver filling, is that the lining of your cheek may be reacting to the metal — we call that a lichenoid reaction, and it's quite common. It's also possible it's from the cheek-biting you mentioned, which can cause the skin inside the mouth to thicken and turn white. There's also a condition called leukoplakia — a white patch that doesn't have an obvious cause — which is something we need to rule out. And because I want to be honest with you without alarming you: there is a small possibility that a white patch like this could be an early sign of something more serious, which is exactly why I don't want to just leave it and hope it goes away.

title: index
text: Most white patches in the mouth are completely benign — but the only way to know for certain is to have it properly assessed." Differential diagnosis in weighted order: (1) Contact lichenoid reaction to adjacent amalgam — most anatomically plausible given proximity; (2) Frictional keratosis from cheek biting under stress; (3) Leukoplakia — diagnosis of exclusion once other causes ruled out; (4) Oral squamous cell carcinoma — must be named and must not be omitted, framed as a condition to exclude rather than a likely diagnosis. I'd also like to discuss replacing that silver filling at some point, because if the patch is a reaction to the metal, removing the filling may help it resolve — but I want the specialist to see it first before we change anything. I'll also check the lymph nodes in your neck as part of a thorough examination. I know this might feel a bit worrying, Hanna, but I want to reassure you — the vast majority of white patches like this are completely harmless. We're doing this because we want to be thorough and look after you properly, not because I think something is seriously wrong." text: PQ-51 Perio Patient — Replacement Options for Missing Teeth (OPG, Bone Loss) Module 10 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors CANDIDATE BRIEF 45-year-old male, new patient. Has been seeing another dentist. Presenting for a second opinion regarding missing teeth and replacement options. Examination Findings: OPG provided showing generalised bone loss and multiple missing posterior teeth. Patient is known to have significant bone loss. Has not been formally diagnosed at this visit. Task: Gather information. Advise on investigations required. Give appropriate replacement options for missing teeth. No need to provide a formal diagnosis. Focus on patient communication, exploring options (implants, bridges, partial dentures), and realistic expectations given bone loss. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Focused History (0–3 min) Introduce yourself and acknowledge David's reason for attending. Take a structured history: previous dental attendance and any periodontal treatment, recall compliance, oral hygiene habits. INFLECTION 1 Ask directly about flossing — when David reveals he stopped because his gums bled, correct this misconception clearly: bleeding is a sign of inflammation, not a reason to stop. Ask about smoking (pack history), alcohol, and medical history including diabetes screening. Stage 2 — OPG Explanation (3–5 min) Explain the OPG in plain language. Use accessible phrasing: "The bone that holds your teeth in place has reduced by roughly half in most areas — this is the result of longstanding gum disease." Note multiple missing posterior teeth and widened ligament spaces. Avoid jargon. INFLECTION 2 Be honest about severity without catastrophising — this is significant but not end-stage. Stage 3 — Replacement Options (5–8 min) Address all three modalities. Implants: best long-term outcome but not immediately available — periodontal disease must be controlled first, smoking doubles failure risk, bone grafting may be needed. Fixed bridge: possible in principle but unsuitable here as adjacent teeth are periodontally compromised. Removable partial denture: immediately available, no surgery, but least preferred for comfort and stability. Stage 4 — Treatment Sequence and Closing (8–10 min) Lay out the sequence clearly: treat gum disease first, re-evaluate bone and tooth stability, then plan replacements. Strongly advise smoking cessation. Reassure David that options remain — this is not hopeless — but commitment from both sides is required.

title: index
text: KEY POINTS ✅ Identify and correct the flossing misconception — bleeding gums indicate inflammation, not a reason to stop interdental cleaning ✅ Elicit full social history including smoking (10 cigarettes/day × 20 years), alcohol, and ask specifically about diabetes ✅ Explain OPG findings in plain language — approximately 40–50% generalised horizontal bone loss as a consequence of longstanding periodontal disease ✅ Discuss all three replacement modalities (implants, fixed bridge, removable partial denture) with honest pros, cons, and patient-specific caveats ✅ State clearly that active periodontal disease must be stabilised before any replacement option is pursued, and that smoking approximately doubles implant failure risk — smoking cessation is strongly recommended KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "I understand you're here for a second opinion, and I want to give you straight answers today — can I ask a few questions first so I have the full picture?" Smokers have approximately double the implant failure rate compared to non-smokers — that is not a reason to rule implants out, but it is a reason to take smoking cessation seriously before we go down that path. Bleeding when you floss is not a sign that flossing is causing damage — it is a sign that the gum tissue is inflamed and infected. Stopping flossing actually allows the disease to get worse, not better. Before we can place any implant or bridge, we need to get the gum disease under control first. Placing an implant into an environment with active periodontal disease significantly increases the risk of peri-implantitis and implant failure. In areas where significant bone has already been lost, we may need a bone graft to build up enough volume to support an implant — that is an additional procedure but it is a well-established pathway. Just give it to me straight.' → Respond directly without hedging: 'Yes, implants are on the table for you — but not yet, and not without some important steps first.

text: We need to treat the gum disease, get that stable, and I would strongly recommend you stop smoking before we proceed. Before I look at the X-ray with you, I need to ask you a few questions so I have the full picture. Is that okay?" Proceed with focused history. Ask about previous dental attendance: how long with the previous dentist, whether any specific gum treatment was ever done, and whether he kept up with recall appointments. When David admits he did not comply with recall, acknowledge this without judgment and note it as a risk factor. Ask about oral hygiene: "Do you floss or use anything between your teeth?" When David explains he stopped flossing because his gums bled, respond directly: "I am glad you told me that, because this is actually a really common misunderstanding and it is important to correct it. Bleeding when you clean between your teeth is not a sign that the flossing is causing damage — it is a sign that the gum tissue is inflamed and infected. When you stop cleaning there, the bacteria build up and the disease gets worse, not better. We will need to get you back into a routine with interdental cleaning as part of the treatment." Ask about smoking: "Do you smoke?" Note ten cigarettes per day for twenty years. Ask about alcohol — four to five standard drinks on weekends is moderate and noted.

title: index
text: Ask about medical history, specifically: "Have you ever been tested for diabetes or told your blood sugar is high?" — David has not been tested; note this and explain that uncontrolled diabetes is a significant risk factor for gum disease and implant healing, and recommend a GP review. This is a panoramic X-ray — it gives us a full view of all your teeth, the bone around them, and the jaw. What I want you to notice is the level of bone here — you can see it has dropped significantly around most of your teeth. In a healthy mouth, the bone comes right up close to the neck of the tooth. In your case, the bone has reduced by roughly half of the root length in most areas. That bone is what anchors your teeth in place, so when it reduces, the teeth become less stable. This is the result of longstanding gum disease — it has been progressing quietly over many years, often without much pain, which is why it can go undetected. I can also see that you have several missing teeth in the back of both jaws, and the remaining teeth show some signs of stress on the ligament that connects them to the bone. There is no acute infection or abscess showing up, which is reassuring — but the overall picture tells me this has been going on for a long time and needs to be addressed properly." The first is dental implants. These are titanium posts that go into the jawbone and act like artificial tooth roots — you then get a crown on top. They are the gold standard for replacing missing teeth because they are fixed, they feel natural, and they do not rely on the neighbouring teeth. For you, implants are a realistic goal — but not right now, and there are some important conditions. First, we need to get the gum disease under control before placing any implant. Putting an implant into a mouth with active gum disease significantly increases the risk of the implant failing.

title: index
text: Second, in areas where the bone has reduced significantly, we may need a bone graft to build up enough volume to support the implant — that is an additional procedure but it is well-established and routinely done. That is not a reason to rule them out, but it is a strong reason to seriously consider stopping smoking before we go ahead. The second option is a fixed bridge. The downside is that most patients find it the least comfortable and least stable long-term. It is a valid option, particularly as a short-term measure while we work on the gum disease." STAGE 4: Treatment Sequence and Close "So here is the sequence I would recommend. Step one: we do a thorough assessment of your gum disease — probing depths, full charting — and then we start active treatment, which involves a deep clean to remove the bacteria and deposits from below the gumline. That usually takes a few appointments. Step two: we review how the gums have responded, reassess the bone, and see which teeth are stable and which may be at risk long-term. Step three: once the gum disease is stable, we plan the replacements — and at that point, implants become a much more viable and predictable option. PQ-58 Drug-Seeking Behaviour — Opioid Request for Dental Pain Module 9 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors CANDIDATE BRIEF Female patient.

title: index
text: Tooth known to need RCT — previous dentist diagnosed irreversible pulpitis and recommended root canal treatment. Scenario: Patient presents demanding strong prescription painkillers (specifically fentanyl, oxycodone, or tramadol) for toothache. Claims her regular dentist is away and she cannot contact him. States normal painkillers are not effective. She also has a physiotherapist-prescribed pain relief patch for chronic back pain. Has an appointment with her regular dentist next week. Insisting she needs strong medication urgently. Key Complexity: Drug-seeking behaviour. Task: Manage the patient's request. Address her concerns without prescribing opioids. Provide safe and appropriate alternatives. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Recognition and Empathic Opening Identify red flags. Acknowledge pain. Set a calm, non-accusatory tone. Stage 2 — Decline Opioids with Clinical Rationale Explain why opioids are contraindicated. Reference patch interaction. Maintain boundary firmly but respectfully. Stage 3 — Offer Alternatives, Safety-Net, Document Prescribe non-opioid analgesia. Arrange urgent dental referral. Advise on red flag symptoms. Document everything. KEY POINTS ✅ Recognise drug-seeking red flags: requesting opioids by name, regular dentist unavailable, claims standard analgesia ineffective, existing opioid patch ✅ Empathise with genuine dental pain (irreversible pulpitis is severely painful) without validating the opioid request ✅ Decline opioids clearly and professionally — cite interaction risk with existing fentanyl patch, dependence risk, and lack of dental indication ✅ Offer evidence-based non-opioid analgesia: alternating ibuprofen 400 mg + paracetamol 1000 mg every 3–4 hours, and arrange urgent dental referral ✅ Document refusal with clinical rationale, red flags noted, alternatives offered, and safety-net advice given KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "I can see you're in a lot of pain and you've come in hoping for something strong — let's talk about what's actually going to fix this properly." Why it works: Names her expectation directly and non-judgementally before pivoting to safe alternatives, avoiding a defensive standoff at the start. Clinical Authority Ibuprofen 400 mg combined with paracetamol 1000 mg alternating every 3–4 hours provides superior analgesia to opioids for acute dental pain and is the evidence-based first-line regimen per Australian Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) and ADA guidance.

text: Prescribing opioids alongside an existing fentanyl transdermal patch creates a clinically significant risk of opioid toxicity and respiratory depression — this combination is contraindicated without specialist review. text: PQ-59 MIH in an 11-Year-Old — Second Opinion on GA Extraction Module 9 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management) CANDIDATE BRIEF 11-year-old boy, attending with his parents. Chief Complaint: Sensitivity to cold in his back teeth. History: Mother took him to a public hospital previously. General dentist at the hospital suggested extracting the back teeth under general anaesthesia. Parents seeking a second opinion. Examination Findings / Clinical Image: Photograph showing hypomineralised (chalky/opaque) first permanent molars and incisors. Baby teeth appear normal. Diagnosis: Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation (MIH) — affects permanent molars and incisors, primary dentition unaffected. Task: Diagnose and manage. Address parent's concern about the hospital dentist's recommendation for GA extraction. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Introduction and History (0–3 min) Greet Liam first, then his parents. Confirm the chief complaint. Ask Liam directly: "Does the pain happen on its own, or only when you have something cold?" Elicit no spontaneous or nocturnal pain — a critical negative finding. Ask Wei about early childhood illnesses; she will disclose bronchiolitis hospitalisation at eight months. INFLECTION 1 — linking the febrile illness to the mineralisation window demonstrates aetiological understanding and opens the reassurance conversation. Stage 2 — Diagnosis and Explanation (3–6 min) Name the condition: "Liam has something called Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation — MIH for short." Explain in lay terms that the enamel did not harden properly during early childhood. Distinguish from caries (not caused by bacteria or sugar in the same way), fluorosis (not caused by fluoride), and amelogenesis imperfecta (not hereditary; primary teeth are normal — point to the photograph). Explicitly reassure Wei that this is not caused by diet, brushing, or anything she did during pregnancy. INFLECTION 2 — this reassurance is the emotional pivot of the station; a strong candidate delivers it with eye contact and pauses to let it land. Stage 3 — Conservative Management Plan (6–9 min) Present the staged ladder: (1) high-fluoride toothpaste (5000 ppm, e.g. Colgate Neutrafluor 5000) and desensitising agents; (2) fissure sealing with resin composite or GIC; (3) GIC or composite restorations for surface breakdown; (4) Hall-technique preformed metal crowns for significantly broken-down molars. Extraction is the last resort — not indicated today.

title: index
text: Stage 4 — Addressing the GA Recommendation and Recall (9–12 min) Acknowledge the hospital dentist's recommendation without criticism: "The team there may have been working with a different clinical picture or resource constraints — that recommendation makes sense in some situations." Explain that because Liam has no spontaneous pain and his teeth remain restorable, conservative management should be trialled first. Set recall at three to six months. Address David's cost and prognosis questions honestly. KEY POINTS ✅ Elicit absence of spontaneous/nocturnal pain — supports conservative management and argues against irreversible pulpitis ✅ Name MIH explicitly and distinguish it from caries, fluorosis, and amelogenesis imperfecta using the intact primary dentition as a discriminating feature ✅ Reassure parents that MIH is developmental — not caused by diet, brushing, or parental actions — and deliver this with genuine empathy directed at Wei ✅ Present the conservative management ladder in logical order (fluoride/desensitising → fissure seal → GIC/composite → Hall crown) before any mention of extraction ✅ Address the GA recommendation diplomatically without criticising the hospital dentist, and set a three-to-six-month recall with explanation of post-eruptive breakdown risk KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Opening Line — First 30 Seconds "I hear your back teeth have been giving you trouble — when do they hurt, is it all the time or does something set it off?" Why it works: Talks directly to the child patient first, even though most of the substantive discussion will be with his parents about the GA decision.

title: index
text: Clinical Authority "Because Liam has no spontaneous pain and no pain at night, the pulps of these teeth are most likely still healthy — that means extraction is not indicated at this stage." "MIH affects only the permanent teeth because the mineralisation disturbance occurs in early childhood, after the primary teeth have already formed — that's why his baby teeth look completely normal in the photograph." "The Hall technique — placing a stainless steel crown over the tooth without drilling — is one of the most evidence-supported options for a significantly broken-down MIH molar in a child, and it can be done in the chair without general anaesthesia in most cases." "High-concentration fluoride toothpaste — 5000 parts per million, available on prescription in Australia — can significantly reduce the sensitivity Liam is experiencing and help remineralise the porous enamel surface." "If extraction ever becomes necessary in the future, we would need orthodontic input to manage the space — ideally this decision is made around ages eight to ten when the second molars are forming, so timing becomes more complex now that Liam is eleven." Curveball Deflectors Wei asks: "So the hospital dentist was wrong? Should we complain?" → Do not agree that the dentist was wrong, and do not encourage a complaint. Say: "I can't speak to exactly what the team saw on that day — there may have been clinical findings or resource factors I'm not aware of. What I can tell you is that based on what I'm seeing today, Liam's teeth are still restorable and I'd like to try a conservative approach first. If that changes, we'll reassess together." This is diplomatic, non-critical, and keeps the focus on Liam's current management. Candidate agrees that extraction under GA is appropriate and begins planning referral without exploring conservative options → This is the most common wrong turn. The absence of spontaneous pain, absence of cavitation, and restorable status of the teeth all contraindicate immediate extraction. A strong candidate explicitly states: "Before we consider extraction, I want to make sure we've tried everything we can to save these teeth — they are Liam's permanent molars and we only get one set." Extraction without trialling conservative management is a mark-losing response. ✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ► STAGE 1: Introduction and History "Hi Liam — I'm Dr [Name]. Thanks for coming in today. I hear your back teeth have been giving you some trouble.

title: index
text: Can I ask you directly — when do they hurt? Is it all the time, or does something set it off?" Address Liam first to build rapport and signal to the examiner that the child is included. Wait for Liam to confirm cold-triggered sensitivity and deny spontaneous or nocturnal pain. Then turn to Wei: "Mrs Chen, has Liam ever woken up at night with toothache, or complained of pain just sitting quietly?" Confirm the answer is no — this is a critical negative finding. Ask Wei: "Can I ask — did Liam have any significant illnesses in his first year or two of life? Anything that required a hospital stay?" When she mentions the bronchiolitis hospitalisation at eight months, acknowledge it: "Thank you — that's actually a really helpful piece of the puzzle, and I'll explain why in a moment." STAGE 2: Diagnosis and Reassurance "So, looking at the photographs and what you've told me, I can give you a clear diagnosis today. Liam has a condition called Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation — most people call it MIH. What that means in plain language is that the enamel — the hard outer layer of his back teeth and his front teeth — didn't harden up properly when it was forming during early childhood. It's a bit like concrete that didn't set quite right. The enamel is more porous, more sensitive, and more fragile than it should be. That's why cold air and cold drinks set it off." Pause, then address Wei directly with eye contact: "I want to be really clear about something, because I know this kind of news can make parents wonder what they did wrong. MIH is not caused by diet, not caused by too much sugar, and not caused by how you brushed Liam's teeth. It is a developmental condition — it happens during a specific window when the teeth are mineralising, usually in the first three years of life. The bronchiolitis Liam had at eight months — that kind of significant illness during that window is associated with MIH in the research literature. You didn't cause this. This is not your fault." Allow a moment for this to land. Then distinguish from other conditions: "This is different from tooth decay, which is caused by bacteria and acid. It's different from fluorosis, which comes from too much fluoride. And it's different from a hereditary condition called amelogenesis imperfecta — we know it's not that because Liam's baby teeth are completely normal, which you can see in the photograph.

title: index
text: MIH only affects the permanent teeth." STAGE 3: Conservative Management Plan "Now, here's the good news — there is a lot we can do before we even think about removing these teeth. I want to walk you through the plan step by step. First, we're going to tackle the sensitivity. I'll prescribe a high-strength fluoride toothpaste — it's called Neutrafluor 5000, and it has about ten times the fluoride of regular toothpaste. Used twice a day, it can really calm things down for Liam. We'll also apply a fluoride varnish here in the chair today. Second, for the surfaces of the molars that haven't broken down yet, we can place fissure sealants — a thin protective coating — to stop them from getting worse. Third, if there are any areas where the enamel has already chipped or broken away, we can restore those with a tooth-coloured filling material or a glass ionomer cement. And if a molar is significantly broken down, there's a very effective technique called the Hall technique, where we place a small stainless steel crown over the tooth — no drilling required — which protects it completely. That can be done right here in the chair." Turn to Liam: "Liam, I also noticed you might be a bit self-conscious about the front teeth — the white-ish patches. We can look at options to improve how those look as you get older, once your teeth have fully come through. You're not stuck with them the way they are." This directly acknowledges Liam's embarrassment and earns marks for child engagement. STAGE 4: Addressing the GA Recommendation, Prognosis, and Recall "I want to address what the hospital team suggested, because I understand that's a big part of why you're here. Extraction under general anaesthesia is a legitimate option in some situations — for example, if a tooth has irreversible nerve damage, or if it simply can't be saved. But based on what I'm seeing today — no spontaneous pain, no pain at night, and teeth that are still restorable — I don't think we're at that point with Liam. The team at the hospital may have been working with different information, or different resources, and I'm not here to second-guess them.

title: index
text: What I can tell you is that my recommendation today is to try conservative treatment first, because these are Liam's permanent molars and we want to keep them if we possibly can." Address David directly: "You asked about cost — the treatments I've described range from relatively low-cost options like fluoride varnish and sealants through to restorations and crowns if needed. I'll give you a written treatment plan with estimates so there are no surprises. As for the long-term outlook — MIH teeth can deteriorate over time, which is why I want to see Liam back every three to six months so we can catch any changes early. Many children with MIH keep their molars into adulthood with good management. I won't promise that extraction will never be needed, but it is not where we are today, and we will make that decision together if it ever comes to that." Close by confirming the recall appointment and providing written instructions for the fluoride toothpaste. PQ-60 Caries Risk Assessment in a Cooperative 8-Year-Old Station 60 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management) CANDIDATE BRIEF Mehmet Askoff, an 8-year-old boy, attends today with his father. His father is worried about black holes in Mehmet's teeth. On examination you find multiple grossly carious primary molars — an intraoral photo is provided, and a bitewing radiograph may sometimes be given. Mehmet is a cooperative child. Conduct a consultation with the father covering the caries risk assessment and management. MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE Stage 1 — Rapport and History (0–3 min) Greet Mehmet directly before turning to his father — signals to the examiner that the child is included, not just discussed over his head. Take a structured caries-risk history: drinks (type, frequency, sipped vs with meals), snacks (type and frequency between meals), brushing (frequency, toothpaste, supervised or not), fluoride exposure (toothpaste strength, home water source), and last dental visit. INFLECTION 1 — Asking specifically about the home water source (town supply vs tank/bore) is the differentiating question here; most candidates ask about diet but skip fluoride exposure entirely. Stage 2 — Explain the Diagnosis (3–5 min) Use the photo (and X-ray if taken) to show the father the carious lesions.

title: index
text: Explain the mechanism in plain language: bacteria feed on sugars/carbohydrates and produce acid that breaks down enamel — and critically, it is the frequency of exposure through the day, not the total amount of sugar, that drives the disease. Reassure the father this is common and very manageable, without assigning blame. Stage 3 — Address "Can We Just Watch Them?" (5–7 min) INFLECTION 2 — This is the key pivot of the station. The father will ask whether cavitated primary teeth need active treatment given they'll fall out anyway. The candidate must explain the real consequences of leaving them untreated: progression to pulpal involvement and abscess, space loss for the permanent successor if a primary molar is lost early, and impact on eating, nutrition and sleep from ongoing pain. Stage 4 — Management Plan (7–9 min) Restorative: glass ionomer or composite restorations for the carious primary molars under local anaesthetic given Mehmet's cooperation; consider a stainless steel crown (Hall technique or conventional) for more extensively broken-down teeth. Preventive: standard-strength fluoride toothpaste (1000–1450 ppm, appropriate for age 8) twice daily supervised, in-chair fluoride varnish today, water as the default drink with sugary drinks/snacks confined to mealtimes, and fissure sealants for permanent first molars as they erupt. Stage 5 — Recall and Close (9–10 min) Arrange a 3-monthly recall given the high caries risk identified today. Give the father one or two concrete, realistic first steps rather than an overwhelming list. Check understanding and invite questions.

title: index
text: KEY POINTS ✅ Takes a structured dietary and oral hygiene history — frequency of sugary/acidic drinks and snacks, brushing supervision, and fluoride exposure via toothpaste and water source — not a generic "what does he eat" question ✅ Explains the diagnosis in plain, non-judgemental language using the photo as a visual aid, without assigning blame to the father ✅ Explicitly identifies frequency (not total amount) of sugar/acid exposure as the key driver, and connects this to the reported snacking and drinking pattern ✅ Identifies the non-fluoridated home water supply as a risk factor and recommends an age-appropriate standard-strength fluoride toothpaste plus in-chair varnish ✅ Outlines a restorative plan appropriate for a cooperative child (GIC/composite, or stainless steel crowns for extensive breakdown) and considers sealants for erupting permanent molars ✅ Directly answers "they're just baby teeth, can we watch them?" with the real consequences of non-treatment — pain, abscess risk, space loss, nutrition/sleep impact KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS Clinical Authority What drives caries is how often teeth are exposed to sugars and acids through the day, not just the total amount — sipping juice or cordial between meals keeps the mouth in an acid attack for most of Mehmet's waking hours, which overwhelms his saliva's ability to repair the enamel in between. A non-fluoridated home water supply is a real, addressable risk factor here — I'd recommend a standard-strength fluoride toothpaste, 1000 to 1450 parts per million, which is appropriate at Mehmet's age, used twice daily, plus a fluoride varnish application today and at each future visit. Because Mehmet is cooperative, most of these carious primary molars can be restored under local anaesthetic with glass ionomer or composite; where breakdown is more extensive, a stainless steel crown gives a more predictable, longer-lasting result than a large filling in a primary tooth. Primary molars aren't replaced until around age 10 to 11 — losing one early to untreated decay can cause the neighbouring teeth to drift into the space, which affects how the permanent premolar comes through underneath. Given the risk factors identified today, I'd like to see Mehmet every three months rather than the standard six, until we've confirmed the new habits are sticking and no new lesions are appearing.

title: index
text: Curveball Deflectors Father asks: 'They're just baby teeth though — can't we just keep an eye on them and let them fall out naturally?' → Acknowledge the logic in his question, then explain clearly: 'I understand why that seems reasonable, but these particular teeth won't be replaced for another two to three years, and if we leave the decay to progress, it can reach the nerve and cause a real infection — which means pain, possible swelling, and sometimes an emergency extraction. If a molar is lost early because of that, the teeth around it can drift into the gap, which affects how his adult tooth comes through underneath. Treating them now is actually about protecting his comfort today and his bite later on.' Candidate focuses only on "less sugar" without asking about frequency or fluoride exposure → This is the most common shortfall in this station. A candidate who only advises "cut down on sugar" misses the two highest-yield points: that frequency of exposure matters more than total amount, and that the family's water source is non-fluoridated. Always ask directly: "How often through the day does he have something sugary or acidic?" and "What's your water supply at home — town water, tank, or bore?" ✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ► STAGE 1: Rapport and History "Hi Mehmet — I'm just going to have a look at your teeth in a minute, and I bet you're going to do a great job. Mr Askoff, thanks for bringing him in — I can see you're worried, and I want us to work out together what's going on and what we can do about it. Can I ask a few questions first? What does Mehmet usually drink through the day — is it mostly water, or juice and cordial too? And roughly how often? Does he snack between meals — things like lollies, chips, or biscuits — and how often would that be, say after school? How's his brushing going — how many times a day, and is it supervised, or does he mostly do it himself? What toothpaste does he use, and — this one might seem like an odd question — what's your water supply at home? Town water, tank, or bore? And when was his last dental check-up?" Listen for: frequent juice/cordial, afternoon snacking on lollies/chips after school, once-daily unsupervised brushing, non-fluoridated bore/tank water, and a check-up gap of over 18 months. Note these as a cluster of modifiable risk factors rather than singling out any one as "the cause." STAGE 2: Explaining the Diagnosis "Thank you — that's really helpful.

title: index
text: So looking at this photo of Mehmet's teeth, these dark areas are decay. What happens is that the bacteria naturally living in the mouth feed on sugars from food and drink and produce an acid, and that acid slowly breaks down the tooth. The important thing to understand is that it's not really about how much sugar he's having overall — it's about how often his teeth are exposed to it through the day. Every time he has something sugary or acidic, the teeth are under acid attack for a little while afterwards, and if that keeps happening again and again, the mouth doesn't get a chance to recover in between. I want to reassure you — this is really common, and it doesn't mean you've done anything wrong. It just means there are a few things we can adjust that will make a real difference." Deliver this in a warm, non-judgemental tone. Avoid language that implies parental blame. Use the photo as a visual anchor throughout. STAGE 3: Addressing "Can We Just Watch Them?" "Mr Askoff, I imagine you might be wondering — since these are baby teeth, could we just keep an eye on them and let them fall out on their own? It's a really fair question, and I want to explain why I wouldn't recommend that here. These particular back teeth won't actually be replaced by adult teeth for another two to three years, so they've got an important job to do in the meantime — chewing, holding space, and guiding his adult teeth into the right position. If we leave this decay untreated, it can progress deeper into the tooth and reach the nerve, which causes real pain and can lead to a dental abscess — that's a proper infection, sometimes with swelling, and in a young child it can mean an emergency visit or even having the tooth taken out under more difficult circumstances. If a molar is lost too early because of that, the teeth on either side can drift into the gap, which then affects how his adult tooth comes through underneath. So treating these now is really about protecting his comfort today and setting his adult teeth up properly for later." This is the highest-yield section of the station — do not skip or rush it. Address the question directly rather than waiting to be asked. STAGE 4: Management Plan "Here's what I'd suggest. Because Mehmet's such a cooperative little patient, we can treat most of these teeth in the chair with a local anaesthetic — a numbing injection — and a tooth-coloured or cement filling.

title: index
text: For a couple of the more broken-down teeth, I'd actually recommend a small stainless steel crown rather than a filling — it fits over the whole tooth like a cap, and for a baby molar with this much decay it tends to last much better and more predictably than a large filling would. On the prevention side: let's make water his main drink through the day, and keep the juice and cordial to mealtimes only rather than sipping between meals. For snacks, swapping the afternoon lollies and chips for things like cheese, fruit, or plain crackers makes a real difference. I'd like him on a regular-strength fluoride toothpaste — that's the normal adult-strength one, which is actually right for his age — twice a day, and I'll apply a fluoride varnish to his teeth today as an extra layer of protection. As his adult back teeth come through over the next year or two, we'll also put protective sealants on them before they have a chance to decay." Prescribe/recommend standard 1000–1450 ppm fluoride toothpaste (not the low-fluoride under-6 formulation). Apply fluoride varnish in the same visit. Plan restorative treatment appropriate to each tooth's extent of breakdown. STAGE 5: Recall and Closing "Because of what we've found today, I'd like to see Mehmet every three months for a little while, rather than the usual six — just until we're confident the new routine is sticking and no new spots are appearing. I know that's a few changes at once, so if it helps, let's start with just two things: swap the after-school snack for something like cheese or fruit, and keep the juice to mealtimes only. We can build on that at the next visit. Does that all make sense? Do you have any questions for me before you go?" Give the father a manageable, prioritised starting point rather than an overwhelming list. Confirm understanding, book the restorative appointment and the 3-month recall, and document the diet, hygiene and fluoride-exposure history along with the management plan. PQ-61 Post-Extraction Instructions — Patient on Apixaban (Eliquis) Station 61 | Past Questions ■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning CANDIDATE BRIEF Mr Amaro, 70, regular patient. You have just extracted a mobile tooth 23 (upper left canine). Haemostasis gel has been applied and a suture placed. He takes apixaban (Eliquis) to prevent stroke; you did not stop the medication prior to extraction, having consulted with his GP beforehand. He had a previous extraction 3 years ago, before he was started on Eliquis.

title: index
text: He smokes 25 cigarettes a day. Task: give him post-extraction instructions and explain the possible complications that may happen. text: This is combination syndrome — also called Kelly's syndrome — where lower anterior teeth biting directly against an upper complete denture concentrate force anteriorly, driving flabby-ridge formation and progressive supra-eruption/mobility of the lower teeth. Osteoporosis compounds bone loss but isn't the primary driver; the biomechanical imbalance, worsened by ten years without a denture remake, is. MRONJ risk is biological, not jurisdictional — having extractions done overseas doesn't remove the risk, and elective treatment abroad also means compromised continuity of care, no local access to records for follow-up, and no insurance or indemnity cover if something goes wrong. A patient who has already refused a recommendation once needs a genuinely new angle — a concrete replacement plan or the time-sensitive clearance reasoning — not the same advice delivered more firmly. text: There are really two separate reasons. First, on examination, your four remaining teeth have quite severe mobility and the gum around them has pulled back significantly — the bone supporting them has been lost to the point where they're not salvageable, regardless of anything else going on. Second, because your GP has referred you for clearance before starting your osteoporosis medication, there's a time-sensitive safety issue: I can't give clearance while these teeth are still there untreated, because if we needed to remove them after you'd started the medication, that carries a real risk of a condition called MRONJ, where the jawbone doesn't heal properly. The safe time to deal with this is now, before you start — not something we can simply monitor and revisit later." Document: 32/31/41/42 grade III mobile, generalised recession, radiographically hopeless if imaging available. STAGE 3: The Mechanism "There's also a connection between your loose upper denture and what's happening with these four teeth. They're biting directly against your upper denture instead of against back teeth, which puts a lot of concentrated force right at the front of your jaw. Over time — especially with your denture being about ten years old — that's worn away the bone at the front of your upper ridge, made the gum there soft and loose, and let the front of the denture tilt, which has pushed these four teeth further out and loosened them. This is called combination syndrome, sometimes also called Kelly's syndrome." If she asks what happens if she keeps the teeth: explain the dentures will keep failing to fit and surgery may eventually be needed to correct the bone. STAGE 4: A Concrete Alternative and Her Fear "I don't want to just tell you what has to go without telling you what we'd replace it with. Once those four teeth come out, I'd really recommend an implant-retained option — either an implant-supported bridge or an implant-retained overdenture — which gives much better support and specifically stops this from happening again.
